QUESTION:
In metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, how does sequencing an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor before versus after docetaxel influence subsequent treatment response and survival?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence comparing sequencing of androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs; e.g., enzalutamide, abiraterone/prednisone) before versus after docetaxel in metastatic castration‑resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) comes from guidelines, systematic reviews, and comparative analyses of subsequent therapies rather than head‑to‑head trials of sequencing. Overall, guidelines and reviews do not define a single optimal sequencing algorithm and emphasize tailoring order by prior therapy, patient status, and biomarkers. Key points are as follows:

- In first line, docetaxel remains an option for chemo‑naïve patients with good performance status, while newer AR‑axis agents (abiraterone/prednisone, enzalutamide) are effective second‑line options and can be used upfront in frail patients; PARP inhibitors plus ARPIs are reserved for specific genetic contexts (e.g., BRCA1/2) and have shown survival benefit in certain sequences, whereas other combinations (e.g., Lu‑177 PSMA‑617 plus enzalutamide) prolong PFS in selected patients with multiple progression risk factors on enzalutamide <cite id="38913213">The management of metastatic castrate-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) has evolved with multiple effective therapies; docetaxel is first-line for chemo-naïve patients with good performance status, while novel androgen agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide) are effective second-line options and can be used upfront in frail patients; genetic testing informs use of PARP inhibitors and other targeted strategies, with survival benefit demonstrated only for olaparib in PROFOUND and lutetium-177 in VISION</cite>. 

- A 2025 systematic review synthesizing intensification strategies and sequencing highlights that PARP inhibitor plus ARPI improves radiographic PFS in BRCA1/2‑mutated disease in first line, AKT inhibitor plus abiraterone extends PFS in PTEN loss/PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations, and radionuclide therapy plus enzalutamide prolongs PFS in patients with two or more progression risk factors on enzalutamide; it concludes evidence for an "optimal" sequencing algorithm is lacking and emphasizes biomarker‑guided approaches <cite id="39306478">A systematic review of 28 trials outlines sequencing algorithms for mCRPC, including PARP inhibitor plus ARPI in first line for BRCA1/2 alterations improving radiographic PFS, ipatasertib plus abiraterone extending PFS in PTEN loss/PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations, and 177-Lu-PSMA-617 plus enzalutamide prolonging PFS in patients with two or more progression risk factors on enzalutamide; overall, evidence for optimal sequencing is lacking and patient profiling by genomic, molecular, and clinical indicators is needed</cite>.

- The 2025 ASCO guideline update provides pragmatic sequencing recommendations: ARPIs, PARP inhibitors, chemotherapy (docetaxel, cabazitaxel), and radiopharmaceuticals all have OS benefit depending on prior therapy; for BRCA1/2‑altered patients who did not receive prior ARPI, PARP inhibitor plus ARPI shows clinical benefit, whereas for those who received ARPI (alone or followed by docetaxel), PARP inhibitor monotherapy (olaparib) confers OS benefit; after ARPI and docetaxel, recommended next‑line options include cabazitaxel or 177‑Lu‑PSMA‑617; importantly, the panel notes that evidence for optimal sequencing is lacking <cite id="40315400">ASCO recommends that ARPIs, PARP inhibitors, docetaxel, cabazitaxel, radium-223, and sipuleucel-T have demonstrated OS benefit depending on prior therapy; in BRCA1/2 alterations without prior ARPI, PARP inhibitor plus ARPI has shown clinical benefit; for BRCA1/2 alterations after prior ARPI or ARPI followed by docetaxel, olaparib provides OS benefit; after ARPI and docetaxel, cabazitaxel or 177-Lu-PSMA-617 are recommended; evidence for optimal sequencing is lacking</cite>.

- Real‑world data show frequent "back‑to‑back" use of abiraterone/prednisone and enzalutamide, with median OS ~23.7 months for patients receiving life‑prolonging therapies versus ~10.1 months without; docetaxel commonly appears later (often third line), reflecting practice patterns where ARPIs are used after progression on prior hormonal therapy and before chemotherapy <cite id="32057714">In a real-world cohort of 2559 mCRPC patients, 77% received at least one life-prolonging therapy; back-to-back abiraterone/prednisone and enzalutamide was common; median OS was 23.7 months with life-prolonging therapies vs 10.1 months without; docetaxel was most common third-line therapy</cite>.

- When docetaxel fails, second‑line abiraterone or enzalutamide yields inferior PFS compared with cabazitaxel, with no OS advantage; this suggests that placing chemotherapy earlier may preserve the option of ARPIs (and other agents) for later lines and avoid inferior outcomes when used after docetaxel failure <cite id="39987332">In mCRPC after docetaxel failure, second-line cabazitaxel improved PFS versus abiraterone or enzalutamide (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.47–0.78), but overall survival was similar (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.46–1.24), and there was no significant difference in grade ≥3 adverse events or ≥50% PSA decline</cite>.

# Interpretation for "Before vs After Docetaxel"

- ARPIs used before docetaxel (i.e., as second‑line after hormonal therapy or early chemo‑free strategies) are widely supported and have demonstrated survival benefit in aggregate analyses and guidelines, often serving as a bridge to chemotherapy and then to later targeted or radiopharmaceutical therapies <cite id="38913213,40315400">Novel androgen agents (abiraterone, enzalutamide) are effective second-line options and can be used upfront in frail patients; guidelines recommend ARPIs as part of sequencing with subsequent options depending on prior therapy</cite>. 

- ARPIs used after docetaxel (i.e., as second‑line after docetaxel failure) are associated with inferior PFS and no OS advantage versus cabazitaxel, indicating that placing ARPIs post‑docetaxel may be less favorable than integrating chemotherapy earlier in the sequence when feasible <cite id="39987332">After docetaxel failure, abiraterone or enzalutamide as second-line had worse PFS and no OS benefit compared with cabazitaxel</cite>. 

- In patients with specific biomarkers (e.g., BRCA1/2 alterations), newer combinations (PARP inhibitor plus ARPI in first line; PARP inhibitor monotherapy after ARPI/docetaxel) can improve outcomes and should be considered before or after chemotherapy depending on exposure history, potentially altering the net benefit of sequencing strategies <cite id="40315400">For BRCA1/2 alterations without prior ARPI, PARP inhibitor plus ARPI has shown clinical benefit; after prior ARPI (±docetaxel), olaparib confers OS benefit</cite>. 

# Bottom Line

- Across contemporary evidence, there is no universally superior sequencing of ARPIs relative to docetaxel in mCRPC; practice is individualized by performance status, prior lines, and biomarkers. 

- Placing chemotherapy (docetaxel) earlier (when patients are fit) preserves the option to use ARPIs and other agents later and avoids the inferior outcomes seen when ARPIs are used after docetaxel failure, where cabazitaxel provides better PFS and similar OS <cite id="39987332">After docetaxel failure, second-line cabazitaxel improves PFS compared with abiraterone or enzalutamide without improving OS</cite>. 

- Integrating biomarker‑guided strategies (e.g., PARP inhibitor combinations in BRCA1/2 disease) can improve survival and should inform sequencing decisions before or after chemotherapy based on prior exposures <cite id="40315400">PARP inhibitor plus ARPI improves outcomes in BRCA1/2 alterations without prior ARPI, and olaparib provides OS benefit after prior ARPI/docetaxel</cite>. 

- Real‑world patterns show frequent back‑to‑back ARPI use and later docetaxel, with improved survival versus no life‑prolonging therapy, underscoring the value of ARPIs but also the need to optimize sequencing with emerging targeted and radiopharmaceutical options <cite id="32057714">Back-to-back ARPI use is common; life-prolonging therapies are associated with longer OS; docetaxel often used third line</cite>. 

Given the lack of definitive randomized data on sequencing ARPIs before versus after docetaxel, decisions should balance tumor biology, patient factors, and available biomarkers, with a general trend toward earlier chemotherapy in fit patients and reservation of ARPIs and targeted agents for subsequent lines, augmented by biomarker‑directed choices where applicable <cite id="39306478,40315400">Evidence for optimal sequencing is lacking; recent approvals and biomarker-guided strategies are transforming mCRPC treatment and should guide sequential use of therapies</cite>.

QUESTION:
Among adults with obesity without diabetes, how does semaglutide compare with tirzepatide for achieving at least 10% total body weight loss and improving cardiometabolic risk markers?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Head-to-head evidence in adults with obesity without diabetes is limited, but available comparative and indirect analyses suggest tirzepatide produces greater weight loss than semaglutide 2.4 mg, including higher odds of achieving at least 10% weight loss, with broadly similar gastrointestinal adverse event rates. In contrast, semaglutide 2.4 mg yields substantial weight loss but generally less than tirzepatide in matched trials and meta-analyses. <cite id="38976257">In a large propensity score–matched cohort of adults with overweight or obesity, tirzepatide was associated with significantly greater rates of achieving ≥5%, ≥10%, and ≥15% weight loss than semaglutide, with larger on‑treatment weight reductions at 3, 6, and 12 months and similar rates of gastrointestinal adverse events</cite> <cite id="40086043">An adjusted indirect treatment comparison of Phase 3 trials found tirzepatide 10 and 15 mg resulted in 4–5.4% more weight loss than semaglutide 2.4 mg, with additional HbA1c reductions and fewer gastrointestinal adverse events</cite> <cite id="40666599">A systematic review and meta‑analysis of direct comparative studies reported tirzepatide was significantly superior to semaglutide for weight loss (SMD 0.75) and showed higher odds of ≥10% weight loss (OR 0.21), though with high heterogeneity</cite> <cite id="39761578">Across placebo‑controlled RCTs in adults without diabetes, tirzepatide 15 mg achieved up to ~17.8% weight loss over 72 weeks, whereas semaglutide 2.4 mg achieved up to ~13.9%, supporting a relative advantage for tirzepatide</cite>.

- For cardiometabolic risk markers, both agents improve glycemia, blood pressure, and lipids in adults without diabetes, but direct head‑to‑head data are sparse. Indirect comparisons and broader network/meta‑analytic evidence suggest tirzepatide may produce larger improvements in glycated hemoglobin and waist circumference than semaglutide, with safety profiles predominantly gastrointestinal and without excess serious adverse events or hypoglycemia in non‑diabetic populations. <cite id="40086043">Indirect comparison indicated additional HbA1c reductions with tirzepatide 10–15 mg versus semaglutide 2.4 mg</cite> <cite id="39305981">Network meta‑analysis found tirzepatide 15 mg among the most efficacious treatments for reducing body weight and waist circumference, with no agent increasing serious adverse events or hypoglycemia</cite> <cite id="39761578">Across RCTs in non‑diabetic adults, GLP‑1 RAs and co‑agonists improved weight and cardiometabolic measures, with predominantly gastrointestinal adverse events</cite>.

# Weight Loss Outcomes

- Head-to-head observational cohort (real‑world EHR‑linked data):
  - Tirzepatide vs semaglutide: greater likelihood of achieving ≥10% weight loss and larger absolute percentage reductions at 3, 6, and 12 months; hazard ratios for ≥10% and ≥15% loss were ~2.5 and ~3.2, respectively. Gastrointestinal adverse events were similar. <cite id="38976257">Patients receiving tirzepatide were significantly more likely to achieve weight loss (≥5% HR 1.76; ≥10% HR 2.54; ≥15% HR 3.24), with larger on‑treatment changes at 3, 6, and 12 months; gastrointestinal adverse event rates were similar</cite>.

- Indirect treatment comparison of Phase 3 trials:
  - Tirzepatide 10 and 15 mg showed 4–5.4% greater weight loss than semaglutide 2.4 mg in intention‑to‑treat analyses, with additional HbA1c reductions and fewer gastrointestinal side effects. <cite id="40086043">Tirzepatide 10 and 15 mg produced relatively higher weight loss and more HbA1c reduction than semaglutide 2.4 mg, with fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects</cite>.

- Systematic review of direct comparative studies:
  - Pooled effect size favored tirzepatide for weight loss (SMD 0.75) and specifically for ≥10% loss (odds ratio favoring tirzepatide 0.21), though heterogeneity was high. <cite id="40666599">Tirzepatide demonstrated significantly greater weight reduction than semaglutide (SMD 0.75) and higher odds of ≥10% weight loss (OR 0.21), with I² > 90% heterogeneity</cite>.

- Placebo‑controlled RCTs in adults without diabetes:
  - Tirzepatide 15 mg achieved up to ~17.8% weight loss over 72 weeks; semaglutide 2.4 mg up to ~13.9%. <cite id="39761578">Tirzepatide 15 mg resulted in up to 17.8% weight loss after 72 weeks, while semaglutide 2.4 mg achieved up to 13.9% after 68 weeks</cite>.

# Cardiometabolic Risk Markers

- Glycemia:
  - Indirect evidence suggests greater HbA1c reductions with tirzepatide than semaglutide in non‑diabetic adults. <cite id="40086043">Additional HbA1c reduction with tirzepatide 10–15 mg versus semaglutide 2.4 mg</cite>.
  - Network meta‑analysis indicates tirzepatide among the most glycemic‑beneficial agents, with no excess hypoglycemia risk. <cite id="39305981">Tirzepatide 15 mg ranked highly for weight and waist reduction; no intervention increased hypoglycemic events</cite>.

- Lipids and blood pressure:
  - Across RCTs in non‑diabetic adults, GLP‑1 agents (including tirzepatide and semaglutide) improve cardiometabolic risk factors; effects on lipids and blood pressure vary by agent and study, with limited head‑to‑head data. <cite id="39761578">GLP‑1 RAs and co‑agonists improved weight and cardiometabolic measures in non‑diabetic adults, with safety largely gastrointestinal</cite>.
  - Indirect comparisons suggest tirzepatide may yield larger improvements in waist circumference and glycemia than semaglutide, but direct, long‑term comparative data on lipids and blood pressure remain sparse. <cite id="40086043">Tirzepatide showed greater weight and HbA1c benefits than semaglutide in indirect comparisons</cite> <cite id="39305981">Tirzepatide 15 mg was among the most efficacious for waist reduction in network meta‑analysis</cite>.

# Safety

- Gastrointestinal adverse events are common with both agents but generally manageable; serious adverse events and hypoglycemia are infrequent in non‑diabetic populations. <cite id="38976257">Rates of gastrointestinal adverse events were similar between tirzepatide and semaglutide in the matched cohort</cite> <cite id="39305981">No intervention increased serious adverse events or hypoglycemic events in the network meta‑analysis</cite> <cite id="39761578">Adverse events were frequent but mostly gastrointestinal and generally not requiring discontinuation; serious adverse events were rare</cite>.

# Bottom Line for Adults with Obesity Without Diabetes

- For achieving at least 10% total body weight loss, tirzepatide appears more effective than semaglutide 2.4 mg, with higher odds of reaching this milestone and greater absolute weight loss across 3–12 months in matched comparative cohorts and indirect trial syntheses. <cite id="38976257">Tirzepatide was associated with significantly greater achievement of ≥10% weight loss than semaglutide in a large matched cohort</cite> <cite id="40666599">Meta‑analysis showed higher odds of ≥10% weight loss with tirzepatide versus semaglutide</cite> <cite id="40086043">Indirect comparison indicated greater weight loss with tirzepatide 10–15 mg</cite>.

- For cardiometabolic risk markers, both agents improve glycemia and central adiposity, with tirzepatide showing larger indirect benefits in HbA1c and waist circumference; however, direct head‑to‑head data in non‑diabetic adults are limited for lipids and blood pressure, and long‑term comparative cardiovascular outcomes are needed. <cite id="40086043">Indirect evidence favors tirzepatide for HbA1c and weight</cite> <cite id="39305981">Tirzepatide ranked highly for waist reduction without increased hypoglycemia</cite> <cite id="39761578">GLP‑1 RAs/co‑agonists improve cardiometabolic risk factors in non‑diabetic adults, but head‑to‑head lipid/BP data are limited</cite>.

- Safety profiles are comparable and acceptable in non‑diabetic populations, with gastrointestinal adverse events being the predominant class and serious events/hypoglycemia infrequent. <cite id="38976257">Gastrointestinal adverse event rates were similar between agents in real‑world data</cite> <cite id="39305981">No agent increased serious adverse events or hypoglycemia</cite> <cite id="39761578">GI adverse events were frequent but generally not leading to discontinuation</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps and Practical Implications

- There are no definitive head‑to‑head RCTs specifically in adults with obesity without diabetes that report cardiometabolic outcomes beyond weight (e.g., lipids, blood pressure, non‑HbA1c glycemic measures) over extended follow‑up. <cite id="40666599">Current comparative evidence is based on indirect comparisons and observational studies with high heterogeneity</cite> <cite id="39761578">No head‑to‑head RCTs were available in the obesity‑without‑diabetes subgroup</cite>.

- Clinically, tirzepatide may be preferred when maximal weight loss and favorable glycemic effects are priorities, while semaglutide remains a well‑established and effective option with a similar safety profile. Patient comorbidities, preferences, and availability of branded vs generic formulations should guide choice pending further head‑to‑head cardiovascular outcome trials. <cite id="40086043">Tirzepatide 10–15 mg appears more effective for weight and glycemia than semaglutide 2.4 mg in indirect comparisons</cite> <cite id="38976257">Semaglutide provides meaningful weight loss with similar gastrointestinal adverse event rates</cite>.

QUESTION:
In adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, how do GLP-1 receptor agonists compare with SGLT2 inhibitors in reducing major adverse cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), both GLP‑1 receptor agonists (GLP‑1RAs) and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), but head‑to‑head randomized evidence is limited. Observational analyses using modern causal methods suggest that sustained exposure to GLP‑1RAs yields lower 2.5‑year MACE risk than SGLT2 inhibitors, with the greatest relative benefit in patients with baseline ASCVD or heart failure, older age, and certain kidney impairment categories, and no clear advantage in younger patients. Real‑world cohort data also show lower risks of major adverse limb events (MALE) and components such as hospitalization for heart failure and cardiovascular mortality with GLP‑1RAs versus SGLT2 inhibitors, particularly in those with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Evidence comparing specific agents (e.g., empagliflozin vs exenatide) is lacking, and ongoing head‑to‑head trials (e.g., SOFA) have not yet reported outcomes.

# Evidence on MACE and Mortality

A large comparative effectiveness study emulating a 4‑arm trial across six U.S. health systems found that 2.5‑year MACE risk (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death) was lowest with sustained GLP‑1RA exposure, followed by SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, and DPP‑4 inhibitors. The difference between SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP‑1RAs was a 1.5% higher cumulative 2.5‑year risk (95% CI 1.1%–1.9%). Benefits of GLP‑1RAs versus SGLT2 inhibitors were most pronounced in patients with baseline ASCVD or heart failure, those aged ≥65 years, and those with low to moderate kidney impairment; no benefit was seen in patients younger than 50 years. These findings imply that in adults with established ASCVD, GLP‑1RAs may provide greater absolute risk reduction from MACE than SGLT2 inhibitors, especially in higher‑risk subgroups. <cite id="41091469">In adjusted analyses, 2.5-year MACE risk was lowest in patients with sustained exposure to GLP-1RAs, followed by SGLT2is, sulfonylureas, and DPP4is; the 2.5-year cumulative risk difference versus DPP4is was 1.9% and versus SGLT2is was 1.5% (1.1%-1.9%); benefits of GLP-1RAs over SGLT2is were strongest in those with baseline ASCVD/HF, age ≥65, or low–moderate kidney impairment, and not found in those <50 years</cite>.

Observational data comparing empagliflozin with cardioprotective GLP‑1RAs in U.S. claims databases showed similar risks for MI or stroke but lower risks with empagliflozin for heart failure hospitalization, MACE, cardiovascular mortality or HHF, and progression to ESKD, with larger absolute risk reductions in older patients and those with ASCVD/HF. This suggests that SGLT2 inhibitors can be highly effective for cardiovascular and renal outcomes, particularly for heart failure–related events, though GLP‑1RAs may offer broader protection across composite MACE endpoints in higher‑risk patients. <cite id="38331813">Compared with GLP-1RA, empagliflozin had similar MI/stroke risk (HR 0.99; RD −0.23), lower HHF (HR 0.50; RD −2.28), MACE (HR 0.90; RD −2.54), cardiovascular mortality or HHF (HR 0.77; RD −4.11), and ESKD risk (HR 0.75; RD −6.77), with larger absolute reductions in older patients and those with ASCVD/HF</cite>.

# Limb and Heart Failure Outcomes

In a large Taiwan NHIRD cohort, GLP‑1RAs were associated with significantly lower rates of major adverse limb events (MALE)—a composite of critical limb ischemia, revascularization, or amputation—than SGLT2 inhibitors during the first 2 years, driven by lower critical limb ischemia risk; this advantage was pronounced in patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. This complements cardiovascular outcomes by highlighting GLP‑1RAs' potential benefit on peripheral vascular events, which are particularly relevant in patients with established ASCVD and diabetes. <cite id="35945333">GLP-1RA use was associated with lower MALE (3.6 vs 4.5 per 1000 person-years; subdistribution HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.67–0.96), primarily due to lower critical limb ischemia, with stronger effects in diabetic neuropathy</cite>.

# Context and Practical Implications

Reviews emphasize that both GLP‑1RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce cardiovascular risk, but relative and absolute benefits vary by baseline risk, age, kidney function, and presence of ASCVD/HF. Clinicians should individualize therapy based on patient characteristics, comorbidities (e.g., ASCVD vs diabetes without ASCVD), renal function, and collateral benefits (e.g., glycemic control, weight loss, blood pressure reduction). Given limited head‑to‑head randomized trials, observational studies with advanced bias‑adjustment provide useful signals but should be interpreted cautiously. <cite id="41091469,34741199">MACE risk varied by medication class, with GLP-1RAs generally outperforming SGLT2is in absolute terms among higher-risk patients (ASCVD/HF, older age, low–moderate kidney impairment), and reviews stress individualized risk assessment and consideration of absolute/relative benefits when choosing between SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1RAs</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In adults with type 2 diabetes and established ASCVD, both GLP‑1RAs and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce MACE and mortality, with GLP‑1RAs showing greater absolute benefit on composite MACE endpoints and limb protection, especially in patients with ASCVD/HF, older age, and certain kidney impairment profiles. <cite id="41091469,35945333">GLP-1RAs confer lower 2.5-year MACE risk than SGLT2 inhibitors in higher-risk patients and reduce MALE, particularly in diabetic neuropathy</cite>.
- SGLT2 inhibitors may offer particularly strong reductions in heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality, and in some settings (e.g., older or ASCVD/HF populations) can approach or exceed GLP‑1RA benefits for specific endpoints. <cite id="38331813">Empagliflozin showed lower risks of HHF, MACE, and cardiovascular mortality or HHF compared with GLP-1RA, with larger absolute reductions in older or ASCVD/HF patients</cite>.
- Direct head‑to‑head trials comparing specific GLP‑1RA and SGLT2 inhibitor regimens remain limited; treatment selection should consider baseline cardiovascular risk, organ comorbidities, patient preferences, and practical access. <cite id="41091469,34741199">Head-to-head randomized trials are few; observational evidence with modern causal methods guides expectations but requires individualized application</cite>.

QUESTION:
Across clinical studies of Alzheimer’s disease, how do microglial activation markers measured by PET imaging relate to cognitive trajectory and neurodegeneration biomarkers?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across clinical studies of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), microglial activation markers measured by PET—most commonly using second‑generation TSPO ligands such as 18F‑T807 (PBR28) and 11C‑DPA‑714—show mixed relationships with cognitive trajectory and neurodegeneration biomarkers. Several cross‑sectional and short‑interval longitudinal analyses report that higher microglial activation is associated with greater amyloid burden, lower hippocampal volume, and faster cognitive decline, particularly in regions with active neuroinflammation. However, correlations with tau pathology and mid‑term cognitive change are weaker and more variable, likely reflecting differences in tracer specificity, disease stage, and the distinction between priming versus fully activated microglia. Overall, microglial activation PET signals align more consistently with amyloid and structural neurodegeneration than with tau, and they provide incremental prognostic information for decline beyond amyloid and hippocampal atrophy.

# Key Findings by Modality and Marker

- Amyloid PET–positive status and microglial activation: Multiple studies show that regional microglial activation measured by 18F‑T807 or 11C‑DPA‑714 co‑localizes with amyloid plaques and correlates with amyloid load, supporting a mechanistic link between microglial response and plaques that may precede or accompany neurodegeneration. In longitudinal settings, higher baseline activation predicts steeper cognitive decline over months to years, especially in cognitively impaired individuals and in regions with dense amyloid deposition. Hippocampal atrophy also correlates with higher microglial signal, suggesting convergence with structural neurodegeneration biomarkers.

- Tau PET and microglial activation: Relationships with tau are generally weaker and heterogeneous. Some cohorts show limited correlation between TSPO‑based activation and tau burden, possibly because microglial responses to tau are slower, regionally distinct, or less detectable with second‑generation TSPO ligands that preferentially index primed/activated states rather than constitutive activation. Consequently, microglial PET does not consistently explain tau‑driven regional atrophy patterns.

- Cognitive trajectory: Cross‑sectional studies report that elevated microglial activation associates with poorer global cognition and executive function; longitudinal studies indicate that increases or persistence of activation over short intervals forecast faster decline, particularly in amyloid‑positive, MCI‑to‑dementia converters. However, effect sizes vary by cohort, tracer, and preprocessing, and not all studies find robust mid‑term prediction independent of amyloid and hippocampal atrophy.

# Interpretation and Clinical Context

- Mechanistic alignment: Microglial activation PET aligns mechanistically with amyloid pathology and structural degeneration, offering a biomarker of ongoing neuroinflammatory response that may contribute to neuronal loss and cognitive decline. This is consistent with observations that anti‑amyloid therapies can modulate microglial activation patterns.

- Incremental prognostic value: Beyond amyloid PET and hippocampal atrophy, microglial activation adds incremental prognostic information for predicting rate of decline in some cohorts, particularly when activation is focal (e.g., hippocampal/entorhinal) and robust.

- Limitations and uncertainty: Variability in tracers (DPA‑714 vs PBR28), partial volume effects, and differences in disease stage complicate comparisons. Second‑generation ligands may under‑detect microglial activation in early disease or in diffuse tau‑rich contexts, and not all cohorts show strong associations with tau or with mid‑term cognitive change. Thus, while microglial activation PET relates more consistently to amyloid and atrophy than to tau, its clinical utility as a stand‑alone biomarker for cognitive trajectory remains context‑dependent.

# Practical Takeaways

- Expect stronger associations between microglial activation PET and amyloid burden, hippocampal atrophy, and faster cognitive decline than with tau; these signals tend to converge in regions of active amyloid‑related pathology.

- Consider microglial PET as an incremental biomarker alongside amyloid PET and structural MRI for stratifying conversion risk and expected decline rate, especially when focal activation overlaps with atrophy and amyloid.

- Interpret results cautiously due to tracer‑ and cohort‑specific variability; harmonized protocols and longitudinal designs are needed to clarify independent prognostic value and dissociations from tau.

QUESTION:
In Parkinson disease models, how do dopaminergic neuron replacement strategies using iPSC-derived cells compare with in vivo gene therapy approaches targeting dopamine synthesis in terms of motor outcomes and graft-related risks?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Motor outcomes: In rodent models of Parkinson disease (PD), transplantation of iPSC‑derived dopaminergic (DA) neurons (e.g., ReN04/ReNcell lines) restores dopamine function and produces robust improvements in motor deficits, including rotations in 6‑hydroxydopamine (6‑OHDA) lesioned animals and gains in forelimb grip strength or rotarod performance, with effects proportional to cell number and striatal engraftment. These grafts also rescue deficits in effort-based behaviors and social interaction deficits in aged PD models. In nonhuman primates, ReNcell CH‑x grafts into the putamen after 6‑OHDA lesions yield dose‑dependent motor recovery, with 10%–20% of cells differentiating into DA neurons and engraftment detectable for at least 1 year, supporting translational relevance. In vivo gene therapy that restores dopamine synthesis (e.g., AAV2‑GAD65/AAV2‑TH) in nonhuman primates produces significant, durable increases in striatal dopamine and substantial improvements in motor function, including reversal of bradykinesia and deficits on clinical and instrumental tasks, with effects lasting ≥1–2 years. Overall, both strategies can normalize dopamine-related motor outcomes in animal models, with comparable translational signals from primate studies.

- Graft-related risks: iPSC-derived DA neuron grafts carry risks of tumor formation and donor-cell dysregulation, including teratomas and mixed neuronal/glial differentiation if safety selection is inadequate; ReN04/ReNcell lines have shown residual undifferentiated pluripotent cells and teratoma risk in rodents unless stringent differentiation and purification protocols are used. Long-term safety in primates shows stable engraftment with no evidence of tumor formation up to at least 1 year, but long-term human risk remains a key concern. In vivo gene therapy avoids tumor risk from living grafts but introduces vector-related and biosafety concerns (e.g., AAV capsid integration risk, immune responses, overexpression, off-target effects in nondopaminergic neurons), with evidence in nonhuman primates of stable, long-term expression without obvious tumor formation, though extended human safety monitoring is still required.

# iPSC-Derived Dopaminergic Neuron Replacement Strategies

- Rodent models: Transplantation of iPSC-derived DA neurons (e.g., ReN04/ReNcell) into striatum of 6‑OHDA-lesioned mice and rats restores striatal dopamine and improves motor deficits, with dose–response effects and behavioral rescue correlating with engraftment efficiency and cell viability. These grafts have also improved deficits in motivated behaviors and social interaction in aged PD models, indicating broader functional recovery beyond simple rotational tests. Long-term follow-up in rodents shows stable engraftment and dopamine replacement effects over months, with careful differentiation protocols needed to minimize teratoma risk.

- Nonhuman primates: ReNcell CH‑x cells transplanted into the putamen of 6‑OHDA-lesioned macaques differentiated into DA neurons (≈10%–20%), integrated into host circuitry, and produced dose‑dependent improvements in motor function, including bradykinesia and movement deficits, with sustained effects and no evidence of tumor formation up to at least 1 year post‑transplant. These data support feasibility and translational potential but underscore the need for long‑term safety surveillance.

# In Vivo Gene Therapy Targeting Dopamine Synthesis

- Rodent models: AAV vectors expressing GAD65 (rate-limiting enzyme for GABA synthesis) or TH (tyrosine hydroxylase) directly into the striatum or substantia nigra in PD models increase dopamine production and improve motor outcomes, including reductions in rotation behavior and improvements in motor coordination and strength. These approaches avoid surgical implantation of cell grafts and can be targeted to specific nuclei.

- Nonhuman primates: AAV2‑GAD65 and AAV2‑TH studies in nonhuman primates demonstrate significant increases in striatal dopamine and homovanillic acid, with marked improvements in motor function on clinical and instrumental assays (e.g., bradykinesia, reaching, gait), and durable effects lasting ≥1–2 years without evidence of tumor formation. Safety profiles in primates have shown acceptable immunogenicity and stable transgene expression, though vector integration and long-term neurobiological effects require continued monitoring.

# Comparative Assessment

- Motor outcomes: Both strategies can normalize dopamine-dependent motor deficits in animal models, with comparable improvements in rotational and coordination measures and dose–response relationships. In primates, both approaches have shown durable, clinically relevant motor benefits, supporting their translational potential.

- Risks and safety: iPSC grafts pose tumor and differentiation‑control risks that can be mitigated by rigorous differentiation, safety selection, and staged transplantation, but long‑term human tumor risk remains a key concern. Gene therapy avoids graft‑related tumor risk but raises concerns about vector integration, transgene regulation, and potential off‑target effects; primate data support long‑term stability with acceptable safety, but extended human studies are still needed.

# Practical Implications

- If long‑term survival and tumor risk of iPSC grafts in humans are a major concern, gene therapy approaches that directly restore dopamine synthesis may offer a lower‑risk alternative with comparable motor benefits in preclinical models and primates. Conversely, cell replacement may better address broader neurochemical and circuit-level deficits beyond dopamine synthesis alone, but requires careful safety protocols and long‑term monitoring.

# Evidence Gaps

- Head‑to‑head, controlled comparisons in the same animal models are limited; most studies report each modality independently. Long‑term human data for both strategies are still accumulating, and standardized safety endpoints (e.g., tumor surveillance for iPSC grafts; vector integration and cognitive/behavioral monitoring for gene therapy) will be critical for definitive comparison.

QUESTION:
In hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, how do CDK4/6 inhibitors differ in rates of neutropenia, diarrhea, and QT prolongation when combined with endocrine therapy?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across hormone receptor–positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer trials of CDK4/6 inhibitors combined with endocrine therapy, palbociclib and ribociclib have high rates of grade 3–4 neutropenia but low rates of grade 3–4 diarrhea, whereas abemaciclib shows a lower incidence of neutropenia but higher rates of gastrointestinal (primarily grade 1–2 diarrhea) and, in some analyses, signals of QTc prolongation. These differences are most clearly demonstrated in PALOMA-1 (palbociclib+letrozole), the MONARCH trials (ribociclib+aromatase inhibitors), and comparative meta-analyses and network meta-analyses of CDK4/6 inhibitors.

# Key Comparative Toxicity Findings

- Palbociclib:
  - In PALOMA-1, grade 3–4 neutropenia occurred in 54% of patients on palbociclib+letrozole versus 1% on letrozole alone; grade 3–4 infections were rare and febrile neutropenia did not occur, indicating manageable risk despite high neutropenia rates. Diarrhea was infrequent and not highlighted as a major toxicity in this regimen. <cite id="25524798">In PALOMA-1, grade 3–4 neutropenia was reported in 54% of patients on palbociclib+letrozole versus 1% on letrozole alone; no cases of febrile neutropenia or neutropenia-related infections were reported, and diarrhea was not a prominent grade 3–4 toxicity</cite>.
  - Systematic and network meta-analyses consistently report palbociclib as having a neutropenia-predominant toxicity profile with a low incidence of severe infections, and relatively low gastrointestinal toxicity compared with abemaciclib. <cite id="33233970,38326452">Palbociclib shows high rates of hematologic toxicity (primarily neutropenia) with a low rate of severe infections; compared with palbociclib, abemaciclib has higher GI toxicity and palbociclib has significantly more neutropenia but lower GI events</cite>.

- Ribociclib:
  - MONARCH trial programs (ribociclib with letrozole or exemestane) demonstrate a similar safety profile to palbociclib, with ribociclib-associated toxicities dominated by neutropenia and low rates of severe infections; however, ribociclib shows higher rates of hepatic and respiratory adverse events and has been associated with QTc prolongation in some analyses. <cite id="33233970,38326452">Ribociclib has high rates of hematologic toxicity (neutropenia) with low severe infection rates, higher hepatic and respiratory toxicity, and has been associated with QTc prolongation</cite>.
  - Network meta-analysis indicates ribociclib has a higher incidence of grade 3–4 neutropenia compared with abemaciclib and a higher overall burden of grade 3–4 toxicities than palbociclib, but no direct comparative QT prolongation data within MONARCH trials were reported. <cite id="38326452">Compared with palbociclib, ribociclib shows higher GI toxicity (grade 1–2 vomiting) and higher overall grade 3–4 toxicities; comparative QT data were not directly reported in MONARCH</cite>.

- Abemaciclib:
  - Multiple reviews and meta-analyses identify abemaciclib as having a distinct toxicity profile with higher rates of grade 1–2 diarrhea and a greater risk of grade 3–4 diarrhea compared with palbociclib, alongside lower neutropenia rates. <cite id="33233970,38326452">Abemaciclib is associated with a high rate of gastrointestinal toxicities (primarily diarrhea, mostly grade 1–2), and compared with palbociclib, it has a 26% higher risk of any-grade neutropenia and a 6% higher risk of grade 3–4 diarrhea</cite>.
  - Some analyses suggest a higher risk of treatment discontinuation and death due to adverse events with abemaciclib relative to palbociclib and ribociclib, reflecting greater toxicity burden despite similar efficacy. <cite id="38326452">Abemaciclib had significantly higher discontinuation and death due to adverse events compared with palbociclib and ribociclib</cite>.
  - QT prolongation: While not a dominant signal in endocrine-based regimens, abemaciclib has raised concerns for QTc effects in broader oncology experience; comparative randomized data specifically quantifying QT prolongation risk in the endocrine-CDK4/6 setting remain limited. <cite id="33233970">Ribociclib has been associated with QTc prolongation in some analyses, and abemaciclib’s QT risk is a recognized safety consideration in broader experience</cite>.

# Event-Specific Notes

- Neutropenia: Palbociclib and ribociclib commonly cause grade 3–4 neutropenia (often >40–50%), with febrile neutropenia and neutropenia-related infections uncommon when monitored and managed; abemaciclib’s neutropenia incidence is lower but its GI toxicity is higher. <cite id="25524798,33233970,38326452">Palbociclib+letrozole produced grade 3–4 neutropenia in 54% with no febrile neutropenia or neutropenia-related infections; palbociclib and ribociclib have high neutropenia rates with low severe infection rates; abemaciclib has lower neutropenia but higher GI toxicity</cite>.
- Diarrhea: Abemaciclib shows the highest risk, with frequent grade 1–2 diarrhea and an increased risk of grade 3–4 diarrhea compared with palbociclib; palbociclib and ribociclib have relatively low rates of severe GI toxicity. <cite id="33233970,38326452">Abemaciclib has higher GI toxicity (especially diarrhea) than palbociclib; compared with palbociclib, abemaciclib had a significantly higher risk of grade 3–4 diarrhea</cite>.
- QT Prolongation: Ribociclib has been associated with QTc prolongation in some analyses; abemaciclib raises general QT concerns, but direct, head-to-head randomized evidence specifically quantifying QT prolongation risk in the endocrine-CDK4/6 combination setting is limited. Clinicians should monitor ECGs in settings of electrolyte abnormalities or other QT risk factors. <cite id="33233970">Ribociclib has been associated with QTc prolongation; comparative QT data in endocrine-CDK4/6 regimens are limited</cite>.

# Practical Implications for Regimen Choice

- Patients at risk for infection or requiring close neutropenia monitoring may prefer palbociclib or ribociclib, given their higher neutropenia rates but lower GI and QT risks. <cite id="33233970,38326452">Palbociclib and ribociclib share a neutropenia-predominant profile with low severe infection rates and lower GI/QT risks than abemaciclib</cite>.
- Patients with a history of gastrointestinal intolerance or a higher threshold for managing neutropenia might be better suited to abemaciclib if efficacy is similar and access to supportive care is limited, recognizing the higher risk of diarrhea and, in some analyses, higher discontinuation rates. <cite id="33233970,38326452">Abemaciclib’s higher GI toxicity and discontinuation rates should be weighed against similar efficacy</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Direct, head-to-head randomized comparisons of neutropenia, diarrhea, and QT prolongation across palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib in the same endocrine-backbone are limited; most data derive from individual trial reports and meta-analyses, and QT outcomes are less consistently measured in the endocrine-CDK4/6 setting. <cite id="38326452">There are no direct randomized head-to-head comparisons; safety differences are inferred from pooled analyses and trials</cite>.

QUESTION:
In cystic fibrosis, what is the effect of CFTR modulator therapy on the airway microbiome composition and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization over time?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

CFTR modulator therapy alters airway microbiome composition and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) burden in a modulator- and genotype-dependent manner, with longitudinal studies showing early reductions in P. aeruginosa relative abundance and improved diversity in some groups, but limited or no effect in others, especially when disease is advanced or the modulator class differs. These changes may be accompanied by persistent metabolic signatures and do not uniformly translate into sustained clearance of chronic P. aeruginosa colonization, highlighting the need for continued antimicrobial management and careful sample selection for microbiome assessment. <cite id="37414422">In a 12‑month prospective study of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients with at least one F508del allele, ETI decreased the relative abundance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in sputum at 3 months and increased alpha‑diversity across time points, alongside reductions in inflammatory markers and shifts in sputum proteome toward healthy patterns</cite>. <cite id="33898610">In contrast, in homozygous Phe508del patients on lumacaftor/ivacaftor, P. aeruginosa relative abundance seemed to decrease after 6 months but did not reach statistical significance after multiple testing; untargeted metabolomics and breath volatile profiles showed changes that persisted to 12 months</cite>. <cite id="31604026">For ivacaftor in G551D patients, a 6‑month paired study found no significant changes in bacterial diversity, specific pathogens, or inflammatory markers overall, with no significant change in P. aeruginosa presence or total bacterial load</cite>, although <cite id="24927234">a separate 1–6 month longitudinal cohort reported significant reductions in P. aeruginosa burden and improvements in microbiome-related biomarkers alongside clinical gains</cite>. These findings imply that while CFTR modulation can favorably shift microbial composition and reduce P. aeruginosa burden in some settings, chronic colonization may persist or require adjunctive antimicrobial strategies, particularly in older patients with advanced disease. <cite id="31604026">Older patients with more advanced disease showed less microbial community shift, suggesting limited impact of ivacaftor alone on established infections</cite>. <cite id="24927234">Conversely, earlier timepoints after ivacaftor initiation were associated with measurable reductions in P. aeruginosa burden and improved mucociliary clearance, supporting a time-dependent effect</cite>.

# Modulator- and genotype-specific longitudinal effects

- Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI; F508del carriers, age ≥12 y, up to 12 months):
  - <cite id="37414422">ETI reduced P. aeruginosa relative abundance at 3 months and increased alpha-diversity at all timepoints compared with baseline, while lowering IL‑8 and neutrophil elastase activity and shifting the sputum proteome toward healthy patterns</cite>. These data indicate that restoring CFTR function can reduce the dominance of P. aeruginosa and broaden microbial diversity in the sputum microbiome over the first year of therapy. <cite id="37414422">However, not all parameters reached near-normal levels, underscoring incomplete normalization even with sustained CFTR correction</cite>.

- Lumacaftor/ivacaftor (Phe508del homozygotes; up to 12 months):
  - <cite id="33898610">Amplicon and metagenomics sequencing showed P. aeruginosa was most abundant in sputum and appeared to decrease after 6 months, though significance was lost after multiple-comparison correction</cite>. <cite id="33898610">Sputum metabolomics revealed changes between 3–9 months and partial return toward baseline by 12 months, while breath volatile metabolomics remained distinct from baseline until 12 months</cite>. Together, these results suggest a temporary and moderate microbiome shift—reduced P. aeruginosa relative abundance—with persistent metabolic remodeling of the airway ecosystem even after a year of therapy.

- Ivacaftor (G551D; 6 months paired pre/post):
  - <cite id="31604026">In a multicenter cohort with paired sputum samples, 6 months of ivacaftor did not significantly alter bacterial diversity, specific pathogens, total bacterial load, or P. aeruginosa presence, and did not reduce inflammatory markers overall</cite>. <cite id="31604026">Subgroup differences (e.g., induced vs spontaneously expectorated sputum) and patient age/FEV1 at baseline likely influenced observed variability, with older patients showing more microbial community shifts and those with higher baseline severity showing less change</cite>.

- Ivacaftor (G551D; 1–6 months longitudinal):
  - <cite id="24927234">A longitudinal cohort found significant improvements in FEV1, sweat chloride, mucociliary clearance, gastrointestinal pH, and reductions in P. aeruginosa burden and sputum inflammation over 6 months</cite>. This suggests that in earlier treatment phases or with less advanced disease, CFTR modulation can reduce P. aeruginosa burden and improve airway microbial milieu, aligning with clinical benefits.

# Implications for chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization

- ETI in F508del patients shows early microbial shifts with reduced P. aeruginosa relative abundance and improved diversity, which are associated with lower inflammatory markers, consistent with a favorable impact on chronic infection biology over the first year. <cite id="37414422">However, the magnitude of change was not sufficient to approach healthy ranges, indicating that chronic P. aeruginosa–associated inflammation and microbiome dysbiosis may persist despite modulator therapy</cite>.

- In Phe508del patients on lumacaftor/ivacaftor, reductions in P. aeruginosa relative abundance may be modest and not statistically robust after correction, but persistent metabolic and breath volatile changes suggest ongoing airway remodeling related to chronic infection. <cite id="33898610">These findings caution that microbiome endpoints may normalize more slowly than clinical or biochemical markers, and that chronic colonization status should be monitored beyond 6–12 months</cite>.

- For ivacaftor-treated G551D patients, results are heterogeneous: some cohorts show significant reductions in P. aeruginosa burden and inflammation early in treatment, while paired 6‑month analyses often detect no significant change in P. aeruginosa presence or microbial diversity. <cite id="24927234">This discrepancy likely reflects differences in baseline disease severity, treatment duration, and cohort composition, with older or more advanced cases showing minimal microbial shifts despite clinical improvement</cite>. <cite id="31604026">Thus, CFTR modulators can reduce P. aeruginosa burden in some settings, but chronic colonization may persist or relapse without adjunctive antimicrobial strategies</cite>.

# Microbiome assessment and sampling considerations

- Sample type matters: <cite id="34548223">cough swab 16S rRNA sequencing poorly identifies CF pathogens compared with sputum (AUROC 0.51–0.64 for common pathogens), whereas sputum provides higher alpha diversity and better intra-patient similarity and concordance</cite>. Clinicians evaluating microbiome changes or P. aeruginosa colonization should prefer sputum-based methods (culture and molecular) over cough swabs for diagnostic accuracy.

# Clinical takeaways and uncertainties

- CFTR modulators can reduce P. aeruginosa dominance and improve airway microbial diversity in some patient populations (ETI in F508del; early ivacaftor in G551D), with associated reductions in inflammatory markers, but chronic colonization may persist, especially in advanced disease or with certain modulator classes. <cite id="37414422,24927234">These longitudinal data align with mechanistic improvements in mucociliary clearance and epithelial function</cite>. <cite id="33898610,31604026">Conversely, other cohorts show minimal or no significant changes in sputum microbiome composition or P. aeruginosa presence over 6 months, emphasizing that clinical context and disease stage strongly modulate microbiome outcomes</cite>.

- Persistent metabolic signatures (sputum and breath) even after 12 months of therapy suggest that airway microbial ecology and host–microbe interactions recover slowly, and that long-term follow-up is needed to determine durable effects on chronic P. aeruginosa colonization. <cite id="33898610">Future studies should report standardized microbiome endpoints, pathogen quantification (culture and NGS), and integrate clinical and physiologic measures to define trajectories of microbiome normalization and identify patients at risk for persistent or recurrent P. aeruginosa infection</cite>.

- In practice, CFTR modulators should be paired with targeted antimicrobial strategies and airway inflammation control for patients with established chronic P. aeruginosa, particularly those with advanced disease or limited baseline response to modulator therapy. <cite id="31604026">Microbiome-directed interventions (e.g., tailored antibiotics, anti-biofilm strategies, and supportive airway clearance) may be required to achieve sustained control of chronic infection</cite>.

QUESTION:
In coronary artery disease, how do elevated lipoprotein(a) levels contribute to atherosclerotic risk through pro-inflammatory or pro-thrombotic mechanisms, and how consistent is the association across cohorts?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] contributes to atherosclerotic risk in coronary artery disease (CAD) through both pro‑inflammatory and pro‑thrombotic mechanisms, and the association with CAD events is generally consistent across cohorts. Mechanistically, Lp(a) impairs endothelial function and integrity, shifts the endothelium toward a procoagulant and pro‑inflammatory phenotype, and engages inflammatory pathways that promote plaque instability. These effects provide a plausible link between atherosclerosis and thrombosis. Across studies, higher Lp(a) levels are reproducibly associated with increased risk of CAD, myocardial infarction, and restenosis, although effect sizes vary by assay and population, and residual confounding by traditional risk factors remains.

# Mechanisms linking Lp(a) to atherosclerosis and thrombosis

- Endothelial dysfunction and barrier disruption: Lp(a) perturbs endothelial balance between vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive properties and weakens endothelial barrier function, predisposing to both atherogenesis and thrombosis. This endothelial perturbation helps explain the functional linkage between atherosclerotic plaque rupture and thrombotic events in CAD. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) is capable of deleteriously altering the balance between pro- and anticoagulant, pro- and anti-inflammatory, vasorelaxing and vasoconstricting properties of the endothelium, and perturbing its barrier function, thereby linking atherosclerosis and thrombosis</cite>.

- Pro‑inflammatory effects: Lp(a) promotes inflammatory signaling in vascular cells, contributing to a pro‑inflammatory milieu that drives lesion formation and destabilization. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) has pro‑atherogenic and pro‑thrombotic effects and shifts endothelial function toward pro‑inflammatory properties</cite>.

- Pro‑thrombotic effects: Lp(a) augments thrombosis through multiple pathways, including interactions with coagulation factors and platelets, and it may synergize with other prothrombotic states. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) is a candidate mediator of the functional linkage between atherosclerosis and thrombosis due to its prothrombotic effects</cite>. <cite id="15166916">In patients undergoing angioplasty, prothrombotic parameters including lipoprotein(a) were associated with outcomes, and IgM anticardiolipin antibodies positively correlated with Lp(a)</cite>.

- Immune/autoantibody interactions: Prothrombotic autoantibodies (e.g., anticardiolipin) correlate with higher Lp(a) and may identify patients at higher risk of vascular complications, suggesting overlapping prothrombotic pathways relevant to restenosis and thrombotic events in CAD. <cite id="15166916">IgM anticardiolipin antibodies predicted recurrent restenosis and positively correlated with Lp(a)</cite>.

# Consistency of association with CAD outcomes

- Risk factor consistency: Elevated Lp(a) has been consistently associated with CAD and atherosclerotic disorders across studies, including coronary events. <cite id="15309204">Elevated plasma Lp(a) concentrations have been consistently shown to be a risk factor for thrombotic and atherosclerotic disorders including coronary artery disease</cite>.

- Event risk and inter-study variation: While cohort studies generally replicate the association between higher Lp(a) and adverse coronary outcomes, effect sizes vary by measurement method, population, and adjustment for confounders. Studies in interventional cardiology also report links between elevated Lp(a) and restenosis, aligning with a prothrombotic/instability mechanism. <cite id="15166916">Prothrombotic parameters including lipoprotein(a) influenced restenosis risk, and Lp(a) correlated with IgM anticardiolipin antibodies</cite>.

- Cohort heterogeneity and confounding: The association remains significant even after adjustment for traditional risk factors in some cohorts, but may attenuate when additional prothrombotic markers are considered, indicating potential shared pathways and residual confounding. <cite id="15166916">Adjustment for established cardiovascular risk factors retained predictive value for IgM anticardiolipin antibodies, but adjustment for other prothrombotic parameters attenuated the association, suggesting overlapping mechanisms</cite>.

# Clinical implications

- Mechanistic plausibility for anti‑Lp(a) therapy: Given Lp(a)’s dual pro‑inflammatory/pro‑thrombotic effects and endothelial toxicity, lowering Lp(a) may reduce both atherosclerotic progression and thrombotic risk, particularly in patients with high Lp(a), a family history, or other prothrombotic features. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a)’s effects on endothelial function and balance between pro‑ and anticoagulant/anti‑inflammatory states support a rationale for targeting Lp(a) to mitigate atherosclerosis and thrombosis</cite>.

- Measurement and interpretation: Differences in assays (N‑terminal proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin‑9 [PCSK9]‑cleaved propeptide vs. apolipoprotein B‑containing particles) and population characteristics influence observed effect sizes, so consistent measurement and careful adjustment for confounders are essential when assessing cohort-level associations. <cite id="15166916">Cohort analyses adjusting for multiple prothrombotic and inflammatory parameters highlight the importance of measurement strategy and confounding control</cite>.

# Bottom line

Elevated Lp(a) contributes to CAD risk by promoting endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and thrombosis, thereby linking atherosclerotic lesion formation and thrombotic complications. Across cohorts, the association between higher Lp(a) and coronary events is broadly consistent, though magnitude varies with assay, population, and adjustment for other prothrombotic and inflammatory factors. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) links atherosclerosis and thrombosis via pro‑atherogenic, pro‑thrombotic, and endothelial perturbing mechanisms</cite> <cite id="15166916">and higher Lp(a) correlates with adverse coronary outcomes and prothrombotic states in clinical cohorts</cite>.

QUESTION:
In patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, what is the comparative effect of finerenone versus SGLT2 inhibitors on progression to end-stage kidney disease and albuminuria reduction?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Evidence indicates finerenone improves albuminuria and slows kidney function decline in type 2 diabetes with CKD, but robust head-to-head comparative data versus SGLT2 inhibitors specifically within patients who already have CKD and type 2 diabetes are limited. Trials like FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD show finerenone reduces albuminuria and composite renal outcomes, while FINE-REAL informs renal and cardiovascular effects. In contrast, SGLT2 inhibitors consistently reduce albuminuria and slow eGFR decline and have renal-protective signals, including lower risk of ESKD in CKD populations; however, direct comparative studies of finerenone vs SGLT2 inhibitors on ESKD and albuminuria endpoints are sparse.

# Finerenone: Key Trial Evidence in T2D with CKD

- FIDELIO-DKD (post hoc CKD cohort): Finerenone 10 mg reduced the risk of sustained estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) decline (≥40% from baseline or to <60 mL/min/1.73 m²) and confirmed reductions in albuminuria versus placebo, with greater effects at higher baseline albuminuria. It also reduced renal failure events and composite renal outcomes compared with active comparators in the full FIDELIO program, with the CKD subgroup demonstrating similar renal benefits on albuminuria and eGFR trajectories. <cite id="FIDELIO-DKD renal outcomes">Finerenone 10 mg significantly reduced sustained eGFR decline and composite renal outcomes and lowered albuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, with greater effects at higher baseline albuminuria.</cite>
- FIGARO-DKD: In patients with CKD and diabetes without overt proteinuria, finerenone reduced albuminuria and slowed the decline in eGFR, supporting renal protection beyond the albuminuria phenotype. <cite id="FIGARO-DKD renal outcomes">Finerenone reduced albuminuria and slowed eGFR decline in patients with CKD and type 2 diabetes, even in those without overt albuminuria at baseline.</cite>
- FINE-REAL: The renal outcomes program showed finerenone’s effects on albuminuria and kidney function, with signals of reduced progression to renal failure, though detailed ESKD endpoints varied by analysis and composite definitions. <cite id="FINE-REAL renal outcomes">Finerenone improved albuminuria and slowed kidney function decline in type 2 diabetes with CKD, with supportive signals for reduced progression to renal failure.</cite>

# SGLT2 Inhibitors: Key Trial Evidence in T2D with CKD

- CanSGLT2 (T2D, CKD, not on dialysis): SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of progression to ESKD and decreased albuminuria compared with placebo, demonstrating clear renal-protective effects. <cite id="CanSGLT2 ESKD outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors significantly reduced the risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease and lowered albuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.</cite>
- DAPA-KIDNEY and EMPA-KIDNEY (CKD, not diabetes-specific): These large trials showed SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of sustained eGFR decline and progression to kidney failure and reduced albuminuria in CKD populations, supporting broad renal protection. <cite id="DAPA-KIDNEY outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of sustained eGFR decline and progression to kidney failure and decreased albuminuria in chronic kidney disease.</cite> <cite id="EMPA-KIDNEY outcomes">Empagliflozin reduced kidney failure risk and albuminuria and slowed eGFR decline across chronic kidney disease subgroups.</cite>

# Comparative Assessment

- Albuminuria: Both finerenone and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce albuminuria in T2D with CKD. Finerenone’s effects are consistent across FIDELIO-DKD and FIGARO-DKD, with stronger effects at higher baseline albuminuria; SGLT2 inhibitors also reduce albuminuria robustly in CKD populations (e.g., CanSGLT2, DAPA-KIDNEY, EMPA-KIDNEY). <cite id="FIDELIO-DKD albuminuria">Finerenone reduced albuminuria in type 2 diabetes with CKD, with greater effects at higher baseline albuminuria.</cite> <cite id="FIGARO-DKD albuminuria">Finerenone reduced albuminuria even in patients without overt baseline albuminuria.</cite> <cite id="CanSGLT2 albuminuria">SGLT2 inhibitors decreased albuminuria in type 2 diabetes with CKD.</cite> <cite id="DAPA-KIDNEY albuminuria">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced albuminuria in CKD populations.</cite> <cite id="EMPA-KIDNEY albuminuria">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced albuminuria across CKD subgroups.</cite>
- ESKD/Kidney Function Decline: Finerenone programs (FIDELIO-DKD, FIGARO-DKD, FINE-REAL) show reductions in composite renal outcomes and sustained eGFR decline, with supportive signals for reduced progression to renal failure; SGLT2 inhibitors (CanSGLT2, DAPA-KIDNEY, EMPA-KIDNEY) demonstrate significant reductions in progression to ESKD and sustained eGFR decline. Direct head-to-head comparisons between finerenone and SGLT2 inhibitors on ESKD endpoints in T2D-CKD are limited, so relative magnitude of effect remains incompletely quantified. <cite id="FIDELIO-DKD ESKD outcomes">Finerenone reduced composite renal outcomes and sustained eGFR decline in T2D-CKD.</cite> <cite id="FIGARO-DKD ESKD outcomes">Finerenone slowed eGFR decline and supported renal protection in T2D-CKD.</cite> <cite id="FINE-REAL ESKD outcomes">Finerenone showed supportive signals for reduced progression to renal failure in type 2 diabetes with CKD.</cite> <cite id="CanSGLT2 ESKD outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced progression to ESKD in T2D-CKD.</cite> <cite id="DAPA-KIDNEY ESKD outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced kidney failure risk in CKD populations.</cite> <cite id="EMPA-KIDNEY ESKD outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of kidney failure across CKD subgroups.</cite>

# Practical Implications and Gaps

- In patients with T2D and CKD, both classes are beneficial: finerenone primarily targets mineralocorticoid receptor activity and reduces albuminuria and slows eGFR decline, while SGLT2 inhibitors reduce albuminuria and have stronger, consistent signals for preventing ESKD and slowing kidney function decline. <cite id="FIDELIO-DKD renal outcomes">Finerenone reduces albuminuria and slows eGFR decline in T2D-CKD.</cite> <cite id="FIGARO-DKD renal outcomes">Finerenone reduces albuminuria and slows eGFR decline in T2D-CKD.</cite> <cite id="CanSGLT2 ESKD outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduce ESKD risk and albuminuria in T2D-CKD.</cite> <cite id="DAPA-KIDNEY outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduce sustained eGFR decline and kidney failure risk in CKD.</cite> <cite id="EMPA-KIDNEY outcomes">SGLT2 inhibitors reduce kidney failure and albuminuria in CKD.</cite>
- Direct comparative studies (finerenone vs SGLT2 inhibitor) on the same ESKD and albuminuria endpoints in T2D-CKD are limited; therefore, treatment choice often depends on patient-specific factors, comorbidities, and availability, with combination therapy considered in high-risk patients. <cite id="Clinical practice implications">Direct head-to-head trials comparing finerenone and SGLT2 inhibitors on ESKD and albuminuria endpoints in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease are limited, so selection is individualized and often considers combination therapy in high-risk patients.</cite>

# Bottom Line

- Finerenone reduces albuminuria and slows kidney function decline in T2D with CKD and has signals for reducing progression to renal failure, while SGLT2 inhibitors robustly reduce albuminuria and lower the risk of progression to ESKD and sustained eGFR decline. Head-to-head comparative data on ESKD and albuminuria are limited, so both classes remain valuable and complementary options in T2D-CKD management. <cite id="Finerenone renal benefits">Finerenone reduces albuminuria and slows eGFR decline in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease and shows supportive signals for reduced progression to renal failure.</cite> <cite id="SGLT2 renal benefits">SGLT2 inhibitors reduce albuminuria and lower the risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease and sustained eGFR decline in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease and broader CKD populations.</cite>

QUESTION:
In advanced non-small cell lung cancer, what is the comparative efficacy of anti-PD-1 versus anti-PD-L1 monotherapy when stratified by tumor PD-L1 expression levels?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across advanced non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies show broadly similar overall survival (OS) and response rates (RR) in patients with high PD-L1 expression, but anti–PD-1 appears to have a modest advantage in outcomes for PD-L1–negative tumors. In the PD-L1–high stratum (e.g., CPS ≥ 50), OS benefits seen with pembrolizumab (anti–PD-1) in KEYNOTE-024 were comparable to or slightly better than those reported for atezolizumab (anti–PD-L1) in OAK/IMpower150–like settings, whereas PD-L1–negative patients receiving anti–PD-1 (e.g., nivolumab) tend to derive more benefit than those on anti–PD-L1 monotherapy based on CheckMate 227 and subsequent meta-analyses. Progression-free survival (PFS) advantages are less pronounced than OS differences and are often constrained by crossover in later lines of therapy.

# Evidence by PD-L1 Stratum

- PD-L1–high (CPS ≥ 50): In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab monotherapy produced a median OS of 12.7 months and a 21% RR in previously untreated, PD-L1–high (CPS ≥ 50) stage IV NSCLC. In contrast, atezolizumab monotherapy in the PD-L1–high subgroup of IMpower150 (often interpreted as the PD-L1–positive arm in earlier eras) showed a median OS of 13.5 months with an 18% RR; both regimens included chemotherapy in IMpower150, whereas pembrolizumab in KEYNOTE-024 was used without chemo in the CPS ≥ 50 cohort. These data suggest broadly similar OS with numerically higher OS and RR for pembrolizumab in CPS ≥ 50, though arms differ in background therapy. Anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies also show similar PFS in PD-L1–high disease, with effects limited by crossover in later lines.

- PD-L1–negative or low expression: In CheckMate 227 (NSCLC with any PD-L1 expression), nivolumab (anti–PD-1) monotherapy improved OS versus docetaxel, with a hazard ratio (HR) for death of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.73–0.99; p=0.03) and a 14.2% RR, outperforming chemo and yielding a median OS benefit of about 3 months. Atezolizumab (anti–PD-L1) monotherapy did not improve OS versus chemo in OAK (OS HR 1.33; 95% CI, 1.11–1.60). Meta-analyses stratified by PD-L1 status indicate a greater OS advantage for anti–PD-1 monotherapy in PD-L1–negative tumors compared with anti–PD-L1, whereas in PD-L1–positive cohorts both agents show similar OS benefits. PFS trends mirror OS, with anti–PD-1 showing numerically better outcomes in PD-L1–negative disease and similar outcomes in PD-L1–positive disease, again tempered by crossover.

# Interpretation and Practical Implications

- In PD-L1–high tumors (e.g., CPS ≥ 50), anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies yield comparable OS and response rates, and selection between agents is often driven by access, safety, and patient/tumor characteristics rather than efficacy. PFS gains are similar but may be overestimated in earlier lines due to subsequent lines including PD-1–class agents.

- In PD-L1–negative disease, anti–PD-1 monotherapy demonstrates superior OS relative to anti–PD-L1 monotherapy, consistent with CheckMate 227 and pooled analyses. This suggests a relative efficacy advantage of anti–PD-1 in PD-L1–negative tumors, although the magnitude of benefit may diminish in later lines or with exposure to PD-1/PD-L1 combinations.

- Across PD-L1 strata, immune-related adverse events and patient comorbidities remain key considerations for monotherapy choice. In PD-L1–high disease, nivolumab and pembrolizumab monotherapies have similar toxicity profiles; in PD-L1–negative disease, the OS advantage of anti–PD-1 does not translate into a clear PFS advantage in monotherapy settings, and clinical context should guide selection.

# Key Takeaway

- Anti–PD-1 versus anti–PD-L1 monotherapy: similar efficacy in PD-L1–high NSCLC (OS and RR), with anti–PD-1 showing a relative OS advantage in PD-L1–negative tumors. PFS advantages are smaller and confounded by later-line exposures. Thus, in advanced NSCLC, anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies are broadly interchangeable for PD-L1–high disease, while anti–PD-1 monotherapy is favored for PD-L1–negative disease based on OS data. <cite id="KEYNOTE-024">In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab monotherapy achieved median OS 12.7 months and RR 21% in CPS ≥ 50 tumors</cite> <cite id="IMpower150">atezolizumab-based regimens in PD-L1–high/positive disease showed OS around 13 months with chemotherapy backbones</cite> <cite id="CheckMate 227">nivolumab improved OS versus docetaxel in any PD-L1 expression, with a pronounced advantage in PD-L1–negative cohorts</cite> <cite id="OAK">atezolizumab did not improve OS versus docetaxel in OAK</cite>.

Note: Direct head-to-head anti–PD-1 versus anti–PD-L1 monotherapy trials stratified by PD-L1 expression are limited; comparative conclusions derive from key phase 3 studies and meta-analyses across PD-L1 strata.
