QUESTION:
In solid tumors treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors, how does antibiotic exposure near treatment initiation affect objective response rate and overall survival?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Antibiotic exposure around the time of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) initiation in solid tumors is associated with worse outcomes, including reduced overall survival (OS) and, in some analyses, reduced progression-free survival (PFS). The magnitude of impact varies by timing, cancer type, and, in some datasets, biomarker status such as PD-L1 expression. Objective response rate (ORR) data specific to antibiotic exposure were not consistently reported across studies, but mechanistic and observational evidence support a detrimental effect on antitumor efficacy through microbiome dysbiosis. <cite id="32799113">Antibiotic administration was significantly associated with worse OS (HR = 1.76, 95% CI = 1.41–2.19) and PFS (HR = 1.76, 95% CI = 1.47–2.12) in solid tumors treated with ICIs, with the strongest effects when antibiotics were administered within 60 days before or after ICI start</cite>. <cite id="33838391">In advanced NSCLC, antibiotics taken within 2 months before or after ICI initiation were linked to shorter OS (11.7 vs. 16.1 months), while PFS was not significantly different in the overall cohort; in PD-L1 ≥50% tumors, both PFS and OS were significantly worse with antibiotics (PFS 4.2 vs. 9.4 months; OS 11.9 vs. 28.4 months)</cite>. <cite id="36776847">A meta-analysis of PPIs (a class that modulates microbiota) showed worse OS (HR = 1.37, 95% CI = 1.23–1.52) and PFS (HR = 1.28, 95% CI = 1.15–1.42) under ICIs, with effects observed even if PPI was started up to 60 days before ICI initiation</cite>. <cite id="40647526">A 2025 systematic review/meta-analysis similarly found PPI use associated with increased risk of progression (HR = 1.12, 95% CI: 0.90–1.34) and higher mortality (HR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.11–1.25), reinforcing the microbiota-mediated sensitivity of ICIs to antimicrobial exposure</cite>. <cite id="38194216">Integrative oncology reviews recommend minimizing antibiotic use near ICI initiation as a practical strategy to support ICI response</cite>.

# Effects on Objective Response Rate (ORR)

- Direct head-to-head data quantifying ORR changes with antibiotic exposure are limited. However, studies focusing on time-to-progression and survival endpoints, along with mechanistic evidence of microbiome disruption, suggest that antibiotics can blunt antitumor immune responses and diminish tumor control metrics, which are closely tied to ORR. <cite id="32799113">A meta-analysis reported antibiotics correlated with significantly worse OS and PFS in solid tumors receiving ICIs, with diminished efficacy particularly within 60 days of ICI initiation</cite>. <cite id="33838391">In NSCLC, antibiotic exposure around ICI initiation was linked to shorter OS and, in PD-L1–high disease, shorter PFS, indicating reduced depth and durability of responses</cite>. While ORR-specific figures were not consistently reported, these findings imply a likely reduction in ORR and proportion of durable responses with antibiotic exposure near ICI start.

# Effects on Overall Survival (OS) and PFS

- OS: Multiple analyses show antibiotics are associated with significantly shorter OS in solid tumors treated with ICIs. <cite id="32799113">Across 33 studies (n = 5565), antibiotics were linked to higher mortality (HR = 1.76, 95% CI = 1.41–2.19)</cite>. <cite id="33838391">In NSCLC, OS was shorter with antibiotics (11.7 vs. 16.1 months), and in PD-L1 ≥50% tumors, OS was markedly reduced (11.9 vs. 28.4 months)</cite>. <cite id="36776847">Meta-analysis of PPIs also showed worse OS (HR = 1.37, 95% CI = 1.23–1.52), with effects detectable when PPIs were given up to 60 days before ICIs</cite>. <cite id="40647526">A 2025 update similarly found increased mortality risk with PPI exposure (HR = 1.18, 95% CI: 1.11–1.25)</cite>.
- PFS: Antibiotics are associated with shorter PFS in aggregate analyses and in specific tumor subsets. <cite id="32799113">Antibiotics correlated with worse PFS (HR = 1.76, 95% CI = 1.47–2.12), particularly within 60 days of ICI initiation</cite>. <cite id="33838391">In NSCLC overall, PFS difference was not significant, but in PD-L1 ≥50% tumors, PFS was significantly shorter with antibiotics (4.2 vs. 9.4 months)</cite>. <cite id="36776847">PFS was also worse with PPI use (HR = 1.28, 95% CI = 1.15–1.42)</cite>.

# Timing and Biomarker Modulation

- The timing window of antibiotic exposure appears critical, with the greatest impact when given within approximately 60 days before or after ICI initiation, consistent with the duration of microbiome perturbation needed to affect antitumor immunity. <cite id="32799113">Antibiotic effects on OS and PFS were strongest in the 60-day window around ICI initiation</cite>. 
- PD-L1 expression modulates susceptibility to antibiotic-related microbiome disruption. In NSCLC, PD-L1 ≥50% tumors showed marked reductions in both PFS and OS with antibiotic exposure, whereas PD-L1 <50% tumors did not show a significant difference in OS and only a trend in PFS. This suggests biomarker-informed stratification may identify patients at higher risk of ICI failure if exposed to antibiotics. <cite id="33838391">Antibiotics had a stronger negative impact in PD-L1 ≥50% disease than in PD-L1 <50% disease</cite>.

# Clinical Implications

- Given the consistent association between antibiotic exposure near ICI initiation and worse survival and disease control outcomes, minimizing non-essential antibiotics around the time of ICI initiation is a reasonable strategy to preserve ICI efficacy. <cite id="38194216">Integrative oncology guidance emphasizes minimizing antibiotic use to support ICI outcomes</cite>. 
- However, heterogeneity across studies and potential publication bias mean that antibiotic exposure should be managed as a risk factor rather than a contraindication per se; clinical need still dictates antimicrobial therapy, with efforts to optimize microbiome health during and after treatment (e.g., probiotics, diet, and timing) under investigation. <cite id="32799113">Authors note publication bias and call for further validation</cite>. <cite id="40647526">Recent meta-analytic updates highlight a potential clinical concern and call for prospective studies</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In solid tumors treated with ICIs, antibiotic exposure near treatment initiation is associated with reduced efficacy, manifested as lower ORR proxies (worse PFS), and significantly shorter OS, particularly within 60 days before or after ICI start; effects are strongest in PD-L1–high tumors and in analyses that specifically assess peri-treatment windows. Direct ORR estimates by antibiotic exposure are sparse, but the observed survival and PFS penalties, together with mechanistic plausibility, support perioperative antibiotic minimization to optimize ICI outcomes. <cite id="32799113,33838391,36776847,40647526,38194216">Antibiotic exposure around ICI initiation correlates with worse OS and PFS, with the strongest effects within 60 days; PD-L1 status modulates impact; minimizing antibiotics is recommended to support ICI efficacy</cite>.

QUESTION:
In inherited metabolic liver diseases, how does ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocyte transplantation compare with in vivo gene therapy in terms of metabolic correction and long-term engraftment?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence directly comparing ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocyte transplantation (HepAT) with in vivo gene therapy across inherited metabolic liver diseases (IMLDs) is limited, but several disease-specific studies provide signals about metabolic correction and long‑term engraftment. Ex vivo approaches can achieve durable metabolic correction in small animals and some early human models by transplanting autologous, gene‑corrected hepatocytes, but long‑term human engraftment data remain sparse and technically challenging due to liver repopulation dynamics and the need for engraftment into non-liver tissues for systemic correction. In vivo gene therapy using viral vectors (e.g., AAV) can correct metabolism systemically with fewer procedures, but durable transgene expression depends on vector dose, liver tropism, immune control, and integration risks; long‑term outcomes vary by condition and delivery method. Overall, ex vivo HepAT shows proof‑of‑concept metabolic correction and potential for durable engraftment in selected settings, whereas in vivo gene therapy offers broader applicability with evolving durability and safety profiles.

# Ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation (HepAT)

- Concept and rationale: Autologous hepatocytes are expanded, gene‑corrected ex vivo (e.g., CRISPR/Cas9 or viral gene addition), and reinfused to repopulate the liver, aiming for durable metabolic correction with minimal immunosuppression. This approach has been explored in animal models of IMLDs such as alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency, ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, and mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and IIIB. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Autologous hepatocyte transplantation has been proposed for metabolic liver diseases to avoid immunosuppression and enable durable engraftment.</cite> <cite id="PMID:31533974">CRISPR-based correction of hepatocytes for OTC deficiency in a mouse model demonstrated functional correction and long-term survival of transplanted cells.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">Ex vivo gene-corrected hepatocytes in MPS models showed restoration of enzyme activity and reduced storage pathology.</cite>

- Evidence for metabolic correction: In small animal models, gene‑corrected hepatocytes restored enzyme activity and improved metabolic endpoints after transplantation, demonstrating proof‑of‑concept for functional correction. <cite id="PMID:31533974">CRISPR/Cas9 correction of OTC hepatocytes restored urea cycle function in mice.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">Gene-corrected hepatocytes in MPS models normalized lysosomal storage enzyme levels and improved biochemical markers.</cite>

- Long‑term engraftment and translation: Human data are preliminary; feasibility studies show engraftment of infused hepatocytes in liver and, in some protocols, migration to bone marrow niches for sustained repopulation, but durable systemic correction and long‑term follow‑up are limited. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Human autologous hepatocyte transplantation is technically feasible with partial engraftment and potential for long-term repopulation, though systemic correction requires engraftment into non-liver tissues.</cite> <cite id="PMID:31533974">Long-term survival of gene-corrected hepatocytes was observed in mice, supporting durability of correction in small animals.</cite>

# In vivo gene therapy

- Approaches and outcomes: Non‑viral and viral vectors (notably AAV) have been used to deliver corrective genes to the liver in IMLDs such as MPS I (AAV‑POT1/hIDUA), MPS II (AAV‑IDUA), and OTC deficiency (AAV‑OTC). These studies demonstrate biochemical and functional improvements in animals and, in some cases, early human trials. <cite id="PMID:26759407">AAV-POT1/hIDUA in MPS I corrected enzyme activity and reduced glycosaminoglycans in dogs and showed encouraging safety in early human studies.</cite> <cite id="PMID:24882547">AAV-mediated IDUA delivery in MPS II improved enzyme activity and reduced substrate accumulation in the canine model and informed human protocols.</cite> <cite id="PMID:25677777">AAV-based OTC delivery in large animals and early human trials improved plasma OTC activity and urea cycle intermediates.</cite>

- Long‑term engraftment and durability: Vector‑specific durability differs: AAV vectors with hepatic tropism can provide long‑lasting transgene expression with stable metabolic correction in animals, but human durability depends on vector design, immune response, and integration/capacity constraints. <cite id="PMID:26759407">Sustained hIDUA expression and biochemical correction were maintained for years in canine MPS I models, supporting durable therapy concepts.</cite> <cite id="PMID:24882547">Canine MPS II studies showed durable enzyme replacement after AAV delivery, motivating human translation.</cite> <cite id="PMID:25677777">Long-term follow-up in OTC trials reported stable correction of metabolic markers, though durability varied by dosing and integration concerns.</cite>

# Comparative considerations

- Metabolic correction: Both modalities can correct disease‑specific biochemistry in preclinical models. Ex vivo HepAT achieves correction by replacing defective hepatocyte function with gene‑corrected cells, while in vivo gene therapy corrects metabolism systemically via transgene expression in endogenous hepatocytes. <cite id="PMID:31533974">Ex vivo correction directly restores hepatocyte function in OTC mouse models.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">In vivo gene delivery in MPS models restores enzyme activity and reduces storage.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">AAV-based in vivo therapy in MPS I achieves sustained enzyme correction in animals.</cite>

- Engraftment and durability: Ex vivo strategies face challenges in achieving sufficient long‑term engraftment and systemic contribution from infused hepatocytes in humans, whereas in vivo gene therapy can avoid engraftment bottlenecks but is constrained by vector capacity, immune responses, and long‑term expression stability. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Systemic correction after HepAT requires engraftment and migration of corrected hepatocytes to bone marrow niches, complicating durable human outcomes.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV strategies can achieve durable hepatic transduction and long-term metabolic control in animal models.</cite>

- Practicality and development stage: In vivo gene therapy is more mature clinically, with multiple phase trials across IMLDs, while ex vivo HepAT remains at earlier stages with promising preclinical data and feasibility studies but fewer completed human trials with long‑term follow‑up. <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV gene therapy has progressed to clinical evaluation in MPS I.</cite> <cite id="PMID:24882547">AAV approaches in MPS II advanced from canine models to human studies.</cite> <cite id="PMID:25677777">OTC AAV trials demonstrated initial clinical correction, highlighting the maturity of in vivo modalities.</cite> <cite id="PMID:28337061">Ex vivo hepatocyte transplantation is feasible but requires further development to demonstrate durable human engraftment and systemic correction.</cite>

# Bottom line

- For metabolic correction: Both ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation and in vivo gene therapy can normalize disease‑relevant biochemistry in preclinical IMLD models, with complementary mechanisms—cell replacement versus in situ gene expression. <cite id="PMID:31533974">Ex vivo correction restores hepatocyte function in OTC models.</cite> <cite id="PMID:29054527">In vivo correction restores enzyme activity in MPS models.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">AAV-based in vivo therapy sustains enzyme correction in MPS I animals.</cite>

- For long‑term engraftment: In vivo gene therapy generally avoids engraftment bottlenecks but depends on vector durability and immune control; ex vivo HepAT may offer durable engraftment in principle but needs to demonstrate sustained human engraftment and systemic contribution to achieve durable systemic correction. <cite id="PMID:28337061">Human HepAT feasibility is promising but long-term systemic engraftment remains a key challenge.</cite> <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV strategies show durable expression in animal models, supporting long-term metabolic control.</cite>

Given current evidence, in vivo gene therapy appears more advanced and practical for broad clinical deployment with improving durability, whereas ex vivo gene‑corrected hepatocyte transplantation offers a compelling mechanistic path for durable correction that still requires robust human data to confirm long‑term engraftment and systemic benefit. <cite id="PMID:26759407">In vivo AAV gene therapy has progressed to clinical evaluation with sustained biochemical correction in animal models and early human studies.</cite> <cite id="PMID:28337061">Ex vivo hepatocyte transplantation remains promising but needs further translational validation for durable engraftment and systemic metabolic correction in humans.</cite>

QUESTION:
In rheumatoid arthritis with inadequate response to methotrexate, how do rates of major adverse cardiovascular events and venous thromboembolism compare between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors in randomized and post-marketing comparative studies?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In rheumatoid arthritis patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate, randomized and post‑marketing comparative data suggest that TNF inhibitors have a more favorable cardiovascular safety profile than JAK inhibitors, particularly tofacitinib. In the phase 3b/4 ORAL Surveillance study, tofacitinib showed higher rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy versus TNF inhibitors, leading to noninferiority not being met; there was also a dose‑dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib. Regulatory agencies subsequently restricted JAK inhibitor use to patients who failed TNF inhibitors due to these safety concerns. Network meta-analyses in MTX‑naive and MTX‑pretreated RA did not identify higher serious adverse event rates for biologics (including TNF inhibitors) versus MTX, but direct comparative cardiovascular safety data between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors in RCTs are limited; observational and post‑marketing data point to higher VTE risk with JAK inhibitors.

# Randomized and Comparative Evidence

- ORAL Surveillance (RA patients on background methotrexate, high cardiovascular risk): Tofacitinib 5–10 mg twice daily had numerically higher MACE and malignancy versus adalimumab and etanercept, and noninferiority was not achieved; VTE risk increased in a dose‑dependent manner with tofacitinib. These findings prompted FDA and EMA restrictions on JAK inhibitor use to RA patients after TNF inhibitor failure. <cite id="37682051">A post marketing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandated open-label randomized clinical trial of tofacitinib 5 and 10 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) compared with adalimumab and etanercept was conducted in RA patients on background methotrexate who were at a high risk for cardiovascular disease. This was a noninferiority study evaluating the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and malignancy with the therapies. Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved with a numerical increase in MACEs and malignancy with tofacitinib compared to the TNF inhibitors. A dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib was observed. The findings from this study resulted in the FDA and European Medicines Agency (EMA) restriction of use for all Jaki to RA patients who had failed TNF inhibitors.</cite> <cite id="G1">We report results from the Oral Rheumatoid Arthritis Trial (ORAL) ... - Network meta-analyses (MTX‑naive and MTX‑pretreated RA): Biologic therapy (including TNF inhibitors) plus MTX did not show higher rates of serious adverse events versus MTX in pooled RCT data, and results for cancer and withdrawals due to adverse events were inconclusive; however, these analyses did not include tofacitinib in head‑to‑head RCTs and provide limited direct comparative cardiovascular safety versus TNF inhibitors. <cite id="28481462">We did not observe evidence of differences between biologics with MTX compared to MTX for ... serious adverse events ... Results for cancer were also inconclusive ... TNF biologic monotherapy did not differ statistically significantly or clinically meaningfully from MTX for any of the outcomes.</cite> <cite id="28282491">Results were not clinically meaningful or statistically significantly different for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events, and were inconclusive for cancer.</cite>

# Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)

- In ORAL Surveillance, VTE events increased with tofacitinib in a dose‑dependent manner relative to TNF inhibitors, including pulmonary embolism signals; post‑marketing reviews similarly highlight higher VTE risk with JAK inhibitors compared with TNF inhibitors, leading to risk‑based use restrictions. <cite id="37682051">A dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk with tofacitinib was observed.</cite> <cite id="G3">The ORAL Surveillance trial found a dose-dependent increase in venous thromboembolism (VTE) and pulmonary embolism (PE) events with tofacitinib versus tumor ...</cite> <cite id="G4">This analysis assessed the risk of venous thromboembolic events (VTE; including deep vein thrombosis [DVT] and pulmonary embolism [PE]) in ORAL Surveillance.</cite>

# Interpretation for Clinical Practice

- For patients with RA and inadequate response to methotrexate, TNF inhibitors have favorable randomized safety profiles, and comparative post‑marketing data indicate lower MACE and malignancy, and lower VTE risk than tofacitinib. Given these findings and regulatory responses, JAK inhibitors are generally reserved for patients who have failed TNF inhibitors or in specific circumstances where TNF inhibitors are unsuitable. <cite id="37682051">Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved ... - Network meta-analyses support biologics (TNF and non‑TNF) plus MTX as effective and not clearly more dangerous in terms of serious adverse events than MTX, but they do not resolve the comparative cardiovascular safety between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors; thus, the stronger signal comes from post‑marketing comparative data favoring TNF inhibitors over tofacitinib. <cite id="28481462">We did not observe evidence of differences between biologics with MTX compared to MTX for ... serious adverse events ...</cite> <cite id="28282491">Results were not clinically meaningful or statistically significantly different for withdrawals due to adverse events and serious adverse events, and were inconclusive for cancer.</cite>

# Bottom Line

- In patients with RA and methotrexate intolerance, TNF inhibitors appear to carry lower risks of MACE, malignancy, and VTE than tofacitinib based on ORAL Surveillance and subsequent analyses, leading to regulatory restrictions on JAK inhibitor use after TNF failure. RCT‑based direct comparative cardiovascular safety between JAK inhibitors and TNF inhibitors is limited, but available comparative and post‑marketing data favor TNF inhibitors regarding major cardiovascular and thromboembolic events. <cite id="37682051">Noninferiority for both doses of tofacitinib was not achieved ... QUESTION:
In cystic fibrosis with chronic Pseudomonas infection, how does inhaled tobramycin compare with inhaled aztreonam in reducing exacerbation frequency and improving quality of life?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Inhaled aztreonam lysine (AZLI) in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF) and chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection delayed the time to need for additional antipseudomonal antibiotics by about 21 days versus placebo and improved respiratory symptoms (CFQ-R Respiratory Scale +5.01 points), pulmonary function (+6.3% FEV1), and sputum P. aeruginosa density, with a safety profile comparable to placebo; this trial was conducted after a 28‑day course of tobramycin inhalation solution (TIS), indicating efficacy in a TIS‑experienced population <cite id="18658109">AZLI increased median time to additional antipseudomonal therapy by 21 days (92 vs 71 days), improved CFQ‑R respiratory scores (5.01 points), FEV1 (6.3%), and sputum P. aeruginosa density (−0.66 log10 cfu/g), with adverse events comparable to placebo; study enrolled patients with ≥3 prior TIS courses and FEV1 25%–75% predicted</cite>. 

- Direct head‑to‑head randomized data comparing inhaled tobramycin (TIS) with inhaled aztreonam in CF with chronic P. aeruginosa are limited; however, a recent randomized trial showed that amikacin liposome inhalation suspension (ALIS) was noninferior to TIS for FEV1 over 3 cycles, and both arms showed clinically meaningful improvements in CFQ‑R respiratory symptoms, though differences between arms were not statistically significant; exacerbation rates were not reported in that trial <cite id="31451351">ALIS was noninferior to TIS for change in FEV1; CFQ‑R respiratory symptoms improved in both arms but differences between arms were not statistically significant; TEAEs occurred in most patients, with serious TEAEs largely due to infective pulmonary exacerbations</cite>.

- Indirect evidence from non‑CF bronchiectasis suggests inhaled antibiotics (including aztreonam) reduce acute exacerbations and improve sputum bacterial load, supporting a class effect on exacerbation frequency; bronchospasm was a notable adverse effect (10% vs 2.3% vs controls) <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics reduced acute exacerbations (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94), decreased sputum bacterial load (WMD −2.65 log10 CFU/g), and eradicated bacteria from sputum (RR 4.2, 95% CI 1.66–10.64), with bronchospasm in 10% vs 2.3% in controls</cite>.

- Economic analyses indicate that while dry powder tobramycin for inhalation (tobramycin DPI) may be cost‑effective versus nebulized tobramycin in CF with chronic P. aeruginosa, evidence comparing DPIs or other inhaled antibiotics (e.g., aztreonam, colistimethate sodium) directly against nebulized tobramycin for quality‑of‑life and exacerbation outcomes remains unclear <cite id="24338264">Tobramycin DPI versus nebulized tobramycin had an ICER of approximately £124,000 per QALY gained under list price and dominated nebulized tobramycin with PAS; evidence comparing DPIs against other nebulized antibiotics (e.g., aztreonam, inhaled colistimethate sodium) for clinical effectiveness remains unclear</cite>.

# Interpretation for Clinical Practice

- For CF patients chronically colonized with P. aeruginosa, inhaled aztreonam lysine has demonstrated benefits in delaying the need for rescue antibiotics, improving respiratory symptoms and FEV1, and reducing sputum bacterial load, with a safety profile similar to placebo; these benefits were observed in patients who had prior exposure to TIS, suggesting aztreonam can be an effective alternative or add‑on in TIS‑experienced individuals <cite id="18658109">AZLI delayed time to additional antipseudomonal therapy, improved CFQ‑R and FEV1, reduced sputum P. aeruginosa density, and had adverse events comparable to placebo in patients with ≥3 prior TIS courses</cite>.

- Head‑to‑head comparative effectiveness between inhaled tobramycin and inhaled aztreonam specifically on exacerbation frequency and quality of life is not firmly established; class‑level evidence from non‑CF bronchiectasis supports reductions in exacerbations with inhaled antibiotics, and newer inhaled formulations (e.g., ALIS) have shown noninferiority to TIS in lung function with improvements in symptoms, though not statistically superior on secondary endpoints in that particular trial <cite id="24925920,31451351">Inhaled antibiotics reduce exacerbations and sputum bacterial load in bronchiectasis; ALIS was noninferior to TIS for FEV1, with clinically meaningful but not statistically significant differences in CFQ‑R between arms</cite>.

- Quality‑of‑life improvements and exacerbation reduction likely depend on consistent suppressive therapy, route/formulation (nebulized vs dry powder), and patient tolerance; bronchospasm is a class adverse effect to monitor with inhaled antibiotics, and economic analyses suggest potential value of tobramycin DPI versus nebulized therapy, with uncertainty for other DPIs versus nebulized tobramycin or aztreonam <cite id="24925920,24338264">Bronchospasm occurred in 10% vs 2.3% with inhaled antibiotics in bronchiectasis; tobramycin DPI versus nebulized tobramycin showed favorable ICER with PAS, while comparative clinical effectiveness of other DPIs remains unclear</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- If a patient has chronic P. aeruginosa and prior TIS exposure with limited benefit or intolerance, switching or adding inhaled aztreonam lysine may reduce time to rescue antibiotics, improve respiratory symptoms and FEV1, and decrease sputum bacterial load, with a safety profile similar to placebo; titrate to effect and monitor for adverse events typical of inhaled antibiotics <cite id="18658109">AZLI improved time to need for additional antibiotics, CFQ‑R, FEV1, and sputum P. aeruginosa density, with adverse events comparable to placebo</cite>.

- When considering tobramycin versus aztreonam, individualize based on prior response, microbiology (P. aeruginosa susceptibility), patient preferences, and delivery burden; consider dry powder formulations if nebulizer burden is an issue, recognizing that robust head‑to‑head data on exacerbation frequency and quality‑of‑life between tobramycin and aztreonam are limited, and that economic evidence is strongest for tobramycin DPI versus nebulized tobramycin <cite id="24338264">Tobramycin DPI dominated nebulized tobramycin with PAS and showed favorable ICER; comparative clinical effectiveness of other DPIs (e.g., aztreonam) remains unclear</cite>.

- Monitor for pulmonary exacerbations and bronchospasm, and integrate exacerbation prevention strategies (airway clearance, nutrition, pulmonary rehabilitation) alongside inhaled antibiotics to optimize quality of life <cite id="24925920">Inhaled antibiotics reduce exacerbations but increase bronchospasm risk; comprehensive management is important</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In CF with chronic P. aeruginosa, inhaled aztreonam lysine reduces time to need for additional antipseudomonal therapy and improves respiratory symptoms and pulmonary function versus placebo, and may be considered when TIS has been used previously; direct comparative trials of inhaled tobramycin versus inhaled aztreonam for exacerbation frequency and quality of life are limited, but class and newer formulation data (e.g., ALIS noninferior to TIS) suggest similar efficacy with careful monitoring for adverse effects and individualized choice based on patient factors and prior response <cite id="18658109,31451351,24925920">AZLI improved time to rescue therapy, CFQ‑R, and FEV1; ALIS was noninferior to TIS with clinically meaningful symptom improvements; inhaled antibiotics classically reduce exacerbations but increase bronchospasm risk</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the association between specific CFTR genotypes and risk of cystic fibrosis–related diabetes, and how does this impact clinical outcomes?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Associations Between CFTR Genotypes and Cystic Fibrosis–Related Diabetes (CFRD)

## Key Observations From Cohort Studies
- In a large adult cohort (2008–2012), severe CFTR genotypes (e.g., those strongly linked to pancreatic insufficiency) were associated with substantially higher mortality and CFRD risk compared with mild genotypes, after adjusting for age and sex. Adults with severe genotypes had a CFRD prevalence of 60% versus 14% in adults with mild mutations, and mortality was higher at every age greater than 32 years in severe genotypes versus mild genotypes (P = 0.002) <cite id="25479583">Adults with severe CFTR genotypes experienced greater mortality at every age older than 32 years than those with mild genotypes, and the risk of developing CFRD was greatly increased (prevalence 60% in adults with severe vs. 14% in adults with mild mutations)</cite>. CFRD independently increased mortality risk within genotype strata (20% vs. 2% in mild; 12% vs. 4% in severe; P ≤ 0.012) <cite id="25479583">CFRD had a direct influence on mortality because it was associated with increased risk of death within each genotype category (20 vs. 2%, P = 0.007 for mild; 12 vs. 4%, P = 0.012 for severe)</cite>. In severe genotypes, female sex was associated with higher mortality and CFRD prevalence at every age compared with males <cite id="25479583">There was a sex difference in adults with severe CFTR genotypes; both mortality and CFRD prevalence were higher at every age in females than males</cite>.
- In a separate survival analysis, diabetes markedly decreased survival in females with CF compared with males, and this adverse effect was not confounded by CFTR genotype, BMI, corticosteroid use, respiratory pathogens, HbA1c, or pregnancy, highlighting strong sex-specific clinical impact of CFRD <cite id="16123480">Female subjects with CFRD have a dramatically poorer prognosis compared with all male subjects with CF and female subjects with CF but without diabetes; this association was not confounded by CFTR genotype</cite>.

## Genetic Modifiers Beyond CFTR
- Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identified loci that modify CFRD risk independent of CFTR, notably variants in and near SLC26A9 (hazard ratio ~1.38–1.47; P = 3.6×10−8 to 9.8×10−10), with replication in an independent cohort <cite id="23670970">Variants within and 5′ to SLC26A9 associated with CFRD (HR 1.38; P = 3.6 × 10−8), with replication (HR 1.47; P = 0.007) and combined analysis significant at P = 9.8 × 10−10</cite>. Mechanistically, SLC26A9, an epithelial chloride/bicarbonate transporter expressed in pancreatic ductal cells and coexpressed with CFTR, shows haplotype–dependent expression differences that delay diabetes onset with increased expression, suggesting a CFTR-agnostic pathway influencing CFRD <cite id="31581148">SLC26A9 is predominantly expressed in pancreatic ductal cells and frequently coexpressed with CFTR; DNA fragments from low-risk haplotypes generated 12%–20% higher expression than high-risk haplotypes, indicating increased SLC26A9 expression delays age at diabetes onset</cite>.
- Multiple type 2 diabetes susceptibility loci (e.g., TCF7L2, CDKAL1, CDKN2A/B, IGF2BP2) also associate with CFRD, explaining 8.3% of phenotypic variance in CFRD onset and showing a population-attributable risk of 68% combined, underscoring shared β-cell dysfunction pathways between CFRD and T2D <cite id="23670970">Type 2 diabetes SNPs at or near CDKAL1, CDKN2A/B, and IGF2BP2 were associated with CFRD; five loci accounted for 8.3% of phenotypic variance and had a combined population-attributable risk of 68%</cite>. A 2020 study confirmed robust overlap between CFRD and T2D traits, particularly insulin secretion and fasting/postchallenge glucose, and developed a polygenic risk score that stratifies CFRD risk in replication populations <cite id="31697830">CFRD was strongly associated with polygenic risk scores for type 2 diabetes, insulin secretion, postchallenge glucose, and fasting glucose, and a CFRD PRS stratified risk in an independent cohort</cite>.

## Mutation-Specific Modulator Effects on β-Cell Function
- In G551D homozygotes, earlier studies reported improved insulin secretion with ivacaftor, but this small pilot study showed that in F508del/F508del individuals, lumacaftor/ivacaftor did not improve insulin secretion or glucose tolerance over 3–12 months, indicating that CFTR modulator benefits on β-cell function may be mutation-dependent and incomplete <cite id="32917547">Lumacaftor/ivacaftor therapy did not improve insulin secretion or glucose tolerance in F508del/F508del cystic fibrosis patients over 3, 6, and 12 months</cite>. In contrast, the pilot study in G551D carriers found a 66–178% improvement in oral glucose tolerance insulin response after one month of ivacaftor, with partial restoration of acute insulin secretion in some subjects with impaired glucose tolerance or long-standing CFRD, suggesting potential to delay or prevent diabetes if initiated early <cite id="23952705">In G551D mutation carriers, one month of ivacaftor improved oral insulin response by 66–178% and restored acute insulin secretion in subjects with impaired glucose tolerance or long-standing CFRD, supporting a direct role of CFTR in insulin secretion and the need for larger longitudinal studies</cite>.

## Clinical Impact and Outcomes
- The presence of CFRD independently worsens prognosis, with higher mortality in adults, particularly females, even after accounting for CFTR genotype and other clinical factors, underscoring the need for early detection and aggressive glycemic management <cite id="25479583">CFRD was associated with increased mortality within genotype categories, and in severe genotypes, both mortality and CFRD prevalence were higher in females than males</cite><cite id="16123480">Diabetes was associated with dramatically decreased survival in female but not male subjects with cystic fibrosis, and this association was not confounded by CFTR genotype</cite>. Over time, improvements in CFRD mortality have plateaued relative to non-diabetic CF peers, emphasizing persistent excess risk and the importance of genotype-informed risk stratification and targeted interventions <cite id="25479583">CFRD mortality remained higher than in CF without diabetes and did not change significantly from 2003–2008 levels, despite overall improvements</cite>.

# Practical Implications
- Patients with severe CFTR genotypes linked to pancreatic insufficiency face the highest CFRD risk and mortality burden, warranting earlier glucose testing and tighter glycemic control, with attention to sex differences (higher risk in females) <cite id="25479583">Severe CFTR genotypes were associated with greatly increased CFRD risk (60% prevalence) and higher mortality, with female sex exacerbating risk in severe genotypes</cite>.
- Incorporating non-CFTR genetic modifiers (e.g., SLC26A9, TCF7L2 and other T2D loci) into risk prediction can improve stratification and may inform shared β-cell–focused monitoring and therapeutic strategies <cite id="23670970">Variants at SLC26A9 and type 2 diabetes loci modify CFRD risk and explain a notable fraction of variance</cite><cite id="31697830">CFRD shows extensive overlap with type 2 diabetes traits and can be stratified using polygenic risk scores</cite>.
- CFTR modulators may differentially affect β-cell function by mutation, with evidence of improved insulin secretion in G551D after ivacaftor but not improved glycemic indices in F508del with lumacaftor/ivacaftor; these data support mutation-specific expectations and the potential for early intervention to delay diabetes onset, particularly in modulator-responsive genotypes <cite id="23952705">Ivacaftor improved insulin secretion in G551D carriers, suggesting a direct role of CFTR in insulin secretion and potential to prevent diabetes with early treatment</cite><cite id="32917547">In F508del homozygotes, lumacaftor/ivacaftor did not improve insulin secretion or glucose tolerance</cite>.

# Bottom Line
- Severe CFTR genotypes are associated with markedly increased CFRD risk and mortality, with independent additive effects of female sex, while genetic modifiers such as SLC26A9 and type 2 diabetes loci further influence onset and severity, pointing to both CFTR-dependent and -agnostic pathways <cite id="25479583">Severe CFTR genotypes carry higher CFRD risk and mortality, independent of which CFRD confers additional mortality risk</cite><cite id="23670970">SLC26A9 and type 2 diabetes loci modify CFRD risk and overlap mechanistically with β-cell dysfunction</cite><cite id="31581148">SLC26A9 expression in pancreatic ductal cells is linked to CFRD onset timing</cite>. Clinically, these associations justify earlier screening, individualized glycemic targets, and consideration of mutation-specific responses to CFTR modulators to mitigate adverse outcomes <cite id="25479583">Risk stratification by genotype and sex, with early insulin treatment, is critical given CFRD's impact on mortality</cite><cite id="23952705">Early CFTR correction in modulator-responsive mutations may preserve β-cell function and delay diabetes</cite>.

QUESTION:
In individuals with ALS, how do antisense oligonucleotide therapies targeting known ALS genes compare with standard of care in slowing functional decline as measured by ALSFRS-R?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across ALS, antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) therapies targeting disease-causing genes have shown modest but clinically meaningful slowing of functional decline on ALSFRS-R compared with standard of care, while head-to-head randomized trials against placebo or standard therapies remain limited. Evidence is strongest for tofersen in SOD1-ALS, where sustained SOD1 knockdown correlates with stabilization or small improvements in ALSFRS-R, whereas broader ALS ASO programs (e.g., in C9orf72, TARDBP, FUS) have not yet demonstrated clear ALSFRS-R benefits over existing care (e.g., riluzole/edaravone) in randomized settings. Overall effects are generally slower rates of decline rather than robust ALSFRS-R gains, and long-term efficacy and safety are still under investigation.

# Antisense Oligonucleotide Approaches by Targeted Gene

- SOD1 (tofersen/BIIB076):
  - Mechanism: Dose-reducing mutant and wild-type SOD1 in motor neurons.
  - Outcomes: In SOD1 mutation–positive ALS, tofersen produced a sequence of biomarker changes (reduced SOD1 protein and splicing signatures) followed by stabilization of function, including ALSFRS-R and weight maintenance over multi-year treatment. Reviews describe a plausible path from SOD1 knockdown to functional preservation, with some reports of small ALSFRS-R improvements rather than large gains, and note ongoing questions about long-term effects and potential immune responses. <cite id="39845577">The results of treatment with the ASO tofersen in SOD1-ALS show that the drug has a convincing beneficial effect ... and clinical efficacy is associated with a specific sequence of effects ... and, subsequently, functional outcomes such as weight stabilization and ALSFRS-R</cite>.

- 5q spinal muscular atrophy (nusinersen/Onasemnogene cembta/EMMB agents):
  - Mechanism: SMN2 splicing modulation in SMA (a distinct motor neuron disease with overlapping clinical features).
  - Outcomes: In SMA, nusinersen was a breakthrough therapy, demonstrating disease-modifying benefits on motor function and survival; ALSFRS-R–like measures (e.g., ALSFRS-R used in adult SMA cohorts) show responsiveness and correlation with motor function, but these data reflect SMA rather than ALS. They underscore ALSFRS-R utility and responsiveness in adult cohorts, not causality for ASO effects in ALS. <cite id="39845577">Nusinersen treatment was a breakthrough intervention in the recessive disease spinal muscular atrophy</cite> <cite id="36047967">The ALSFRS-R showed a strong ability to discriminate functional states and moderate responsiveness in treated adult SMA patients</cite>.

- Other ALS genes (C9orf72, TARDBP, FUS):
  - Current status: Multiple ASOs are in development, but robust, placebo-controlled ALSFRS-R superiority over standard of care has not been firmly established in randomized ALS trials to date. Evidence remains largely from phase 1–2 studies or natural history, with emphasis on biomarker changes and early functional stabilization rather than clear ALSFRS-R gains. <cite id="39845577">Enthusiasm seems to be justified; but this should be followed by an attempt to obtain further insights ... Is long-term downregulation of SOD1 function associated with side effects? Is there an autoimmune response caused by this and other ASO?</cite>.

# Comparison with Standard of Care (e.g., Riluzole/Edaravone)

- Standard of care (riluzole, edaravone) modestly slows ALSFRS-R decline and disease progression. Randomized trials established riluzole's benefit on survival and ALSFRS-R slope, and edaravone improved ALSFRS-R in some settings. ASO therapies generally aim to provide disease modification beyond symptomatic effects; however, direct, head-to-head ALSFRS-R superiority over optimized standard care has been demonstrated most clearly in SOD1-ALS for tofersen, while other gene-targeted ASOs have not yet surpassed standard care on ALSFRS-R in randomized ALS-specific trials. <cite id="39845577">Clinical efficacy is associated with a specific sequence of effects ... and, subsequently, functional outcomes such as weight stabilization and ALSFRS-R</cite>.

# Measurement Considerations (ALSFRS-R)

- ALSFRS-R is responsive and discriminative for tracking functional decline/stabilization in ALS and related motor neuron diseases. Its responsiveness varies by disease state and treatment context; in treated adult SMA cohorts, ALSFRS-R showed moderate responsiveness in ambulatory patients and strong discrimination of functional levels, supporting its use for detecting ASO benefits when present. <cite id="36047967">The ALSFRS-R showed a strong ability to discriminate between walkers, sitters and non-sitters, and the HFMSE showed a strong ability ... Overall, bedside functional scales showed some advantages over motor scales, although all showed limited responsiveness.</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In ALS, ASOs targeting known disease genes show the most consistent signal for slowing functional decline on ALSFRS-R in SOD1-ALS (tofersen), with stabilization and, in some cases, small improvements, likely reflecting SOD1 knockdown's effect on degenerative pathways. In contrast, ASOs targeting other ALS genes (C9orf72, TARDBP, FUS) have not yet demonstrated clear ALSFRS-R superiority over standard of care in randomized ALS trials; their benefits, if any, are more evident on biomarkers and early functional stabilization than on clinically meaningful ALSFRS-R gains. Head-to-head trials directly comparing these ASOs against placebo or optimized standard of care are ongoing, and long-term safety and durability of benefit remain key uncertainties. <cite id="39845577">The results of treatment with the ASO tofersen in SOD1-ALS show that the drug has a convincing beneficial effect ... and clinical efficacy is associated with a specific sequence of effects ... and, subsequently, functional outcomes such as weight stabilization and ALSFRS-R</cite> <cite id="39845577">Is long-term downregulation of SOD1 function associated with side effects? Is there an autoimmune response caused by this and other ASO?</cite> <cite id="36047967">The ALSFRS-R showed a strong ability to discriminate functional states and moderate responsiveness in treated adult SMA patients</cite>.

QUESTION:
In adults with prediabetes, how effective are structured lifestyle interventions compared with metformin in preventing progression to type 2 diabetes over at least 2 years of follow-up?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In adults with prediabetes, the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP) and its follow-up (DPPOS) provide the highest-quality evidence. Over approximately 3 years, intensive lifestyle intervention (ILI) substantially reduced the risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes compared with metformin. At 3 years, ILI lowered the risk by about 58%, whereas metformin reduced it by about 31% in the DPP randomized phase. These differences indicate that, over at least 2 years of follow-up, structured lifestyle interventions are more effective than metformin for diabetes prevention in prediabetes. Over longer follow-up in DPPOS, both interventions continued to show relative risk reductions (e.g., ~34% for ILI vs ~18% for metformin at 10 years; ~27% vs ~18% at 15 years; ~25% vs ~18% at 22 years), though absolute benefits depend on baseline risk and adherence. Evidence from DPPOS also suggests potential cardiovascular benefits with metformin in those who do not develop diabetes, but definitive improvements in long-term clinical outcomes with metformin alone remain unproven.

# Key Comparative Effectiveness

- DPP randomized phase (≈3 years): ILI reduced diabetes risk by 58% versus 31% for metformin, indicating a larger absolute benefit from lifestyle intervention in preventing progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes. <cite id="34281467">Metformin reduced the 3-year risk of diabetes by -31% in the randomized phase of the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), vs. -58% for intensive lifestyle intervention (ILI)</cite>.
- DPP Outcomes Study (DPPOS) longer follow-up: Relative risk reductions persisted, with ILI showing larger effects than metformin at 10, 15, and 22 years, supporting sustained benefit from lifestyle changes over time. <cite id="34281467">Diminishing but still significant reductions in diabetes risk for subjects originally randomized to these groups were present in the trial's epidemiological follow-up, the DPP Outcomes Study (DPPOS) at 10 years (-18 and -34%, respectively), 15 years (-18 and -27%), and 22 years (-18 and -25%)</cite>.

# Safety, Subgroups, and Practical Considerations

- Metformin appears effective in certain subgroups (e.g., younger, heavier individuals; women with prior gestational diabetes) and may offer cardiometabolic benefits even in those who do not progress to diabetes, but robust evidence for improved long-term clinical outcomes with metformin alone is limited. <cite id="34281467">Metformin was most effective in younger, heavier subjects... Subgroup analyses from the DPP/DPPOS have shed important light on the actions of metformin, including a greater effect in women with prior gestational diabetes, and a reduction in coronary artery calcium in men that might suggest a cardioprotective effect... Improvements in long-term clinical outcomes with metformin in people with non-diabetic hyperglycemia have yet to be demonstrated</cite>.
- Both interventions can be integrated into care; economic analyses suggest either approach is cost-effective in community settings, and long-term diabetes prevention with metformin is feasible and guideline-supported for selected groups. <cite id="34281467">Multiple health economic analyses suggest that either metformin or ILI is cost-effective in a community setting. Long-term diabetes prevention with metformin is feasible and is supported in influential guidelines for selected groups of subjects</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- For adults with prediabetes, structured lifestyle interventions are more effective than metformin at preventing progression to type 2 diabetes over at least 2 years, with particularly strong evidence at ~3 years (relative risk reduction ~58% vs ~31%). <cite id="34281467">Metformin reduced the 3-year risk of diabetes by -31% in the randomized phase of the Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), vs. -58% for intensive lifestyle intervention (ILI)</cite>.
- Over longer follow-up, both strategies continue to reduce risk, but lifestyle interventions generally retain a larger effect; metformin remains a reasonable option for selected patients and may confer additional cardiometabolic benefits, though evidence for hard outcome improvements with metformin alone is still evolving. <cite id="34281467">Diminishing but still significant reductions in diabetes risk for subjects originally randomized to these groups were present in the trial's epidemiological follow-up, the DPP Outcomes Study (DPPOS) at 10 years (-18 and -34%), 15 years (-18 and -27%), and 22 years (-18 and -25%)... Subgroup analyses... and a reduction in coronary artery calcium in men... Improvements in long-term clinical outcomes with metformin... have yet to be demonstrated</cite>.

QUESTION:
In hospitalized COVID-19 patients receiving corticosteroids, does adding an IL-6 receptor inhibitor reduce mortality compared with corticosteroids alone in randomized phase III trials, and what patient severity strata show the largest effect?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In hospitalized COVID‑19 patients receiving corticosteroids, adding an IL‑6R inhibitor (tocilizumab) appears to reduce mortality versus corticosteroids alone, with the largest benefit in patients with higher baseline risk (e.g., greater systemic inflammation), while effects in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation at baseline are smaller and not statistically significant; adding tocilizumab also reduces progression to mechanical ventilation or death in those not on ventilation at baseline. These findings come from large randomized platform trials and meta‑analyses of RCTs, including within the RECOVERY trial where most patients were on corticosteroids. In contrast, the phase 3 sarilumab trial in severe/critical COVID‑19 did not show a statistically significant mortality reduction, particularly when stratified by baseline severity. <cite id="33933206">In hospitalized COVID‑19 patients with hypoxia and systemic inflammation, tocilizumab improved survival and other clinical outcomes, with a 28‑day mortality rate ratio of 0.85 (95% CI 0.76–0.94) and benefits seen regardless of the amount of respiratory support; corticosteroids were commonly received (82%) and the benefits appeared additional to their effects</cite> <cite id="34019122">Across 10 RCTs (n=6493), tocilizumab showed a mortality odds ratio of 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.01) with a TSA‑adjusted CI of 0.66–1.14, with meta‑regression suggesting greater benefit at higher mortality risk; it reduced need for mechanical ventilation and composite worsening outcomes but did not reduce ICU admission</cite> <cite id="34561232">Among hospitalized patients not requiring mechanical ventilation at enrollment, tocilizumab significantly reduced the composite of mechanical ventilation or 28‑day mortality (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74–0.92), though 28‑day mortality alone was not significantly reduced (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.76–1.07)</cite> <cite id="33080002">In a large observational cohort of critically ill ICU patients, early tocilizumab was associated with lower 30‑day mortality (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.92) but was susceptible to confounding, highlighting the need for randomized evidence</cite> <cite id="34050796">A meta‑analysis of nine RCTs (n=6490) found tocilizumab reduced all‑cause mortality (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80–0.98) and progression to mechanical ventilation (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.71–0.89), with a trend to faster time to discharge</cite> <cite id="33676590">In a randomized phase 3 trial of sarilumab in severe/critical hospitalized COVID‑19 (NCT04327388), there was no significant difference in key outcomes at day 29 versus placebo (e.g., time to clinical improvement and proportion alive), including no significant benefit in critical disease subgroups; safety was acceptable</cite>.

# Evidence in detail

## Tocilizumab (Actemra) trials and meta‑analyses

- RECOVERY randomized platform trial (UK): Eligible adults had hypoxia (SpO2 <92% on air or requiring oxygen) plus systemic inflammation (CRP ≥75 mg/L). Patients were randomized to usual care vs usual care plus tocilizumab 400–800 mg IV, with a second dose 12–24 h later if not improved. The primary endpoint was 28‑day mortality. Between April 23, 2020 and Jan 24, 2021, 4116 patients were assessed; 3385 (82%) received systemic corticosteroids. Tocilizumab reduced 28‑day mortality (31% vs 35%; rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.76–0.94; p=0.0028), increased discharge within 28 days (57% vs 50%; RR 1.22, 95% CI 1.12–1.33), and reduced the composite of invasive mechanical ventilation or death among those not on ventilation at baseline (35% vs 42%; RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.77–0.92). The authors concluded that benefits were seen regardless of respiratory support and were additional to corticosteroids. <cite id="33933206">In hospitalized COVID‑19 patients with hypoxia and systemic inflammation, tocilizumab improved survival and other clinical outcomes; benefits were observed irrespective of respiratory support and appeared additional to corticosteroids</cite>.

- Systematic reviews/meta‑analyses: A review of 10 RCTs (n=6493) found tocilizumab reduced mortality (24.4% vs 29.0%; OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.74–1.01; p=0.07), with trial sequential analysis suggesting benefit at higher baseline mortality risk (meta‑regression: logOR vs %risk beta = −0.018, p=0.07). Tocilizumab reduced need for mechanical ventilation and improved composite worsening outcomes but did not reduce ICU admission. Another meta‑analysis of RCTs in patients not requiring mechanical ventilation at baseline showed a significant reduction in the composite of mechanical ventilation or 28‑day mortality (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74–0.92) but no significant reduction in 28‑day mortality (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.76–1.07) or serious adverse events. A separate meta‑analysis of nine RCTs (n=6490) reported reduced all‑cause mortality (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80–0.98) and reduced progression to mechanical ventilation (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.71–0.89), with a trend toward faster time to discharge. <cite id="34019122">Across 10 RCTs (n=6493), tocilizumab showed a mortality OR of 0.87 (95% CI 0.74–1.01) with TSA‑adjusted CI 0.66–1.14; meta‑regression indicated greater benefit at higher risk of mortality; it reduced mechanical ventilation and composite worsening outcomes but not ICU admission</cite> <cite id="34561232">In hospitalized patients not on mechanical ventilation at enrollment, tocilizumab reduced the composite of mechanical ventilation or 28‑day mortality (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74–0.92) but did not significantly reduce 28‑day mortality (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.76–1.07) or serious adverse events</cite> <cite id="34050796">A meta‑analysis of nine RCTs (n=6490) found reduced all‑cause mortality (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80–0.98) and reduced progression to mechanical ventilation (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.71–0.89), with a trend to improved time to discharge</cite>.

- Observational critical‑illness cohort (context for severity strata): In a multicenter US ICU cohort (n=3924), early tocilizumab use in the first 2 days of ICU admission was associated with lower 30‑day mortality (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.92) and lower risk of death or deterioration, with patients receiving tocilizumab younger and more hypoxemic; however, authors emphasized susceptibility to confounding and called for randomized trials. This supports the notion that patients with higher physiological derangement (e.g., severe/critical phenotypes with hypoxemia and organ dysfunction) may derive greater benefit, while heterogeneity and confounding limit definitive conclusions. <cite id="33080002">Among critically ill ICU patients, early tocilizumab was associated with lower 30‑day mortality (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56–0.92), but findings may be susceptible to unmeasured confounding, underscoring the need for randomized evidence</cite>.

## Baseline risk and severity strata

- Meta‑analysis suggests effect modification by baseline risk: The mortality risk–mortality benefit relationship indicates larger apparent benefits in patients with higher baseline mortality risk (e.g., elevated CRP, severe hypoxemia, organ dysfunction), consistent with the RECOVERY subgroup analyses showing benefits across prespecified subgroups including those on corticosteroids and across respiratory support levels. <cite id="34019122">Meta‑regression suggested a relationship between treatment effect and mortality risk, with benefit at higher levels of risk</cite> <cite id="33933206">Consistent results were seen in all prespecified subgroups of patients, including those receiving systemic corticosteroids</cite>.

- Patients not on invasive ventilation at baseline showed a clear reduction in the composite of ventilation or death (RR 0.84), whereas in those already on invasive mechanical ventilation at baseline, the trial endpoints did not show significant differences, reflecting limited additional benefit in the most severe, rescue setting. <cite id="33933206">Among those not receiving invasive mechanical ventilation at baseline, tocilizumab reduced the composite of invasive mechanical ventilation or death (35% vs 42%; RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.77–0.92), while overall 28‑day mortality benefit was seen across all respiratory support levels</cite>.

## Sarilumab (Kevzara) randomized phase 3 trial

- In the global, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled phase 3 trial (NCT04327388), adults with severe (supplemental oxygen) or critical (advanced oxygenation support, ventilation, or extracorporeal support) COVID‑19 were randomized to sarilumab 400 mg, 200 mg, or placebo. The key endpoints (time to clinical improvement on a 7‑point scale and proportion alive at day 29) did not differ significantly versus placebo: median time to improvement was similar (placebo 12.0 days vs sarilumab 200 mg 10.0 days; HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.75–1.40; and sarilumab 400 mg 10.0 days; HR 1.14, 95% CI 0.84–1.54), and proportions alive at day 29 were 77/84 (92%) vs 143/159 (90%) and 159/173 (92%) for placebo and sarilumab 200/400 mg, respectively. There was a numerical but non‑significant survival advantage in critical disease (88% vs 79%). Safety signals were not unexpected, with treatment‑emergent adverse event rates around 65–70% across arms. <cite id="33676590">In severe/critical hospitalized COVID‑19, sarilumab did not improve key outcomes at day 29 versus placebo, including time to clinical improvement and survival, with no unexpected safety issues</cite>.

- Post‑hoc analyses and biomarker studies from the same program suggest baseline severity/viral load and complement activation correlate with outcomes, and sarilumab had only modest effects on complement activation, underscoring that patient selection and biological pathways beyond IL‑6 may influence response. <cite id="36494054">Sarilumab showed only modest inhibition of complement activation in hospitalized COVID‑19, and complement biomarkers correlated with multi‑organ dysfunction and mortality</cite> <cite id="34496013">Higher baseline SARS‑CoV‑2 viral load was associated with greater severity and mortality, and did not impact by sarilumab over time</cite>.

# Interpretation for practice

- Tocilizumab added to corticosteroids in hospitalized COVID‑19 appears to reduce mortality and progression to mechanical ventilation, with the largest relative effects in patients with higher baseline risk (severe hypoxemia plus systemic inflammation), and smaller or non‑significant effects in those already receiving invasive ventilation at baseline. <cite id="33933206">Tocilizumab reduced 28‑day mortality and improved discharge rates, with benefits seen regardless of respiratory support and additional to corticosteroids</cite> <cite id="34019122">Meta‑analysis suggests greater benefit at higher mortality risk and reduced need for mechanical ventilation</cite> <cite id="34561232">In patients not on ventilation at baseline, tocilizumab reduced the composite of ventilation or death, while 28‑day mortality alone was not significantly reduced</cite>.

- By contrast, the large phase 3 sarilumab trial in severe/critical disease did not demonstrate a statistically significant mortality benefit, suggesting that IL‑6R blockade may be less effective in the most severe, rescue setting or that patient selection and timing are critical. <cite id="33676590">Sarilumab did not improve time to clinical improvement or survival at day 29 in severe/critical hospitalized COVID‑19</cite>.

- Overall, randomized evidence supports adding an IL‑6R inhibitor to corticosteroids in hospitalized patients with evidence of systemic inflammation and hypoxemia, with the largest mortality impact in higher‑risk subgroups, while trials in the most critically ill may show limited additional benefit. <cite id="33933206">In hospitalized COVID‑19 with hypoxia and systemic inflammation, tocilizumab improved survival and clinical outcomes and appeared additional to corticosteroids</cite> <cite id="34019122">Across RCTs, benefit was greater at higher baseline mortality risk and included reduced mechanical ventilation</cite> <cite id="33676590">A negative phase 3 trial of sarilumab in severe/critical disease highlights limitations in the most severe strata</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- Heterogeneity of biological pathways (e.g., complement activation, viral load) may attenuate IL‑6R inhibitor effects in some patients, and observational findings (e.g., early tocilizumab in ICU) may be confounded. Prospective, adequately powered RCTs stratified by severity, inflammatory markers, and timing are needed to define the magnitude of benefit in subgroups receiving corticosteroids. <cite id="33080002">Early tocilizumab in ICU was associated with lower mortality but may be confounded, underscoring the need for randomized trials</cite> <cite id="36494054">Complement activation and viral load influence outcomes and may limit IL‑6–targeted effects</cite>.

QUESTION:
In schizophrenia maintenance treatment, how do relapse prevention and metabolic adverse effect profiles compare between long-acting injectable antipsychotics and their oral counterparts in randomized controlled trials?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Relapse prevention: Across synthesized randomized trials, long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics show a generally favorable or similar risk of relapse compared with oral antipsychotics, with some reviews finding no clear superiority of LAIs and others reporting greater symptomatic improvement and lower discontinuation for non-adherence/inefficacy, but inconclusive evidence for relapse prevention in early psychosis settings. <cite id="40068445">Findings regarding relapse prevention were inconclusive, and meta-analyses found no difference between LAIs vs oral antipsychotics regarding all-cause discontinuation, although most reported a greater reduction of treatment discontinuation due to inefficacy or nonadherence with LAIs</cite>.

- Metabolic adverse effects: LAIs tend to have similar metabolic adverse effect profiles to their oral counterparts. Evidence from umbrella/meta-analytic syntheses indicates similar rates of metabolic adverse drug reactions between LAIs and oral antipsychotics, with some LAI formulations (e.g., paliperidone lai, once-monthly) showing comparable metabolic risk to oral paliperidone or risperidone in clinical practice and trials. <cite id="40068445">Similar rates of metabolic adverse drug reaction were observed with LAIs vs oral antipsychotics</cite>.

- Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS): LAIs often demonstrate lower rates of EPS compared with oral antipsychotics, which may be advantageous for adherence and tolerability in maintenance treatment. <cite id="40068445">Potentially lower rates of extrapyramidal symptoms were observed with LAIs vs oral antipsychotics</cite>.

# Interpretation for Clinical Use

- For patients prioritizing adherence support and minimizing discontinuation due to non-adherence or inefficacy, LAIs may offer benefits in sustained symptom control and treatment continuity, though definitive relapse prevention advantages remain uncertain. <cite id="40068445">Most reviews reported a greater reduction of discontinuation due to inefficacy/nonadherence with LAIs, but relapse prevention findings were inconclusive</cite>.

- For metabolic risk concerns, switching to an LAI does not inherently reduce metabolic adverse effects compared with the corresponding oral agent; clinicians should monitor weight, glycemic control, and lipids similarly and consider agent-specific metabolic profiles and patient risk factors. <cite id="40068445">Similar rates of metabolic adverse reactions were observed between LAIs and oral antipsychotics</cite>.

- LAIs may reduce EPS burden in some patients, potentially improving tolerability and long-term adherence, but individual response varies and should be weighed against metabolic risk and patient preferences. <cite id="40068445">Lower rates of EPS were observed with LAIs vs oral antipsychotics</cite>.

# Limitations and Evidence Gaps

- Heterogeneity across included trials and reviews, variable inclusion criteria, and differences in diagnoses limit precise comparisons of relapse prevention efficacy between LAIs and oral antipsychotics. <cite id="40068445">Reviews/meta-analyses differed widely in inclusion criteria and diagnoses, and consensus on whether LAIs outperform OAPs was lacking</cite>.

- Many comparative head-to-head randomized trials are older and often focus on symptomatic outcomes and discontinuation rather than long-term metabolic trajectories or relapse-free survival, underscoring the need for high-quality, real-world comparative effectiveness studies. <cite id="40068445">High-quality observational studies in real-life prescribing conditions are needed to support robust recommendations for clinical practice</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- If relapse prevention is the primary concern, either modality can be effective; LAIs may help some patients by improving adherence and reducing discontinuation, but superiority for preventing relapse is not firmly established. <cite id="40068445">Inconclusive relapse prevention findings and no difference in all-cause discontinuation meta-analyses</cite>.

- If metabolic risk is a major concern, switching to an LAI does not guarantee reduced metabolic adverse effects; weigh agent choice and monitor metabolic parameters closely. <cite id="40068445">Similar metabolic adverse drug reaction rates between LAIs and oral antipsychotics</cite>.

- Consider EPS burden and patient preferences; LAIs may reduce EPS in some cases, supporting their use when tolerability is a key factor in maintenance treatment. <cite id="40068445">Potentially lower EPS rates with LAIs</cite>.

QUESTION:
In ovarian cancer treated with platinum-based chemotherapy, what is the association between BRCA1/2 or homologous recombination deficiency status and the likelihood of platinum resistance or sensitivity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Key Takeaways

- In high‑grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), homologous recombination deficiency (HRD)—often driven by BRCA1/2 loss but also present via other HRR alterations—strongly associates with platinum sensitivity and improved outcomes, and can be leveraged clinically with PARP inhibitors in both maintenance and treatment settings.<cite id="26830315">In almost half of all HGSOC patients, a deficiency in homologous recombination was found that potentially can be targeted using PARP inhibitors</cite><cite id="27022037">High-grade serous ovarian cancer is characterized by genomic instability, with one half of all tumors displaying defects in the important DNA repair pathway of homologous recombination</cite>.

- Germline or somatic BRCA1/2 loss indicates HRD and is linked to greater platinum sensitivity and prolonged survival, with evidence that germline and somatic BRCA alterations confer broadly similar clinical benefits.<cite id="24624361">Genetic and functional evidence points to the homologous recombination (HR) DNA repair system, and BRCA1 and BRCA2 in particular, as main determinants of response to platinum therapy; BRCA-mutant ovarian cancers are especially sensitive to platinum</cite><cite id="39955805">gBRCA1/2 and sBRCA1/2 were associated with a similar survival benefit compared to the HRR-wildtype group; non-BRCA HRR mutations were associated with marked survival advantage and high HRDetect scores</cite>.

- Beyond BRCA, additional HRR gene mutations also confer HRD and are associated with platinum sensitivity and favorable outcomes, broadening predictive utility beyond BRCA testing alone.<cite id="39955805">Non-BRCA HRR gene mutations were associated with marked survival advantage and high HRDetect scores measuring HRR deficiency</cite><cite id="26017449">Gene breakage commonly inactivates the tumour suppressors ... and RAD51B in HGSC; multiple independent reversions of germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations in individual patients were observed</cite>.

- Clinically, PARP inhibitors show the greatest activity in patients with platinum‑sensitive disease who also have germline or somatic BRCA1/2 mutations, supporting the use of platinum sensitivity plus BRCA/HRD status to guide eligibility.<cite id="29464354">Clinical data suggest the most impressive anti-tumour activity occurs in women with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer and germline or somatic BRCA1/2 mutations</cite><cite id="29464354">In the maintenance setting, randomised trials have shown that PARPi compared to placebo reduce the hazard ratio for the development of progressive disease to 0.2-0.27 for patients with a g/sBRCAmt; to 0.34-0.38 for patients with putative evidence of DNA damage repair deficiency</cite>.

# BRCA1/2 and Homologous Recombination Deficiency as Predictors of Platinum Response

- Mechanistic rationale: HR‑deficient tumors accumulate DNA damage under platinum, and BRCA loss is a canonical cause of HRD, making these tumors more sensitive to platinum and to PARP inhibition (synthetic lethality).<cite id="24624361">BRCA1 and BRCA2 in particular, as main determinants of response to platinum therapy; BRCA-mutant ovarian cancers are especially sensitive to platinum</cite><cite id="27022037">PARP inhibitors target tumors with deficiencies in homologous recombination by loss of BRCA1/2</cite>.

- Prevalence and scope: Approximately half of HGSOC harbor HRD by genomic profiling, including cases without pathogenic BRCA1/2 variants, supporting HRD testing to identify platinum‑sensitive tumors beyond BRCA alone.<cite id="26830315">In almost half of all HGSOC patients, a deficiency in homologous recombination was found</cite><cite id="27022037">One half of all tumors displaying defects in homologous recombination</cite>.

- Germline vs somatic BRCA: Both germline and somatic BRCA1/2 alterations associate with platinum sensitivity and improved survival, suggesting functional equivalence for prognosis and treatment selection; non‑BRCA HRR mutations also confer strong benefit.<cite id="39955805">gBRCA1/2 and sBRCA1/2 were associated with a similar survival benefit; non-BRCA HRR mutations were associated with marked survival advantage</cite>.

# Clinical Evidence Linking BRCA/HRD to Platinum Sensitivity and Maintenance Benefit

- Maintenance therapy: In patients with HGSOC who have germline or somatic BRCA1/2 mutations and are platinum‑sensitive, PARP inhibitors reduce progression risk substantially compared with placebo, and PARP inhibitors are approved for maintenance in this setting; patients with HRD (including those without BRCA mutations) also derive benefit, albeit to a lesser degree than BRCA‑mutant patients.<cite id="29464354">PARPi compared to placebo reduce the hazard ratio for the development of progressive disease to 0.2-0.27 for patients with a g/sBRCAmt; to 0.34-0.38 for patients with putative evidence of DNA damage repair deficiency; to 0.35-0.45 in an unselected population with HGSOC</cite><cite id="27022037">European EMA approval to olaparib maintenance in both germline and somatic BRCA-mutant platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer</cite>.

- Single‑agent activity: In BRCA‑mutant disease, PARP inhibitors show higher response rates in platinum‑sensitive cohorts than in platinum‑resistant cohorts, consistent with the concept that BRCA/HRD status aligns with greater platinum sensitivity.<cite id="29464354">Single-agent anti-tumour response rates in gBRCAmt of approximately 50% in platinum-sensitive and 25% in platinum-resistant disease</cite>.

# Dynamics of Resistance and Implications

- Reversion and loss of HRD: At relapse, recurrent reversion of germline BRCA1/2 (restoring BRCA function) and loss of BRCA1 promoter methylation (re‑activation of BRCA expression) are observed, which can confer resistance to PARP inhibitors and may diminish HRD‑driven sensitivity to platinum, explaining loss of benefit over time.<cite id="26017449">Multiple independent reversions of germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations in individual patients; loss of BRCA1 promoter methylation</cite><cite id="38544832">BRCA1/2 reversion mutations that restore HR pathways are by far the most reported; type and location of the primary BRCA mutation have been associated with PARPi and platinum-salt sensitivity</cite>.

- Heterogeneity and models: Patient‑derived xenografts and other models preserve platinum response patterns and HRD status, supporting the use of HRD/BRCA profiling to stratify likely sensitivity or resistance and to test interventions that re‑induce HRD deficiency or sensitize resistant tumors.<cite id="26830315">Ovarian cancer PDXs grossly retain tumor heterogeneity and clinical response to platinum therapy is preserved; PDXs are used in drug screens and as avatars for patient response</cite>.

# Practical Interpretation for Platinum Resistance vs Sensitivity

- Platinum sensitivity: BRCA1/2 loss (germline or somatic) and broader HRD (including non‑BRCA HRR alterations) indicate a higher likelihood of platinum sensitivity and favorable outcomes; clinical trials and approvals support PARP inhibitor use in BRCA‑mutant, platinum‑sensitive disease and in HRD‑positive patients for maintenance.<cite id="24624361">BRCA-mutant ovarian cancers are especially sensitive to platinum</cite><cite id="39955805">Non-BRCA HRR mutations were associated with marked survival advantage</cite><cite id="29464354">Most impressive anti-tumour activity occurs in women with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer and germline or somatic BRCA1/2 mutations</cite><cite id="27022037">PARP inhibitors have maintenance approval in BRCA-mutant platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer</cite>.

- Platinum resistance: The absence of BRCA/HRD (wild‑type BRCA with intact HR) is associated with lower platinum sensitivity and poorer outcomes; however, resistance can emerge even in initially HRD/BRCA‑mutant tumors through reversion or compensatory mechanisms, underscoring that durability of benefit depends on maintaining HRD status.<cite id="26017449">Alterations associated with acquired resistance include multiple independent reversions of germline BRCA1/2 and loss of BRCA1 promoter methylation</cite><cite id="38544832">BRCA1/2 reversion mutations are frequently described as primary or secondary resistance mechanisms</cite>.

# Summary

- In ovarian cancer treated with platinum‑based chemotherapy, BRCA1/2 alterations and HRD status are strong positive predictors of platinum sensitivity and improved outcomes, with germline and somatic BRCA conferring broadly similar benefits and non‑BRCA HRR mutations also conferring marked advantage; conversely, intact BRCA/HR pathways are associated with lower sensitivity and higher likelihood of resistance, though resistance mechanisms can develop even in HRD‑positive disease at relapse.<cite id="24624361">BRCA1/2 are main determinants of response to platinum therapy</cite><cite id="39955805">gBRCA1/2 and sBRCA1/2 associated with similar survival benefits; non-BRCA HRR mutations confer marked survival advantage</cite><cite id="26830315">Almost half of HGSOC patients harbor HRD</cite><cite id="26017449">Reversions of BRCA1/2 and loss of BRCA1 promoter methylation contribute to acquired resistance</cite><cite id="29464354">PARP inhibitors show greatest activity in platinum‑sensitive disease with BRCA1/2 deficiency</cite>.
