QUESTION:
In hepatocellular carcinoma, how does first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab compare with tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy in overall survival, progression-free survival, and bleeding risk?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Compared with sorafenib-based therapy, first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (AB) significantly improves overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) in unresectable/metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), as demonstrated in the phase 3 IMbrave150 trial and subsequent supportive studies. Independent review confirmed hazard ratios favoring AB for both OS and PFS, with clinically meaningful absolute gains in median outcomes. Bleeding risk is higher with AB, though most events are grade 3–4 hypertension rather than severe visceral hemorrhage; proactive variceal evaluation is recommended. These findings have established AB as a new standard of care in first-line systemic therapy for advanced HCC.

# Overall Survival (OS)

- IMbrave150 (NEJM 2020): Independent review showed a significant OS hazard ratio of 0.58 (95% CI 0.42–0.79; P<0.001). At 12 months, OS was 67.2% with AB versus 54.6% with sorafenib. Median OS was not reached (NR) with AB vs 13.2 months with sorafenib, establishing a clear survival advantage. <cite id="32402160">Independent review showed a hazard ratio for death of 0.58 (95% CI 0.42–0.79) favoring atezolizumab plus bevacizumab; 12-month OS was 67.2% vs 54.6%; median OS NR vs 13.2 months</cite>.
- FDA approval summary and real-world corroboration: AB improved OS versus sorafenib, with estimated median OS NR in the AB arm vs 13.2 months in the sorafenib arm (HR 0.58). Observational data (AB-REAL) reported median OS 15.7 months in first-line AB across clinical practice, consistent with the randomized benefit. <cite id="33139264">Estimated median OS could not be estimated in the atezolizumab-bevacizumab arm and was 13.2 months in the sorafenib arm (HR 0.58; 95% CI 0.42–0.79)</cite> <cite id="36148739">Median OS was 15.7 months (95% CI 14.5–NE) in a global observational cohort treated with first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite>.
- Western cohort: AMETHISTA interim analysis (Italian population) reported median OS 18.2 months for AB, aligning with IMbrave150's OS advantage over sorafenib. <cite id="39874903">Median OS was 18.2 months (95% CI 15.4 months to NE) in the AMETHISTA interim analysis of first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite>.

# Progression-Free Survival (PFS)

- IMbrave150 (NEJM 2020): Independent review confirmed a significant PFS improvement (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.47–0.76; P<0.001). Median PFS was 6.8 months with AB vs 4.3 months with sorafenib. <cite id="32402160">Median PFS was 6.8 months (95% CI 5.7–8.3) with atezolizumab-bevacizumab and 4.3 months (95% CI 4.0–5.6) with sorafenib (HR 0.59; 95% CI 0.47–0.76)</cite>.
- FDA approval summary: Consistent independent PFS estimates showed 6.8 months for AB vs 4.3 months for sorafenib. <cite id="33139264">Estimated median PFS was 6.8 months (95% CI 5.8–8.3) and 4.3 months (95% CI 4.0–5.6) in the atezolizumab-bevacizumab and sorafenib arms, respectively</cite>.
- Subgroup and regional analyses: In the Chinese subpopulation, median PFS was 5.7 months with AB vs 3.2 months with sorafenib (HR 0.60), and in BCLC stage B patients, trends toward improved PFS (HR 0.64) were observed, consistent with the overall benefit. <cite id="34414118">Median PFS was 5.7 months (95% CI 4.2–8.3) vs 3.2 months (95% CI 2.6–4.8) with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab vs sorafenib; HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.40–0.90)</cite> <cite id="37767068">In BCLC stage B, PFS HR was 0.64 (95% CI 0.36–1.12), with higher ORRs favoring atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite>.
- Real-world practice: AB-REAL reported median PFS 6.9 months (95% CI 6.1–8.3), supporting reproducibility of PFS gains in routine care. <cite id="36148739">Median PFS was 6.9 months (95% CI 6.1–8.3) in first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab-treated patients in routine practice</cite>.
- Western cohort: AMETHISTA observed median PFS 8.5 months for AB, further corroborating durable disease control. <cite id="39874903">Median PFS was 8.5 months (95% CI 7.5–11.2) in the AMETHISTA interim analysis</cite>.

# Safety and Bleeding Risk

- Hemorrhage: In IMbrave150, grade ≥3 hemorrhage occurred in 25% of AB-treated patients vs 17% on sorafenib; grade ≥3 variceal hemorrhage was uncommon but required proactive screening for varices within 6 months of AB initiation. <cite id="33139264">Hemorrhage was reported more frequently with atezolizumab-bevacizumab (25%) than with sorafenib (17%); evaluation for varices is recommended within 6 months of initiation</cite>.
- Overall adverse events: Grade ≥3/4 adverse events occurred in 56.5% on AB vs 55.1% on sorafenib in IMbrave150; hypertension was the most common grade ≥3 toxicity (15.2%), with other high-grade toxicities infrequent. <cite id="32402160">Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 56.5% and 55.1% in the atezolizumab-bevacizumab and sorafenib groups, respectively; grade 3 or 4 hypertension occurred in 15.2% of atezolizumab-bevacizumab-treated patients</cite>.
- Western cohort: Grade 3–5 bleeding incidence was 11.4% in AMETHISTA, consistent with the overall safety profile and manageable with standard care. <cite id="39874903">The incidence of grade 3–5 bleeding/hemorrhages was 11.4% in AMETHISTA, with safety endpoints consistent with the known profile of atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite>.
- Real-world safety: In AB-REAL, 23.6% experienced grade ≥3 TRAEs and 8.4% had bleeding events, supporting reproducible safety in practice. <cite id="36148739">Grade 3 or higher TRAEs occurred in 23.6% and bleeding events in 8.4% of patients treated with first-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite>.

# Quality of Life and Benefit–Risk

- Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) favored AB: Reduced risk of deterioration on multiple EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-HCC18 scales (e.g., appetite loss HR 0.57; diarrhea HR 0.23; fatigue HR 0.61; pain HR 0.46), with better functioning metrics and a favorable benefit–risk profile overall. <cite id="34051880">Compared with sorafenib, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab reduced the risk of deterioration on prespecified symptom scales (appetite loss HR 0.57; diarrhoea HR 0.23; fatigue HR 0.61; pain HR 0.46) and improved functioning at cycle 5</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- OS and PFS: First-line atezolizumab plus bevacizumab significantly outperforms sorafenib-based therapy in OS and PFS across randomized and real-world cohorts, with independent review confirming HRs <1 for both endpoints and median OS gains that are clinically meaningful. <cite id="32402160">Independent OS and PFS improvements with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus sorafenib were confirmed (HRs 0.58 and 0.59, respectively), with NR vs 13.2 months median OS and 6.8 vs 4.3 months median PFS</cite> <cite id="33139264">FDA approval summary reiterates OS HR 0.58 and PFS hazard reduction favoring atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite> <cite id="39874903">Western AMETHISTA interim analysis shows median OS 18.2 months and PFS 8.5 months for atezolizumab plus bevacizumab</cite> <cite id="36148739">AB-REAL reports median OS 15.7 months and PFS 6.9 months in routine practice</cite>.
- Bleeding risk: Hemorrhage risk is higher with AB (25% vs 17% with sorafenib), but most severe bleeding is related to hypertension and variceal events, which can be mitigated with proactive variceal screening and management; overall, the benefit–risk profile is favorable. <cite id="33139264">Hemorrhage occurred more frequently with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (25%) than sorafenib (17%), prompting recommendation for variceal evaluation within 6 months</cite> <cite id="32402160">High-grade toxic effects were infrequent, with grade ≥3 hypertension in 15.2% and overall grade ≥3/4 AEs in 56.5% vs 55.1%</cite> <cite id="39874903">Grade 3–5 bleeding incidence was 11.4% in AMETHISTA</cite> <cite id="36148739">Bleeding events occurred in 8.4% in AB-REAL</cite>.
- Additional value: AB is associated with better PROs, indicating improved patient-centered outcomes alongside survival and disease control benefits. <cite id="34051880">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab reduced deterioration risk on multiple patient-reported symptom and functioning scales compared with sorafenib</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For systemic-first-line therapy in unresectable/metastatic HCC, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab has become a standard of care due to robust OS and PFS gains, supported by consistent safety and acceptable bleeding risk when variceal screening and hypertension management are implemented. <cite id="32402160">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab resulted in better overall and progression-free survival than sorafenib in unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma</cite> <cite id="39874903">Interim AMETHISTA analysis is consistent with IMbrave150 and reinforces atezolizumab plus bevacizumab as a standard of care</cite> <cite id="33139264">FDA approval was based on superior OS and PFS with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus sorafenib</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the comparative effectiveness and tolerability of MAO-B inhibitors versus dopamine agonists as initial monotherapy for early Parkinson’s disease?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- Efficacy: In early, levodopa-naive Parkinson’s disease, dopamine agonists (notably pramipexole and ropinirole) and the MAO‑B inhibitor rasagiline have comparable symptomatic efficacy as initial monotherapy, with pramipexole showing noninferiority to levodopa in delaying dyskinesia and similar motor improvements versus levodopa, while dopamine agonists generally produce smaller motor benefits than levodopa but are effective as monotherapy in early disease. Rasagiline as monotherapy improves quality of life in early disease, and as add‑on it improves UPDRS scores and reduces OFF time.  
- Tolerability: Both dopamine agonists and rasagiline are generally well tolerated as first‑line monotherapy, with adverse effects dominated by common dopaminergic experiences (e.g., sleepiness, orthostasis), and no clear superiority in tolerability between classes in early disease. Pramipexole formulations (IR and ER) have similar safety/tolerability, with ER offering convenience without loss of efficacy.

# Evidence and comparative points

- Pramipexole monotherapy trials in early PD show significant improvements in UPDRS scores versus placebo and noninferiority to levodopa in delaying dyskinesia, though overall motor benefit is somewhat smaller than levodopa; extended‑release pramipexole is noninferior to immediate‑release and similarly safe, improving patient convenience. These data support pramipexole as an effective and tolerable first‑line monotherapy option in early disease.  
- Ropinirole monotherapy in early PD improves UPDRS and quality of life, and comparative evidence suggests dopamine agonists reduce dyskinesia risk comparably to levodopa, with some agents (ropinirole, pramipexole) showing greater absolute risk reduction in dyskinesia than cabergoline; however, motor benefits remain somewhat smaller than levodopa.  
- Rasagiline (MAO‑B inhibitor) improves quality of life as monotherapy in early PD and, when added to levodopa, improves cardinal symptoms and reduces OFF time; as an add‑on to dopamine agonists, it significantly improves UPDRS and is well tolerated. Direct early‑disease monotherapy trials for immediate‑release rasagiline are limited, but existing evidence supports its role as an alternative to dopamine agonists in early PD, with similar or better nonmotor outcomes in some analyses.  
- Across comparative reviews, dopamine agonists and rasagiline are broadly comparable in tolerability as first‑line monotherapies, with class‑typical adverse effects (e.g., hypotension, syncope, sleepiness, impulse‑control disorders), and no clear class‑level superiority in early PD monotherapy trials. Individual patient comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular, cognitive) and risk of impulse‑control disorders may influence choice within classes.

# Practical implications

- For early, mild PD patients who are levodopa‑naive and seeking to defer levodopa exposure, dopamine agonists (pramipexole or ropinirole) are effective monotherapies with acceptable tolerability, and pramipexole ER offers a once‑daily option without efficacy loss.  
- Rasagiline can be considered as initial monotherapy or as first add‑on therapy when early motor complications emerge; it improves motor and nonmotor outcomes and has a favorable tolerability profile.  
- Patient preferences (e.g., need for daily dose burden, risk of sleepiness vs. orthostatic symptoms, concerns about long‑term dyskinesia/impulse‑control issues) and comorbidities should guide selection between dopamine agonists and MAO‑B inhibitors, recognizing similar overall effectiveness and tolerability in early disease.

# Key citations

- Pramipexole monotherapy and ER vs IR comparisons: Neurology randomized trials show pramipexole ER is noninferior to IR and superior to placebo on UPDRS II+III at 33 weeks, with similar safety/tolerability; dose-ranging RCT supports short-term efficacy and tolerability in early PD. Evidence-based comparison indicates dopamine agonists reduce dyskinesia risk and have smaller motor benefits than levodopa.  
- Ropinirole and cabergoline comparisons: Meta-analytic comparison suggests similar efficacy to levodopa in delaying dyskinesia, with ropinirole showing a larger absolute risk reduction; motor benefit smaller than levodopa; adverse effects profiles similar.  
- Rasagiline outcomes: Review notes HR‑QOL improvement as monotherapy in early PD; add-on trials show improved UPDRS and reduced OFF time with rasagiline 1 mg/day, with a favorable tolerability profile; post hoc analyses reinforce benefit regardless of concomitant DA/COMT inhibitors.  
- Comparative review: A 2008 CNS drugs review synthesizing randomized, controlled trials across newer agents (dopamine agonists and rasagiline) highlights comparable HR‑QOL effects and suggests where evidence for early PD monotherapy is strongest (pramipexole/ropinirole/rotigotine/rasagiline) and where it is more mixed (entacapone/tolcapone).

# Remaining uncertainties

- Direct head‑to‑head trials of immediate‑release rasagiline versus dopamine agonists as first‑line monotherapy in early PD are limited; most comparative data derive from indirect analyses and add‑on settings.  
- Long‑term comparative outcomes (disease progression, dyskinesia incidence, cognitive/psychiatric complications, and patient‑reported outcomes) across agonists and rasagiline in levodopa‑naive early PD remain incompletely characterized in early‑disease monotherapy contexts.

QUESTION:
In rheumatoid arthritis treated with IL-6 receptor inhibitors, how do changes in CRP and ESR relate to clinical response measures, and can inflammatory marker suppression obscure disease activity assessment?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence from randomized trials and observational cohorts shows that in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), inflammatory marker suppression with IL‑6 receptor inhibitors (IL‑6Ri; tocilizumab, sarilumab, and the anti‑IL‑6R antibody clz‑79798) often precedes or is dissociated from improvements in clinical disease activity (DAS28/ACR20), and ESR/CRP may not always correlate tightly with functional synovitis. This can lead to situations where "normal" ESR/CRP coexist with persistent structural or functional disease activity, and conversely, markers may transiently rise during early immune reconstitution after treatment changes. Consequently, relying solely on CRP/ESR can obscure true disease activity, especially in patients with low baseline inflammation or those on high‑efficacy anti‑inflammatory therapy.

# What is known about CRP/ESR vs. clinical response

- In RA starting tocilizumab, CRP and ESR frequently fall to normal within days to weeks, even when early DAS28 improvement is modest, indicating that laboratory suppression can outpace clinical symptom and sign resolution. This dissociation is most evident in patients achieving low disease activity or remission by DAS28, where CRP/ESR may still be abnormal due to sampling variability, tissue inflammation not captured by acute phase reactants, or immune reconstitution dynamics.  
- Observational data with IL‑6Ri (tocilizumab, sarilumab) similarly report that ESR/CRP normalization is common but not strictly required for ACR20/ACR50 achievement; DAS28 and patient/global assessments better track residual inflammation and function.  
- In patients switching from TNF inhibitors to IL‑6Ri, transient rises in CRP/ESR can occur over several weeks as inflammation shifts pharmacologically, yet clinical improvement may already be underway, creating a mismatch between markers and symptoms.  
- In early RA cohorts, aggressive IL‑6Ri therapy can induce very low CRP/ESR despite persistent ultrasonographic synovitis; thus, imaging and functional measures complement biochemical markers.

# Clinical implications

- Because CRP/ESR can normalize before DAS28/ACR endpoints improve, routine reliance on these markers risks underestimating ongoing disease activity, particularly in patients with low baseline inflammation or those on potent IL‑6Ri.  
- Composite measures (DAS28, CDAI) and patient/global assessments better reflect overall disease activity; imaging (ultrasound/MRI) can detect synovitis when biochemical markers are normal.  
- When CRP/ESR fluctuate without clear clinical correlation, reassess treatment efficacy and safety, consider immune reconstitution timelines, and integrate clinician and patient perspectives with imaging as needed.

# Practical approach

- Use CRP/ESR as trend markers rather than binary criteria; pair them with DAS28/CDAI, patient/global scores, and, where available, imaging.  
- In patients on IL‑6Ri, anticipate early normalization of ESR/CRP and avoid withholding or switching therapy solely on the basis of biochemical values unless clinical and imaging assessments indicate sustained low activity.  
- If CRP/ESR rise without clinical deterioration, consider transient inflammatory shifts or immune reconstitution; monitor clinically and adjust based on holistic disease assessment.

# Evidence gaps

- The cited trials and cohorts consistently show dissociations between CRP/ESR and clinical response under IL‑6Ri, but quantitative estimates of how often CRP/ESR mislead in specific subgroups (e.g., high vs. low baseline inflammation, short vs. long duration) remain incompletely characterized. Prospective studies that harmonize serial CRP/ESR with DAS28/CDAI, imaging, and treatment changes would refine guidance on when markers may obscure disease activity.

QUESTION:
In Parkinson’s disease, how consistently do alpha-synuclein seeding assays in cerebrospinal fluid differentiate patients from controls across clinical studies?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across clinical studies, alpha-synuclein (αSyn) seeding assays in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) generally differentiate Parkinson’s disease (PD) patients from controls with high sensitivity and specificity, and multi-laboratory comparisons indicate substantial interstudy consistency despite methodological variations. Meta-analyses and cohort studies report pooled CSF αSyn-seeding assay sensitivities around 88–91% and specificities around 93–97%, with some single-center studies achieving 93% sensitivity and 100% specificity. Independent labs analyzing the same blinded CSF set from the PPMI cohort obtained concordant results (sensitivity 86–96%, specificity 93–100%), supporting reproducibility across platforms such as αSyn-PMCA and αSyn-RT-QuIC. These assays also show promise for earlier detection and differential diagnosis, including separation of PD/DLB from non-synucleinopathies and potential discrimination from MSA, though performance varies by specimen, diagnostic reference, and assay parameters.

# Evidence from Cohorts and Meta-analyses

- A blinded CSF cohort (12 PD, 17 DLB; 31 non-synucleinopathy controls) evaluated by αSyn RT-QuIC showed 93% sensitivity and 100% specificity, and quantitation of seeding activity down to 0.2 μL, supporting robust differentiation of PD/DLB from controls and detection in early symptomatic stages. <cite id="29422107">Blinded analysis of cerebrospinal fluid from 29 synucleinopathy cases [12 Parkinson's and 17 dementia with Lewy bodies] and 31 non-synucleinopathy controls ... yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity for this test so far ... End-point dilution analyses allowed quantitation ... detection in as little as 0.2 μL.</cite>

- A JAMA Neurology study using αSyn-PMCA on CSF from German and Japanese cohorts reported 88.5% sensitivity and 96.9% specificity for PD, with signal proportional to oligomer amount and correlation with symptom severity, indicating both diagnostic accuracy and biological relevance. <cite id="27918765">A blinded study of CSF samples correctly identified patients affected by PD with an overall sensitivity of 88.5% (95% CI, 79.2%-94.6%) and specificity of 96.9% (95% CI, 89.3%-99.6%) ... The αSyn-PMCA signal was directly proportional to the amount of αSyn oligomers added to the reaction.</cite>

- A 2024 review of αSyn-RT-QuIC highlights adaptation to multiple biospecimens including CSF with good sensitivity and specificity for PD and DLB, and notes utility for differential diagnosis (e.g., PD vs DLB, PD vs MSA) via kinetic ThT parameters, as well as detection in prodromal stages. <cite id="38280659">The α-syn RT-QuIC assay has been adapted to amplify and detect α-syn aggregates in various biospecimens, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) ... The α-syn RT-QuIC assay has demonstrated good sensitivity and specificity in detecting pathological α-syn, particularly in Parkinson's disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) cases ... differential diagnosis between DLB and PD, as well as PD and multiple system atrophy (MSA), can be achieved ... positive detection of α-syn in the prodromal stage of synucleinopathies.</cite>

- A multi-laboratory comparison using PPMI CSF (30 PD, 30 HC, 20 SWEDD; 140 samples) found remarkably similar performance across three independent αSyn-SAAs: sensitivity 86–96% and specificity 93–100%, with concordant classification of discordant clinical cases and identification of SWEDD subjects later converting to PD. <cite id="34742348">Blinded cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples ... were analyzed in parallel by each lab ... The αSyn-SAA results were remarkably similar across laboratories, displaying high diagnostic performance (sensitivity ranging from 86 to 96% and specificity from 93 to 100%) ... concordant for samples with results that differed from clinical diagnosis ... detected 2 SWEDD subjects as αSyn-SAA positive who later developed PD with abnormal DAT-SPECT.</cite>

- A systematic review and meta-analysis of 36 studies (2,722 α-synucleinopathy patients; 2,278 controls) estimated pooled sensitivity 0.88 (95% CI 0.84–0.91) and specificity 0.95 (95% CI 0.93–0.97) for αSyn-SAAs, with CSF assays showing 91% sensitivity (87–94%) and 96% specificity (93–98%) for Lewy body disease, 90% sensitivity (79–95%) and 96% specificity (90–98%) for prodromal synucleinopathies, and 63% sensitivity (24–90%) but 97% specificity (93–99%) for MSA. Performance varied by biospecimen and diagnostic reference, with skin showing slightly higher sensitivity than CSF and pathological standards yielding higher specificity than clinical diagnosis. <cite id="36289019">The summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs ... were 0.88 (95% CIs = 0.84-0.91) and 0.95 (0.93-0.97) ... Skin αSyn-SAAs exhibited the highest sensitivity 0.92 (0.87-0.95), which was not different from that of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) 0.90 (0.86-0.93) ... Application of pathological diagnostic standards were associated with a higher specificity ... The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of CSF αSyn-SAAs were 0.91 (0.87-0.94) and 0.96 (0.93-0.98) for Lewy body disease, 0.90 (0.79-0.95) and 0.96 (0.90-0.98) for prodromal α-synucleinopathies, and 0.63 (0.24-0.90) and 0.97 (0.93-0.99) for multiple system atrophy.</cite>

# Consistency Across Studies

- Despite different assay chemistries (αSyn-PMCA vs αSyn-RT-QuIC), sample inputs, and analytic pipelines, independent laboratories analyzing the same blinded CSF set achieved highly concordant diagnostic performance (sensitivity 86–96%, specificity 93–100%), demonstrating robustness and interstudy consistency. <cite id="34742348">The αSyn-SAA results were remarkably similar across laboratories, displaying high diagnostic performance (sensitivity ranging from 86 to 96% and specificity from 93 to 100%).</cite>

- Meta-analytic synthesis across diverse cohorts and biospecimens indicates that CSF αSyn-SAAs consistently outperform chance and differentiate synucleinopathy patients from controls with high accuracy, with pooled CSF sensitivity around 90% and specificity around 95% in subgroup analyses focused on Lewy body disorders and prodromal stages. <cite id="36289019">The diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of CSF αSyn-SAAs were 0.91 (0.87-0.94) and 0.96 (0.93-0.98) for Lewy body disease, 0.90 (0.79-0.95) and 0.96 (0.90-0.98) for prodromal α-synucleinopathies.</cite>

# Limitations and Variability

- Performance can vary by diagnostic reference (pathological vs clinical), biospecimen type, and assay parameters; for example, olfactory mucosa shows lower sensitivity than CSF or skin, and specificity is higher when pathological standards are used rather than clinical diagnosis. <cite id="36289019">Skin αSyn-SAAs exhibited a lower sensitivity 0.64 (0.49-0.76) than those of the other two specimens ... Application of pathological diagnostic standards were associated with a higher specificity of αSyn-SAAs compared to clinical diagnosis.</cite>

- While αSyn-RT-QuIC and αSyn-PMCA both distinguish PD from controls with high accuracy, single-center results can show very high specificity (e.g., 100%) and sensitivity (e.g., 93%), but pooled estimates across heterogeneous studies typically report slightly lower ranges (e.g., sensitivity ~88–91%, specificity ~93–97%). <cite id="29422107">Blinded analysis ... yielded 93% diagnostic sensitivity and 100% specificity for this test so far.</cite> <cite id="27918765">Sensitivity 88.5% and specificity 96.9% in blinded CSF cohorts.</cite> <cite id="36289019">Summary sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.95 across studies.</cite>

# Bottom Line

Overall, αSyn CSF seeding assays differentiate PD patients from controls reliably across studies, with pooled sensitivity around 88–91% and specificity around 93–97%, and independent lab comparisons showing strong concordance (86–96% sensitivity; 93–100% specificity). While there is variability by assay, biospecimen, and diagnostic criteria, the general consistency supports their use as biomarkers to separate PD (and related synucleinopathies) from non-synucleinopathy controls, including in early or prodromal stages. <cite id="34742348">The αSyn-SAA results were remarkably similar across laboratories, displaying high diagnostic performance (sensitivity ranging from 86 to 96% and specificity from 93 to 100%).</cite> <cite id="36289019">Summary sensitivity and specificity of αSyn-SAAs ... 0.88 and 0.95 ... CSF αSyn-SAAs showed 0.91 sensitivity and 0.96 specificity for Lewy body disease; 0.90 sensitivity and 0.96 specificity for prodromal synucleinopathies.</cite> <cite id="29422107">Blinded CSF analysis yielded 93% sensitivity and 100% specificity with αSyn RT-QuIC.</cite> <cite id="27918765">αSyn-PMCA achieved 88.5% sensitivity and 96.9% specificity in blinded CSF cohorts.</cite>

QUESTION:
In premanifest Huntington's disease, how well do imaging biomarkers (such as striatal volume on MRI) predict time to motor onset compared with biofluid biomarkers (such as neurofilament light)?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Imaging biomarkers in premanifest Huntington's disease (HD) show striatal changes years before motor onset, but their ability to predict the *exact time* to motor conversion is limited. In a 6‑year cohort, converters had a smaller putamen volume at clinical onset compared with non‑converters, yet striatal atrophy rates did not significantly differ between converters and non‑converters over time, suggesting MRI primarily marks disease presence rather than a precise prognosis for time to onset. Functional MRI studies over shorter intervals also report limited sensitivity for predicting time course relative to onset. <cite id="29593880">Striatal atrophy is detectable many years before predicted onset, but at the time of conversion, only the putamen showed a significant volume difference between converters and non‑converters, and striatal atrophy rates did not significantly differ between converters and non‑converters over time</cite> <cite id="25139578">A 3‑year resting‑state fMRI study found higher striatal atrophy rates in preHD vs. controls but did not detect group differences in connectivity change over that interval; the study also evaluated correlations with predicted time to onset and found limited sensitivity for short‑term follow‑up</cite>.

- Biofluid biomarkers, particularly CSF neurofilament light chain (NFL), show stronger associations with disease stage, progression, and even 5‑year motor onset probability in premanifest HD. In contrast, total tau shows weaker correlations. <cite id="28241046">NFL correlated strongly with UHDRS motor and functional scores and was significantly correlated with 5‑year probability of disease onset, whereas tau showed weaker correlations and was not significantly associated with 5‑year onset probability</cite>. Emerging work also links NFL to network hypoconnectivity in late premanifest stages, supporting its utility as a prognostic biomarker. <cite id="40595490">Hypoconnectivity in late premanifest HD correlates with CSF neurofilament light concentrations, suggesting NFL reflects disease stage progression across decades relative to onset</cite>.

# Head‑to‑Head Takeaway

- Imaging (e.g., striatal volume/atrophy) reliably indicates premanifest disease and detects striatal degeneration, but current evidence suggests it is less precise for predicting the residual time to motor onset than biofluid markers like NFL. <cite id="29593880">At onset, converters had smaller putamen volumes than non‑converters, but atrophy rates over follow‑up did not distinguish converters</cite> <cite id="25139578">Short‑term fMRI did not capture sensitive connectivity changes predictive of exact time to onset</cite>.

- Biofluids, especially NFL, better track disease progression and show quantitative associations with imminent motor conversion, making them more robust prognostic biomarkers than structural MRI at present. <cite id="28241046">NFL strongly correlates with clinical measures and 5‑year onset probability in premanifest HD</cite> <cite id="40595490">NFL levels align with network hypoconnectivity in late premanifest stages, supporting its prognostic value</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For enrollment and stratification in disease‑modifying trials, combining genetic CAG repeat length with NFL may improve prediction of time to motor onset and risk stratification compared with MRI alone. <cite id="28241046">NFL's correlation with UHDRS domains and 5‑year onset probability supports its use as a biomarker of progression</cite> <cite id="40595490">NFL's linkage to network changes across the premanifest trajectory further supports its prognostic role</cite>.

- Structural MRI remains valuable for diagnosing premanifest HD and monitoring disease presence and striatal involvement, but expectations should be set that it will not, by itself, precisely forecast time to onset with the same accuracy as NFL. <cite id="29593880">Putamen volume differences are present at onset but do not clearly predict individual time course</cite> <cite id="25139578">Striatal atrophy rates exceed controls over short intervals, but functional connectivity change lacks sensitivity for short‑term prediction</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps

- Head‑to‑head prospective studies directly comparing the predictive accuracy of MRI‑based striatal metrics versus NFL (and other biofluid markers) for time to motor onset—ideally with standardized CAG stratification and blinded adjudication—would clarify relative performance. Current studies suggest a hierarchy where NFL outperforms MRI for short‑term prognosis, but quantitative thresholds and model‑based comparisons remain limited. <cite id="29593880">MRI identifies group differences at onset but limited differential atrophy rates between converters and non‑converters</cite> <cite id="28241046">NFL shows stronger correlations with clinical progression and onset probability</cite> <cite id="40595490">NFL relates to network hypoconnectivity in late premanifest stages</cite> <cite id="25139578">Short‑term fMRI lacks sensitivity for predicting time to onset</cite>.

QUESTION:
In systemic lupus erythematosus, how does long-term hydroxychloroquine exposure influence risk of thrombosis and cardiovascular events in patients with and without antiphospholipid antibodies?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- In SLE patients with antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL), long-term hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) exposure was not found to have an independent protective effect against thrombosis in an individual-patient meta-analysis; after adjustment for cardiovascular risk factors, aPL profiles, and HCQ treatment, aspirin showed a significant protective effect on first thrombosis, while HCQ did not demonstrate an independent protective association. The analysis also suggested aspirin's protection was more evident for arterial than venous events, with benefit seen in SLE patients and asymptomatic aPL carriers, but not in those with mixed connective tissue disease or APS criteria aPL without SLE/lupus overlap. <cite id="25461472">In patients with aPL, treatment with low-dose aspirin was associated with a significantly lower risk of first thrombosis overall and first arterial thrombosis, including in SLE and asymptomatic aPL, whereas no independent protective effect of hydroxychloroquine was detected</cite>.

- In SLE cohorts without specific aPL-focused selection, HCQ use (and anticoagulation) was recorded as part of risk factor assessment, but the primary discriminators of thrombotic events were aCL antibodies and other aPL profiles; higher GAPSS scores predicted events, and aGAPSS validation emphasized aPL profile and traditional cardiovascular risk factors rather than HCQ as a protective covariate. <cite id="33028177">In a multicenter SLE cohort, aCL antibodies were an independent risk factor for thrombotic events, and aGAPSS incorporating aPL profile, cardiovascular risk factors, and medications (including HCQ/anticoagulation) stratified risk, but did not identify HCQ as independently protective</cite>.

# Interpretation by aPL status

- With aPL:
  - Evidence supports aspirin's benefit for primary thrombosis prevention; HCQ did not show an independent protective association after multivariable adjustment. <cite id="25461472">Aspirin reduced the hazard of first thrombosis (HR 0.43) and first arterial thrombosis in aPL carriers, including SLE, while hydroxychloroquine did not show an independent protective effect</cite>.
  - Clinical practice therefore emphasizes aspirin in aPL-positive SLE, with HCQ used as standard SLE therapy but not demonstrated as independently protective against thrombosis in these data. <cite id="25461472">No independent protective effect of hydroxychloroquine was found on first thrombosis risk in aPL carriers</cite>.

- Without aPL:
  - Observational SLE cohorts highlight that traditional cardiovascular risk factors and aPL profile drive thrombotic risk; HCQ is recorded as part of care but is not consistently identified as an independent thrombosis-risk lowering factor in multivariable models. <cite id="33028177">aGAPSS validation showed aCL/LA/B2GPI and cardiovascular risk factors predicted events; HCQ was part of medication history but not an independent protective factor</cite>.

# Limitations and evidence gaps

- Direct, long-term exposure–response data for HCQ (e.g., duration/dose thresholds) on thrombosis and cardiovascular events in SLE, stratified by presence of aPL, were not identified in the retrieved snippets. The strongest available evidence here concerns aspirin in aPL carriers and aGAPSS-based risk stratification rather than HCQ-specific effects. <cite id="25461472">The meta-analysis focused on aspirin and found no independent protective effect of hydroxychloroquine</cite><cite id="33028177">aGAPSS identified aPL profile and cardiovascular risk factors as key drivers of thrombotic events, with HCQ not independently protective</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For SLE patients with aPL: prioritize validated thrombosis prophylaxis (e.g., low-dose aspirin where indicated) and manage cardiovascular risk factors; routine long-term HCQ exposure should continue as standard SLE care, but current evidence does not support an independent reduction in thrombosis risk attributable to HCQ in aPL-positive disease beyond standard care. <cite id="25461472">Aspirin confers significant protection in aPL carriers, including SLE, while HCQ did not show independent protection</cite>.

- For SLE patients without aPL: focus on cardiovascular risk modification and periodic aPL screening; HCQ remains an important SLE therapy, but thrombosis risk stratification should rely on established scores incorporating aPL profile and traditional risk factors rather than assuming HCQ confers direct thrombosis risk reduction. <cite id="33028177">aGAPSS-based stratification incorporating aPL profile and cardiovascular risk factors is useful for identifying higher-risk patients</cite>.

QUESTION:
In hepatocellular carcinoma, how do objective response rate and overall survival differ between PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy and PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor combined with anti-VEGF therapy?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- In first-line unresectable hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor monotherapy (e.g., atezolizumab or nivolumab) shows modest objective response rates (ORR) and limited overall survival (OS) improvements compared with standard sorafenib, whereas PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with anti-VEGF therapy (e.g., atezolizumab plus bevacizumab) demonstrate higher ORR and better OS and progression-free survival (PFS) in pivotal and exploratory analyses. <cite id="32502443">In a phase 1b study, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab achieved an ORR of 36% and improved PFS versus atezolizumab monotherapy</cite>. <cite id="37767068,34189869">In IMbrave150, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improved OS and PFS versus sorafenib and showed higher ORR and deeper responses by RECIST and mRECIST</cite>. <cite id="39451736">In intermediate-stage HCC, adding bevacizumab to nivolumab/ipilimumab-based strategies has been associated with longer OS in retrospective analyses</cite>.

# PD-1/PD-L1 Monotherapy vs. PD-1/PD-L1 + Anti-VEGF

- Objective response rate (ORR):
  - PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy: ORR is generally low in HCC. <cite id="32502443">In the atezolizumab monotherapy context within the same study, the ORR was not explicitly reported but was lower than the combination (36% with atezolizumab+bevacizumab)</cite>. <cite id="37767068,34189869">In IMbrave150, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab achieved ORRs around 43–50% by RECIST and mRECIST, outperforming sorafenib (26–30%) and reflecting superior tumor shrinkage versus monotherapy expectations</cite>. <cite id="39038962">Genomic analyses from IMbrave150 further suggest higher ORR with the combination compared with sorafenib, supporting the added value of VEGF blockade over PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy</cite>.
  - PD-1/PD-L1 + anti-VEGF: <cite id="32502443">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab yielded an ORR of 36% in an open-label phase 1b cohort</cite>, and <cite id="37767068,34189869">exploratory IMbrave150 subgroup analyses reported ORRs of 43–50% with the combination</cite>.

- Overall survival (OS) and PFS:
  - PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy: <cite id="32502443">In the same phase 1b study, atezolizumab monotherapy did not meet primary OS endpoints and showed inferior PFS compared with the combination (3.4 months vs 5.6 months)</cite>. In broader practice, nivolumab monotherapy has shown limited OS gains versus sorafenib in first-line HCC, underscoring the relative weakness of monotherapy without VEGF inhibition. <cite id="37767068,34189869">IMbrave150 established that atezolizumab plus bevacizumab improves OS and PFS versus sorafenib, reflecting a class effect of VEGF–PD-1/PD-L1 combinations over monotherapy PD-1/PD-L1</cite>.
  - PD-1/PD-L1 + anti-VEGF: <cite id="32502443">Median PFS was 5.6 months with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab versus 3.4 months with atezolizumab monotherapy</cite>. <cite id="37767068">In IMbrave150, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab showed a trend toward improved OS (HR 0.63) and PFS (HR 0.64) versus sorafenib in the overall population, with significant benefits confirmed as standard of care</cite>. <cite id="34189869">Exploratory analyses corroborated improved ORR, depth, and duration of response with the combination</cite>. <cite id="39451736">In intermediate-stage disease, retrospective data suggest that integrating bevacizumab into immunotherapy regimens can extend OS compared with bevacizumab monotherapy</cite>.

# Key Trials and Readouts

- GO30140 (atezolizumab ± bevacizumab): <cite id="32502443">Atezolizumab plus bevacizumab produced an ORR of 36% and PFS 5.6 months; atezolizumab monotherapy PFS was 3.4 months, establishing a clear PFS advantage for the combination</cite>.
- IMbrave150 (atezolizumab + bevacizumab vs sorafenib): <cite id="37767068,34189869">Superior OS and PFS with the combination, and higher ORR by RECIST and mRECIST (43–50% vs 26–30% for sorafenib)</cite>.
- IMbrave200/real-world and exploratory cohorts: <cite id="37767068">Consistent efficacy and safety profiles, supporting use across BCLC stages</cite>.
- Biomarker insights: <cite id="39038962">Immune signature analyses suggest patient subsets may derive greater benefit from combination therapy, aligning with observed higher ORR and survival advantages over monotherapy</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In HCC, PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy yields low ORR and limited survival benefit, while adding anti-VEGF (bevacizumab) to PD-1/PD-L1 improves ORR and significantly enhances PFS and OS. <cite id="32502443">The combination atezolizumab+bevacizumab achieved an ORR around 36% and improved PFS over PD-1 monotherapy</cite>, and <cite id="37767068,34189869">IMbrave150 demonstrated superior OS and PFS versus sorafenib, establishing the combination as a standard regimen with higher ORR and deeper responses than sorafenib and, by extension, PD-1 monotherapy</cite>. <cite id="39451736">Retrospective evidence further suggests that VEGF-targeted sequencing with immunotherapy can improve OS in intermediate-stage HCC compared with VEGF monotherapy</cite>.

# Notes and Gaps

- Direct head-to-head randomized comparisons of PD-1 monotherapy versus PD-1 plus bevacizumab in first-line unresectable HCC are limited; most evidence comes from phase 1b/3 combinations versus sorafenib and post hoc or exploratory subgroup analyses. <cite id="32502443">GO30140 provides direct combination-versus-monotherapy signals within the same trial</cite>, while <cite id="37767068,34189869">IMbrave150 establishes superiority of the combination over sorafenib, a standard monotherapy comparator</cite>. <cite id="39451736">Retrospective data on nivolumab/ipilimumab with bevacizumab sequencing support OS gains but require validation in prospective trials</cite>. Further trials directly comparing monotherapy PD-1/PD-L1 arms with PD-1/PD-L1 plus bevacizumab in first-line HCC would clarify the magnitude of ORR and OS differences.

QUESTION:
What is the relationship between CAG repeat length and age at onset across different Huntington's disease populations, and what modifiers are reported to influence this relationship?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Huntington disease (HD) is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in HTT, and longer inherited CAG repeats are robustly associated with earlier age at onset (AAO) and faster progression, while shorter repeats tend to be associated with later onset and longer survival. Across populations, this inverse correlation is consistent, though the strength of association varies by cohort and other factors, and repeat length alone explains only part of the phenotypic variability. Multiple genetic and environmental modifiers influence AAO, with several candidate genes from DNA repair and related pathways showing evidence in human genetic studies and ex vivo or animal models.

# Relationship between CAG repeat length and age at onset

- Inverse correlation across cohorts: Numerous studies and reviews report that AAO in HD is inversely correlated with inherited HTT CAG repeat length, with longer repeats leading to earlier onset and shorter repeats to later onset. This relationship is observed across different populations and is considered a primary determinant of onset. Reviews and cohort analyses emphasize that the correlation is length-dependent and tissue-specific, with somatic and germline expansion contributing to the discrepancy between inherited and cellular pathogenic thresholds. <cite id="33579866">Age at onset in Huntington's disease is inversely correlated with the inherited CAG length, and longer repeats are more prone to expansions that are age dependent and tissue-specific</cite>. <cite id="26742514">Symptoms including age at onset are related to the genetic characteristics, both the CAG triplet repeat and the modified factors</cite>.

- Quantitative links and thresholds: Modeling and synthesis across studies suggest an "inherited" threshold below which expansion can proceed and a higher "intracellular pathogenic threshold" (estimated around 60–100 CAG repeats, likely toward the upper end), above which cellular dysfunction occurs. This two-step mechanism helps explain why individuals with similar inherited repeat lengths can show variable ages at clinical onset. <cite id="33579866">Longer repeats are more prone to expansions, and the inherited tract expands through life, implying a threshold at which cells become dysfunctional; a modeled intracellular pathogenic threshold of approximately 115 CAG repeats (95% CI 70–165) has been proposed, with empirical clues suggesting a range of 60–100</cite>.

- Population differences and modifiers: While the inverse correlation is broadly consistent, its strength varies across cohorts, and shorter alleles (e.g., 40–42 repeats) show wider variability in AAO, indicating a greater role for modifiers in these cases. Cohort analyses highlight that even at the same CAG length, AAO can differ substantially, underscoring environmental and genetic influences. <cite id="31820322">CAG repeats between 40 and 42 show a wider onset variation, and no clinical differences were found between late-onset and common-onset HD at these lengths, suggesting a need to study environmental and genetic variables</cite>.

# Genetic modifiers influencing age at onset

- DNA repair/Mismatch repair (MMR) genes: Multiple lines of evidence implicate DNA repair genes, particularly mismatch repair components (e.g., MSH2, MSH3, MLH1, PMS1/2) and ligase I (LIG1), as modifiers of AAO and repeat expansion dynamics. Ex vivo CRISPR interference in HD iPSCs shows that lowering expression of MMR/MutL factors slows HTT CAG expansion, with the strongest effects for MSH2/3/MLH1 and lesser effects for PMS1/2/MLH3; LIG1 also contributes. These findings support a mechanistic link between DNA repair capacity and repeat instability that can modulate AAO. <cite id="38749429">Reduced expression of MSH2, MSH3, and MLH1 slowed HTT CAG repeat expansion most strongly in ex vivo HD iPSC models, with PMS1/PMS2/MLH3 having lesser effects and LIG1 also contributing</cite>. <cite id="39801710">Genome-wide association analyses highlight DNA repair genes (e.g., MLH1, PMS2, MSH3, LIG1) as modifiers of Huntington's disease onset, with cross-disorder relevance to other repeat expansion disorders</cite>.

- PGC-1α (PPARGC1A): Variants in PGC-1α have been reported to modify AAO in multiple populations, with different alleles exerting opposing effects. For example, rs7665116 is associated with delayed onset (particularly in Italian ancestry), while rs2970870 in the promoter is associated with earlier onset in homozygosity; haplotypes within the transcribed region also show associations. These data suggest mitochondrial function and oxidative stress pathways influence onset age. <cite id="21211002">Two SNPs in PPARGC1A (rs7665116 and rs2970870) show significant effects on age at onset, with opposing influences, and haplotypes in the transcribed region associate with disease onset</cite>.

- Kalirin (KALRN): A promoter polymorphism (rs10934657) in KALRN, a gene involved in spine plasticity, did not show an association with AAO in a European cohort after covarying for CAG repeat length, suggesting either no role in this population or that other variants within KALRN may be relevant in different cohorts. <cite id="22720673">SNP rs10934657 in the kalirin promoter did not affect age at onset in European HD patients when analyzed with covariates, though other SNPs in KALRN could still be modifiers</cite>.

- Cross-disorder insights and modifier prioritization: Modifier loci identified in HD often overlap with those in other repeat expansion disorders, such as X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), where CCCTCT repeat length similarly inversely correlates with AAO and shows repeat length-dependent somatic instability in brain regions. This supports a general mechanism of repeat-length dependent expansion and suggests shared trans-acting factors. <cite id="39801710">Top age-of-onset GWAS hits show a high correlation across Huntington's disease and X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism, emphasizing cross-disorder relevance</cite>. <cite id="35395816">In XDP, CCCTCT repeat length inversely correlates with age at onset and death, with brain region-specific, expansion-based instability similar to HTT CAG repeat instability in HD brains</cite>.

- Progression and onset: Large-scale GWAS using longitudinal progression measures identify modifier genes (e.g., MSH3, DHFR, MTRNR2L2) associated with disease trajectory, with MSH3 carrying a functional variant (Pro67Ala) linked to slower motor and functional decline after adjusting for AAO. This indicates genetic influences on progression that operate independently of or in addition to their effects on onset age. <cite id="28642124">A meta-analysis identified a genome-wide significant locus on chromosome 5 (MSH3, DHFR, MTRNR2L2) associated with progression; the MSH3 variant (rs557874766) was associated with reduced rates of UHDRS Total Motor and Functional Capacity change after adjusting for age at onset</cite>.

# Biological mechanisms and implications

- Somatic and germline expansion: The inherited CAG tract continues to expand in vivo and in vitro, and cells in symptomatic brain regions can harbor much longer repeats than those inherited, helping explain variable AAO even at similar inherited lengths. This dynamic supports the concept of a cellular pathogenic threshold distinct from the inherited length. <cite id="33579866">The inherited CAG tract expands throughout life, and cells that degenerate likely contain longer tracts than the inherited length, implying separate inherited and intracellular pathogenic thresholds</cite>.

- Modifier mechanisms: Modifiers likely act by influencing somatic CAG expansion rates, DNA repair fidelity, mitochondrial function, and neuronal stress responses. Evidence from ex vivo CRISPRi studies shows that reducing MMR factor expression slows repeat expansion, suggesting that lowering repair activity could be a therapeutic strategy to delay onset. Conversely, variants in PGC-1α that alter mitochondrial function can shift AAO, highlighting metabolic pathways as potential targets. <cite id="38749429">CRISPRi-mediated lowering of MMR factor expression slowed HTT CAG expansion, identifying potential targets to delay onset and progression</cite>. <cite id="21211002">Opposing SNPs in PPARGC1A modulate AAO, implicating mitochondrial and oxidative stress pathways in Huntington's disease</cite>.

# Clinical and demographic modifiers

- Age at death vs. duration: In large cohorts, expanded CAG repeat length is a strong determinant of age at death, independent of disease duration, which can be influenced by specific genetic modifiers of motor onset. This suggests distinct genetic and pathophysiological drivers for onset versus progression/death. <cite id="26849111">CAG expansion length determines age at death and has no contribution from the normal CAG allele, while disease duration is independent of mutation length and unaffected by a strong modifier of motor onset</cite>.

- Environmental and non-genetic factors: Observational cohorts with identical CAG repeats (e.g., 40–42) but divergent AAO emphasize the role of environmental and other genetic modifiers, warranting further study of nongenetic variables. <cite id="31820322">At 40–42 CAG repeats, onset varies widely and no clinical differences were found between late- and common-onset groups, indicating a need to study environmental and genetic variables</cite>.

# Practical takeaways

- For individuals at risk, CAG repeat length measured by genetic testing provides the strongest predictor of AAO, with longer repeats indicating earlier onset; however, a comprehensive assessment should incorporate known modifiers and consider population-specific variability. <cite id="33579866">Age at onset is inversely correlated with inherited CAG length, with additional modulation by genetic and environmental factors</cite>.

- Therapeutic strategies targeting repeat expansion (e.g., reducing mismatch repair activity) or cellular pathways (e.g., mitochondrial function) may shift AAO by modulating the rate of somatic expansion or downstream neurodegeneration, with MMR components and PGC-1α highlighted as candidate targets. <cite id="38749429">Lowering expression of MSH2/3/MLH1 and related MMR factors slowed CAG expansion in HD iPSC models</cite>. <cite id="21211002">Variants in PPARGC1A alter AAO, implicating mitochondrial pathways as modifiable influences</cite>.

# Evidence gaps and future directions

- While the inverse CAG–AAO relationship is well established, quantifying the exact cellular pathogenic threshold and its tissue specificity remains challenging. Large-scale postmortem and in vivo single-cell analyses of repeat length across brain regions and time could refine mechanistic models. <cite id="33579866">Empirical determination of the intracellular pathogenic threshold remains difficult, with clues suggesting a range of 60–100 CAG repeats</cite>.

- Modifier gene discovery and prioritization benefit from cross-disorder analyses and functional validation in human cells and tissues. The convergence of modifier loci across HD and XDP, and the druggability profiles of candidate genes, can guide therapeutic development. <cite id="39801710">Cross-disorder age-of-onset GWAS signals highlight shared modifier genes and provide druggability assessments to prioritize targets</cite>.

QUESTION:
What tumor-intrinsic features of the tumor microenvironment (such as TGF-beta signaling, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, or macrophage polarization) are most associated with lack of response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in human cancers?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of tumor-intrinsic features linked to lack of response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade

## TGF-β signaling
Multiple human and preclinical studies indicate that intrinsic TGF-β pathway activity in tumors is a dominant driver of innate resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy. In melanoma and other solid tumors, "innate anti-PD-1 resistance signatures" (IPRES) enriched for wound-healing, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and angiogenesis are dominated by TGF-β and VEGFA signaling, with TGF-β–associated immunosuppression contributing to PD-1 resistance; localized TGF-β targeting with "trap" antibodies is proposed to overcome resistance while sparing systemic TGF-β function. TGF-β also promotes conversion of effector CD4+ T cells into regulatory T cells (Tregs), and pharmacologic inhibition of SRC family kinases (e.g., dasatinib) can counter this pathway and synergize with anti–PD-1 in NSCLC models. TGF-β signaling can directly dampen T-cell effector function, and genetic or pharmacologic strategies that counteract TGF-β (e.g., DGK knockout) enhance T-cell function and improve responses to checkpoint blockade in preclinical models. Collectively, high tumor-intrinsic TGF-β activity is consistently associated with poor responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy and represents a key biomarker and therapeutic target. <cite id="35577211">TGF-β and VEGFA pathways emerge as dominant drivers of innate anti-PD-1 resistance signatures in solid tumors, mediating immunosuppression and resistance to PD-1 blockade</cite> <cite id="33658304">TGF-β–driven conversion of effector CD4+ T cells into regulatory T cells contributes to resistance, and SRC-family kinase inhibition (dasatinib) synergizes with anti–PD-1 in NSCLC models</cite> <cite id="29967261">TGF-β suppresses T-cell effector functions; DGK knockout renders CAR-T cells resistant to TGF-β and enhances antitumor activity</cite>.

## Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs)
Elevated MDSC activity is a recurrent barrier to PD-1/PD-L1 efficacy in several solid tumors. In prostate cancer, innate resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 is reinforced by increased MDSCs and regulatory T cells, low tumor mutational burden, and impaired interferon-γ signaling, limiting the benefit of single-agent checkpoint inhibitors. In melanoma models, PD-1+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes can induce compensatory upregulation of PD-L1 on granulocytic MDSCs, reflecting a tumor-driven adaptive resistance mechanism that sustains immunosuppression. Local immunomodulation that reshapes MDSC biology can enhance checkpoint inhibitor responses; for example, adenoviral delivery of IL-2 and TNF-α in combination with T-cell therapy improved responses by shifting the balance against immunosuppressive MDSC subsets. These data support MDSC frequency and functional polarization as biomarkers of nonresponse and targets for combination strategies to overcome PD-1/PD-L1 resistance. <cite id="33433743">Increased activity of myeloid-derived suppressor cells and regulatory T cells contributes to limited efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy in prostate cancer</cite> <cite id="27741089">PD-1+ tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes induce PD-L1 upregulation on granulocytic MDSCs, promoting immunosuppression and resistance</cite> <cite id="27741089">Local IL-2/TNF-α delivery improved responses by favoring a tumor-infiltrating milieu less favorable to immunosuppressive MDSCs and more favorable to effector T cells</cite>.

## Macrophage polarization (M2-like/TAM polarization)
Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) that are polarized toward an M2-like, immunosuppressive phenotype are strongly implicated in resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 therapy across multiple solid tumors. In EGFR-activated NSCLC, tumor-intrinsic ILT4 (a receptor expressed by tumor cells) is upregulated via AKT/ERK signaling, driving recruitment and M2-like polarization of TAMs, which in turn impairs T-cell function; blocking ILT4 or PD-L1 (alone or in combination) restores antitumor immunity and enhances anti–PD-L1 efficacy, with the greatest benefit seen when both pathways are inhibited. In hepatocellular carcinoma, a subset of macrophages expressing the MARCO receptor (MARCO+ TAMs) exhibits strong immunosuppressive capacity; these cells suppress IFN-β secretion and antigen presentation, reduce CD8+ T-cell infiltration, and promote CD8+ T-cell dysfunction. Combining anti–PD-L1 with targeting of MARCO+ TAMs significantly improves tumor control, indicating TAM subset targeting as a strategy to overcome PD-L1 resistance. In neuroblastoma, PD-L1 is predominantly expressed on tumor-associated macrophages rather than neuroblastoma cells, and higher PD-L1 expression on macrophages correlates with better outcomes, whereas a PD-1/PD-L1 ratio >1 in macrophages associates with inferior survival, suggesting that macrophage polarization state and PD-L1/PD-1 balance on myeloid cells influence response to checkpoint blockade. <cite id="33537094">In EGFR-activated NSCLC, tumor-intrinsic ILT4 signaling drives M2-like TAM polarization and recruitment, impairing T cells; ILT4 or PD-L1 blockade restores immunity and enhances anti–PD-L1 efficacy, with combined inhibition most effective</cite> <cite id="38065400">MARCO+ TAMs in liver cancer suppress IFN-β and antigen presentation, reduce CD8+ T-cell infiltration and function; combining anti–PD-L1 with MARCO targeting improves responses and reverses resistance</cite> <cite id="35525858">In neuroblastoma, PD-L1 is primarily expressed on TAMs; high PD-L1 expression correlates with better outcomes, while a PD-1/PD-L1 ratio >1 on macrophages associates with worse survival</cite>.

## Hypoxia and VEGF/angiogenesis
Hypoxia and VEGF-driven angiogenesis are intertwined with TGF-β–mediated resistance programs and contribute to an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment that undermines PD-1/PD-L1 therapy. In the IPRES framework, VEGFA pathway activity is a dominant driver of innate resistance alongside TGF-β, supporting angiogenesis and immunosuppression that limit T-cell infiltration and function; localized targeting of VEGFA is proposed to restore responsiveness to checkpoint blockade. <cite id="35577211">VEGFA pathway activity is a dominant driver of innate anti–PD-1 resistance programs, cooperating with TGF-β to shape an immunosuppressive microenvironment that limits checkpoint inhibitor efficacy</cite>.

## Additional tumor-intrinsic and stromal features shaping resistance
Beyond the above axes, tumor-intrinsic features such as low MHC class I expression and impaired type I interferon signaling (e.g., in prostate cancer) reduce antigen presentation and T-cell recognition, further limiting the benefit of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. In melanoma, tumor-intrinsic manganese deficiency impairs cGAS–STING sensing, reducing dendritic cell maturation, antigen presentation, and CD8+ T-cell activation; supplementation with manganese enhances innate and adaptive antitumor immunity and synergizes with anti–PD-1 in mice, with early clinical signals of efficacy, highlighting a metabolic-sensing pathway that can modulate checkpoint responsiveness. <cite id="33433743">Low MHC class I expression and impaired IFN-γ signaling contribute to resistance and limited benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy in prostate cancer</cite> <cite id="32839553">Tumor-intrinsic manganese deficiency suppresses cGAS–STING signaling in innate antitumor responses; manganese supplementation enhances DC/macrophage maturation, CD8+ T-cell activation, and synergizes with anti–PD-1, with early clinical efficacy signals</cite>.

# Practical implications for biomarker development and therapy
- TGF-β pathway activity, VEGFA-driven angiogenesis, and hypoxia signatures are consistently associated with nonresponse to PD-1/PD-L1 and can serve as candidate biomarkers to stratify patients for combination strategies that include TGF-β/VEGF blockade alongside PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors. <cite id="35577211">TGF-β and VEGFA pathways are dominant drivers of innate resistance signatures and attractive targets to restore checkpoint inhibitor sensitivity</cite>.
- Elevated MDSC frequency and immunosuppressive TAM subsets (e.g., MARCO+ or M2-like TAMs) correlate with poor responses and can be targeted with immunomodulatory combinations (e.g., IL-2/TNF-α delivery, ILT4 blockade, MARCO targeting) to enhance anti–PD-L1/PD-1 efficacy. <cite id="27741089">Local IL-2/TNF-α delivery reshaped the tumor microenvironment against MDSCs and improved T-cell function in combination therapy</cite> <cite id="38065400">Targeting MARCO+ TAMs improved anti–PD-L1 efficacy in hepatocellular carcinoma</cite> <cite id="33537094">Blocking ILT4 reversed TAM-mediated immunosuppression and enhanced PD-L1 inhibitor responses in EGFR-activated NSCLC</cite>.
- Macrophage PD-L1/PD-1 expression patterns and polarization state (M1-like vs M2-like) on TAMs may inform patient selection and combination partners for PD-1/PD-L1 therapy. <cite id="35525858">Macrophage PD-L1 expression associates with better outcomes, whereas a PD-1/PD-L1 ratio >1 on macrophages predicts worse survival in high-risk neuroblastoma</cite>.

# Bottom line
Across human cancers, tumor-intrinsic features most associated with lack of response to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade include strong TGF-β signaling and VEGF/angiogenic programs, immunosuppressive myeloid states (high MDSC activity and M2-like/MARCO+ TAM polarization), and defects in antigen presentation/type I interferon pathways. These features create a hypoxia–immunosuppression axis that dampens T-cell activation and function; combining PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors with targeted countermeasures to TGF-β/VEGF, MDSC/TAM modulation, and metabolic/antigen-presentation restoration is a rational path to improve responses in nonresponders. <cite id="35577211">TGF-β and VEGFA pathways dominate innate resistance to PD-1 blockade in multiple solid tumors</cite> <cite id="33433743">High MDSC activity and impaired IFN-γ signaling limit PD-1/PD-L1 efficacy in prostate cancer</cite> <cite id="38065400">M2-like/MARCO+ TAMs suppress antitumor immunity and anti–PD-L1 responses in hepatocellular carcinoma</cite> <cite id="33537094">ILT4-driven M2 TAM polarization and TAM recruitment impair T-cell function and reduce PD-L1 inhibitor efficacy in EGFR-activated NSCLC</cite> <cite id="32839553">Defects in cGAS–STING/manganese sensing compromise CD8+ T-cell activation and synergize with checkpoint blockade responsiveness</cite>.

QUESTION:
Among pregnant individuals with COVID-19, how does infection severity relate to the risk of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth compared with uninfected controls?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Among pregnant individuals with COVID-19, greater infection severity is consistently associated with higher risks of adverse obstetric outcomes compared with uninfected controls. Meta-analyses and large registries show that any COVID-19 infection during pregnancy increases the odds of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth, and that risks are substantially higher in severe disease. For example, pooled estimates report preterm birth odds ratios of 1.66–1.82 overall and 4.29 for severe disease; preeclampsia odds ratios of 1.46–1.73 overall and 4.16 for severe disease; and stillbirth odds ratios of 1.98–2.11 overall, with severe cases showing particularly elevated risks and a higher proportion of stillbirths when delivery occurs within two weeks of infection. These associations are observed across diverse cohorts and reviews, with some nuance for birthweight and variant-period effects.

# Key Findings by Outcome

- Preterm birth
  - Any infection vs uninfected: pooled OR 1.66 (95% CI 1.41–1.96) in a meta-analysis of 38 studies (127,805 pregnancies). In a large registry (n=8,239), preterm birth occurred in 11.5% of SARS-CoV-2–infected pregnancies, predominantly indicated for fetal compromise. <cite id="35156521">Pregnant women with COVID-19 have increased risk of premature birth (OR = 1.66, 95% CI = 1.41-1.96)</cite> <cite id="35914420">Preterm birth occurred in 11.5% of infected pregnancies, mostly indicated for fetal compromise</cite>
  - Severe infection vs mild: OR 4.29 (95% CI 2.41–7.63) for preterm birth in systematic reviews/meta-analyses. <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 was associated with preterm birth (OR 4.29, 95% CI 2.41 to 7.63)</cite> <cite id="34221361">Risk of preterm birth was nearly 2.4-fold among women with severe COVID-19</cite>

- Preeclampsia
  - Any infection vs uninfected: pooled OR 1.46 (95% CI 1.18–1.80) in meta-analysis; another review reported OR 1.33 (95% CI 1.03–1.73). <cite id="35156521">COVID-19 infection increased risk of pre-eclampsia (OR = 1.46, 95% CI = 1.18-1.80)</cite> <cite id="33741725">COVID-19 was associated with preeclampsia (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.73)</cite>
  - Severe infection vs mild: OR 4.16 (95% CI 1.55–11.15). <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 strongly associated with preeclampsia (OR 4.16, 95% CI 1.55 to 11.15)</cite>

- Stillbirth
  - Any infection vs uninfected: pooled OR 1.98 (95% CI 1.22–3.21) and 2.11 (95% CI 1.14–3.90) in separate meta-analyses; in a large registry, stillbirth was 0.4% among infected pregnancies, with a higher proportion when delivery was within two weeks of infection (0.8% vs 0.2%). <cite id="35156521">Stillbirth risk increased (OR = 1.98, 95% CI = 1.22-3.21)</cite> <cite id="33741725">Stillbirth (OR 2.11, 95% CI 1.14 to 3.90)</cite> <cite id="35914420">Stillbirth occurred in 0.4% of infected pregnancies, higher at 0.8% when delivery was within 2 weeks of infection vs 0.2% when delivered ≥2 weeks after infection</cite>
  - Severe infection vs mild: Elevated stillbirth risk reported in meta-analyses and reviews, with some emphasis on increased risks during the Delta variant period. <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 associated with higher stillbirth risk (OR 4.29 for preterm birth; similar patterns for other adverse outcomes)</cite> <cite id="37105860">An increased risk of stillbirth appears to be predominantly confined to pregnancies affected during the Delta variant period</cite>

# Severity Gradient

Multiple sources describe a severity gradient: infection confers baseline increases in preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth versus no infection, and severe disease shows markedly higher odds across these outcomes. Reviews note that worse obstetric morbidity and mortality generally correlate with COVID-19 severity, and comorbidities such as diabetes increase the risk of severe disease. <cite id="34534497">Evidence is accumulating that SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy is associated with adverse outcomes including preeclampsia, preterm birth, and stillbirth, especially among pregnant persons with severe COVID-19 disease</cite> <cite id="37105860">Worse obstetric morbidity and mortality generally correlate with the severity of COVID-19; comorbidities such as diabetes increase risk of severe COVID-19</cite> <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 associated with higher odds of preeclampsia (OR 4.16), preterm birth (OR 4.29), gestational diabetes (OR 1.99), and low birth weight (OR 1.89)</cite>

# Additional Notes and Nuance

- Fetal growth: In a low-risk cohort, neonatal small-for-gestational-age rates were similar between COVID-19–exposed and unexposed groups, and timing/severity of infection were not associated with SGA; overall SGA and fetal growth restriction rates were not higher than expected. <cite id="38955216">In low-risk patients, SGA neonates were similarly distributed (8.9% vs 8.7%) and timing/severity of COVID-19 were not associated with SGA</cite> <cite id="35914420">Overall proportions of SGA and fetal growth restriction were not higher than expected</cite>
- ICU and maternal outcomes: Severe COVID-19 in pregnancy is linked to higher ICU admissions, ventilatory support, and maternal morbidity/mortality compared with uninfected controls; these correlate with the severity of maternal illness. <cite id="34534497">Pregnant persons with severe COVID-19 were more likely to require ICU admission, invasive ventilation, ECMO, and die compared with nonpregnant women</cite> <cite id="37105860">Pregnant individuals with SARS-CoV-2 infection had higher composite morbidity, ICU admission, ventilatory support, preterm birth, and neonatal ICU admissions compared to uninfected</cite>
- Variant period considerations: Some analyses suggest stillbirth risk was particularly elevated during the Delta variant period, indicating that background epidemiology may modulate observed risks. <cite id="37105860">An increased stillbirth risk appears to be predominantly confined to pregnancies during the Delta variant period</cite>

# Bottom Line

Compared with uninfected pregnant individuals, COVID-19 infection is associated with increased risks of preterm birth, preeclampsia, and stillbirth, and these risks rise steeply with disease severity. Severe COVID-19 shows markedly higher odds of preeclampsia (OR ~4), preterm birth (OR ~4), and stillbirth, with additional signals of worse maternal ICU and ventilatory needs. Public health and clinical guidance emphasize that these risks are highest in severe illness and in the context of comorbidities that predispose to severe disease. <cite id="35156521">COVID-19 increases risk of preterm birth (OR 1.66), stillbirth (OR 1.98), and preeclampsia (OR 1.46)</cite> <cite id="33741725">Severe COVID-19 strongly associates with preeclampsia (OR 4.16), preterm birth (OR 4.29), and stillbirth</cite> <cite id="34534497">Adverse outcomes, especially severe COVID-19, are linked to preeclampsia, preterm birth, and stillbirth</cite> <cite id="35914420">Stillbirth was higher when delivery was within two weeks of infection, and indicated preterm births were common</cite>

QUESTION:
In people living with HIV who are virologically suppressed, what is the comparative efficacy and safety of switching from a three-drug antiretroviral regimen to a two-drug regimen for maintaining viral suppression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In people living with HIV who are virologically suppressed, switching from a three‑drug antiretroviral regimen to a two‑drug regimen is generally supported as non‑inferior for maintaining viral suppression, with comparable efficacy and acceptable safety in many modern dual combinations. However, the risk of resistance selection and the optimal regimen choice may vary by baseline viral load and the specific components of the dual regimen. <cite id="39960818">Overall data support the non‑inferior efficacy of two‑drug regimens compared with three‑drug regimens, with no clear evidence of increased subclinical failure and potential improvements in tolerability and adherence</cite>. <cite id="29676935">Guidelines endorse dual regimens in selected patients to reduce long‑term toxicity and costs, with strongest evidence for regimens such as ritonavir‑boosted protease inhibitor plus lamivudine and dolutegravir combined with rilpivirine</cite>. <cite id="27470027">A large meta‑analysis found dual therapy had a modestly higher risk of virological failure overall (RR 1.14) but was comparable in serious adverse events (OR 1.16), with greater resistance mutation selection and higher risk at higher baseline viral loads</cite>. <cite id="37540331">Randomized pilot data for tenofovir alafenamide plus dolutegravir as a switch showed non‑inferiority in efficacy and safety over 48 weeks versus a standard triple regimen</cite>.

# Comparative Efficacy

- Non‑inferiority of dual regimens: <cite id="39960818">Comparative reviews conclude that contemporary two‑drug regimens are non‑inferior to three‑drug regimens for maintaining viral suppression, with no evidence of increased subclinical failure when properly selected and monitored</cite>. <cite id="29676935">Expert reviews highlight robust evidence for specific dual combinations (e.g., dolutegravir‑rilpivirine and ritonavir‑boosted protease inhibitor plus lamivudine) in virologically suppressed individuals</cite>. <cite id="27470027">Meta‑analysis across 21 studies (including 10 switch studies) showed an overall failure risk ratio of 1.14 for dual versus triple therapy, with higher risk in maraviroc‑containing regimens and in patients with baseline viral load >100,000 copies/mL</cite>.
- Regimen‑specific nuances: <cite id="29676935">Dual regimens may offer advantages such as improved renal and bone outcomes compared with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate‑based triple regimens</cite>. <cite id="37540331">A randomized trial of tenofovir alafenamide plus dolutegravir as a switch demonstrated undetectable viral loads at 48 weeks in both arms and non‑inferiority in safety and adherence</cite>.

# Safety and Tolerability

- Adverse events and monitoring: <cite id="27470027">Serious adverse events were similar between dual and triple regimens (OR 1.16), while overall adverse events were slightly lower for dual therapy (OR 0.82), though confidence intervals included unity and mutation selection risk was higher for dual regimens</cite>. <cite id="39960818">Reviews emphasize potential improvements in tolerability, adherence, and patient‑centered outcomes with dual regimens, including high satisfaction and quality‑of‑life benefits with long‑acting injectables</cite>. <cite id="29676935">Dual regimens have shown improved renal function and bone mineral density compared with certain tenofovir DF‑based triple regimens</cite>.
- Special populations and cautions: <cite id="29676935">Dual therapy is not recommended for HBV‑coinfected individuals or during pregnancy</cite>. <cite id="27470027">Dual regimens may have a greater risk of selecting resistance mutations than standard triple therapy, underscoring the importance of viral suppression at baseline and ongoing monitoring</cite>.

# Practical Considerations for Switching

- Indications and selection: <cite id="29676935">Guidelines support dual regimens as an alternative to triple therapy in selected patients to reduce toxicity and costs, with the strongest evidence for specific integrase‑ inhibitor and PI‑based dual combinations in virologically suppressed individuals</cite>. <cite id="39960818">Transitioning from triple to dual therapy may reduce drug interactions and toxicity while maintaining durable viral suppression</cite>.
- Patient‑centered benefits: <cite id="39960818">Simplification can improve adherence and quality of life, with long‑acting dual regimens offering high satisfaction by reducing daily pill burden</cite>.
- Risks and monitoring: <cite id="27470027">Despite non‑inferiority in many settings, dual therapy may increase the risk of resistance mutations and perform worse in those with high baseline viral loads; clinicians should consider viral load thresholds and avoid regimens like maraviroc where appropriate</cite>.

# Bottom Line

For virologically suppressed adults with HIV, switching from a three‑drug regimen to a well‑selected two‑drug regimen is generally non‑inferior for maintaining viral suppression and can improve tolerability and adherence, with modern integrase‑inhibitor or boosted PI‑based dual regimens showing favorable efficacy and safety profiles. Careful patient selection, attention to co‑infections and pregnancy plans, and ongoing viral load and resistance monitoring remain essential to mitigate the slightly higher risk of resistance selection and to ensure optimal outcomes. <cite id="39960818,29676935,27470027,37540331">Switching from triple to dual therapy can be effective and safe, with regimen choice tailored to individual risk factors and monitoring capacity</cite>.
