QUESTION:
Among individuals with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder, what is the risk and typical time course of conversion to Parkinson’s disease or dementia with Lewy bodies in prospective cohorts?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Prospective cohorts of individuals with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) consistently show a high risk of phenoconversion to synucleinopathies, most commonly Parkinson’s disease (PD) and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), over a mean follow-up of several years. Across multicenter and single-center longitudinal studies, annual conversion rates on the order of 6% are observed, with a large cumulative probability of conversion by 10–12 years. Typical time-to-conversion is on the order of 4–9 years from iRBD diagnosis, and 11–16 years from symptom onset, though this varies by cohort and the presence of soft neurodegenerative signs. Cognitive impairment, olfactory loss, color vision abnormalities, subtle motor dysfunction, and abnormal dopaminergic imaging are the strongest baseline predictors distinguishing those who convert, and cognitive markers can identify those who tend to develop dementia before parkinsonism.

# Risk and Conversion Rates

In a large multicenter International RBD Study Group cohort (n=1,280; mean follow-up 4.6 years; range 1–19 years), the overall phenoconversion rate to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with 73.5% converting by 12 years’ follow-up. Conversion was distributed primarily to PD and DLB, with smaller proportions to multiple system atrophy. Predictors of faster conversion included abnormal quantitative motor testing, objective motor examination, olfactory deficit, mild cognitive impairment, erectile dysfunction, motor symptoms, abnormal DAT scans, color vision abnormalities, constipation, loss of REM atonia, and older age. Notably, in this cohort, those converting to primary dementia versus primary parkinsonism differed at baseline only by cognitive variables, suggesting cognitive profiles may help anticipate dementia-first presentation. Sample size calculations for neuroprotective trials were feasible, requiring roughly 142–366 patients per arm depending on assumptions. <cite id="30789229">In a large multicenter cohort of iRBD followed prospectively, the overall conversion rate to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with 73.5% converting by 12 years; predictors included abnormal motor testing, olfactory loss, color vision abnormalities, constipation, REM atonia loss, age, and abnormal DAT scans</cite>.

An earlier 10-year prospective cohort (n=89) reported high cumulative risk: 30% developed neurodegenerative synucleinopathy by 3 years and 66% by 7.5 years. Strongest predictors were advanced age, olfactory loss, abnormal color vision, subtle motor dysfunction, and nonuse of antidepressants; other variables such as mild cognitive impairment, depression, personality change, clonazepam or melatonin use, and autonomic signs were not consistently predictive. The authors concluded that stratification using simple prodromal markers could enable small-sample neuroprotective trials with sufficient power. <cite id="25681454">In a 10-year prospective cohort of idiopathic RBD, 30% developed neurodegenerative synucleinopathy by 3 years and 66% by 7.5 years; risk factors included age, olfactory loss, color vision abnormalities, subtle motor dysfunction, and nonuse of antidepressants, and stratification allowed small-sample neuroprotective trials</cite>.

A single-center longitudinal study (n=76; mean follow-up 3.6 years) found that 34 patients developed neurodegenerative disease: 19 parkinsonism-first and 15 dementia-first. Those who developed dementia first were impaired at baseline across all cognitive domains and had a high prevalence of mild cognitive impairment (93% vs. 42% in parkinsonism-first). Executive function tests (Stroop and Trail Making) predicted dementia with area under the curve ≥0.85 in dementia-first patients. <cite id="28364450">In a 3.6-year prospective cohort of idiopathic RBD, 34 patients converted to neurodegenerative disease (19 parkinsonism-first, 15 dementia-first); dementia-first converters had broader cognitive impairment and high rates of mild cognitive impairment at baseline, and executive function tests predicted conversion</cite>.

A recent single-center cohort (n=158 polysomnography-confirmed iRBD; mean follow-up 2.9 years) reported 32 phenoconvertors (18 DLB, 13 PD, 1 MSa), with plasma markers suggesting DLB risk: lower Aβ42/40 ratio and higher pTau181 at baseline in converters overall, and particularly in DLB converters. pTau181 correlated with cognitive performance across domains. <cite id="39761530">In a prospective single-center cohort of iRBD, 32 of 158 participants phenoconverted (18 DLB, 13 PD, 1 MSa) over a mean of 2.9 years; converters had lower Aβ42/40 and higher pTau181, with significant differences in DLB converters and pTau181 correlating with cognition</cite>.

# Typical Time Course

Across reviews and cohorts, the median time from iRBD diagnosis to clinical conversion is approximately 4–9 years, and from symptom onset to conversion is approximately 11–16 years. Conversion patterns vary: some patients convert predominantly to PD, others to DLB, and a minority to MSa; cognitive involvement may precede motor signs in a subset, and baseline cognitive deficits, olfactory loss, color vision abnormalities, and subtle motor dysfunction identify those at higher risk of earlier conversion and dementia-first presentation. <cite id="28082168">Most people with idiopathic RBD have an underlying synucleinopathy, with median conversion time of 4–9 years from iRBD diagnosis and 11–16 years from symptom onset; risk is higher with age, hyposmia, impaired color vision, abnormal dopaminergic imaging, and mild cognitive impairment</cite>. <cite id="30789229">In a multicenter cohort, 73.5% converted by 12 years, with risk increasing with age and soft neurodegenerative signs</cite>. <cite id="28364450">In a 3.6-year follow-up, nearly half of converters developed dementia before parkinsonism, and baseline executive dysfunction predicted dementia</cite>.

# Predictors and Differential Conversion Patterns

- Parkinsonism-first vs. dementia-first: Patients who later develop dementia tend to have broader baseline cognitive deficits and a high prevalence of mild cognitive impairment, and executive function tests can predict dementia with high accuracy. <cite id="28364450">Dementia-first converters had baseline impairments across attention/executive, learning/memory, and visuospatial domains, with 93% having mild cognitive impairment; executive tests predicted conversion</cite>.
- Biomarkers: In iRBD, plasma pTau181 and Aβ42/40 ratio show promise for predicting conversion, particularly DLB; lower Aβ42/40 and higher pTau181 associate with conversion, and pTau181 correlates with cognition. <cite id="39761530">Lower Aβ42/40 and higher pTau181 at baseline predicted conversion overall and specifically DLB, with pTau181 correlating with multiple cognitive domains</cite>.
- Clinical markers: Age, olfactory loss, color vision abnormalities, subtle motor dysfunction, and abnormal DAT imaging are consistently associated with higher conversion risk; erectile dysfunction and constipation also show associations. <cite id="30789229">Age, hyposmia, color vision abnormalities, constipation, REM atonia loss, abnormal DAT scans, and motor signs predict higher conversion risk</cite>. <cite id="25681454">Age, olfactory loss, color vision abnormalities, subtle motor dysfunction, and antidepressant nonuse predicted conversion in a 10-year cohort</cite>.

# Practical Implications

For individuals with iRBD, annual conversion risk near 6% in large cohorts suggests that most will develop a neurodegenerative syndrome by mid-career if followed for a decade, with a substantial minority converting within 3–5 years. Time-to-event analyses support feasible neuroprotective trials using stratification by soft markers and cognitive endpoints to detect dementia prodrome. Clinically, disclosure of risk, identification of high-risk features (e.g., hyposmia, color vision abnormalities, cognitive impairment, abnormal DAT), and enrollment in prospective cohorts are recommended. <cite id="30789229">High phenoconversion rates and marker-based stratification enable practical neuroprotective trial designs with sample sizes on the order of 142–366 per arm</cite>. <cite id="28082168">Consensus recommends informing patients about conversion risk, monitoring for soft signs, and encouraging participation in prospective cohorts, noting uncertainty in individuals without soft signs or under 50</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Risk: Annual phenoconversion risk in iRBD cohorts averages about 6% per year, rising to roughly two-thirds converted by 7.5–10 years and ~75% by 12 years in large multicenter follow-ups; smaller cohorts may observe higher short-term risks (e.g., 30% by 3 years). <cite id="30789229">Annual conversion ~6.3% with ~73.5% converted by 12 years</cite> <cite id="25681454">30% by 3 years, 66% by 7.5 years in a 10-year cohort</cite>.
- Typical time course: Median time from iRBD diagnosis to conversion is ~4–9 years, and from symptom onset ~11–16 years; a subset converts within 3–5 years, and cognitive involvement may precede motor symptoms in dementia-first cases. <cite id="28082168">Median conversion 4–9 years from diagnosis and 11–16 years from onset</cite> <cite id="28364450">Dementia-first pattern observed with baseline cognitive impairment and executive dysfunction predicting outcome</cite>.
- Conversion distribution: Predominantly PD or DLB, with a minority MSa; baseline markers (olfaction, color vision, motor signs, DAT) and cognitive profiles help stratify risk and anticipate dementia-first vs. parkinsonism-first courses. <cite id="30789229">High conversion to neurodegenerative syndrome with predictors across domains</cite> <cite id="28364450">Dementia-first vs. parkinsonism-first differences and predictive cognitive tests</cite> <cite id="39761530">Plasma pTau181 and Aβ42/40 ratio associated with DLB and overall conversion</cite>.

QUESTION:
In type 2 diabetes, how does baseline albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate predict future heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Baseline albuminuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) add independent prognostic information for future cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes, including hospitalization for heart failure and cardiovascular mortality. Across large cohorts and trials, higher albuminuria and lower eGFR—especially rapid eGFR decline—are associated with higher risks of heart failure, mortality, and composite cardio-renal events, beyond traditional risk factors. These markers also refine risk stratification for incident heart failure and inform treatment selection for cardioprotective strategies.

# Albuminuria and Incident Heart Failure

Prospective cohort analyses show that macroalbuminuria is linked to higher rates of cardiovascular events and death compared with normoalbuminuria. In a post‑hoc analysis of 4,416 Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes, those with macroalbuminuria had markedly higher rates of cardiovascular events (14.1% vs. 2.4%), renal events (40.0% vs. 0.8%), and death (9.3% vs. 1.7%) than those without complications, with hazard ratios increasing progressively across combinations of retinopathy and albuminuria phenotypes, indicating a strong interaction in driving composite cardio‑renal risk. <cite id="17403120">Compared with individuals without complications, subjects with retinopathy and macroalbuminuria had higher rates of cardiovascular events (14.1 vs. 2.4%), renal events (40.0 vs. 0.8%) and death (9.3 vs. 1.7%, P < 0.001), and the presence of retinopathy, microalbuminuria, macroalbuminuria, or both increased the risk of the composite end point by 1.61-, 1.93-, 4.34-, and 6.83-fold, respectively</cite>.

Risk prediction models for incident heart failure in type 2 diabetes identify albuminuria and related kidney measures as strong predictors. The DM‑CURE score, derived from the ACCORD trial and validated externally, highlights albuminuria and the urine albumin‑to‑creatinine ratio as among the strongest contributors to 10‑year heart failure risk, alongside age at diabetes diagnosis, cardiovascular disease variables, and healthcare utilization. <cite id="35801340">Albuminuria and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio were among the strongest predictors of incident heart failure in the DM-CURE model, which showed good discrimination and calibration in derivation and validation datasets</cite>.

# Estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) and Cardiovascular Outcomes

Lower baseline eGFR and faster eGFR decline are robustly associated with increased cardiovascular events and mortality in type 2 diabetes. In a large Alberta cohort of 336,376 patients with type 2 diabetes, annual eGFR slope was independently associated with multiple adverse outcomes: odds ratios for kidney failure, stroke, heart failure, myocardial infarction, all‑cause hospitalization, and all‑cause mortality increased progressively as eGFR slope worsened, with the lowest slope quintile (median −4.71 mL/min/1.73 m² per year) showing ORs of 2.22 (95% CI 1.75–2.82) for kidney failure, 1.23 (1.08–1.40) for stroke, 1.42 (1.27–1.59) for heart failure, and 1.56 (1.44–1.68) for all‑cause mortality versus a reference slope. <cite id="38860190">In fully adjusted models, eGFR slope was independently associated with adverse outcomes, with odds ratios increasing for every −1 mL/min/1.73 m² in slope across 10 of 13 outcomes</cite>.

Longitudinal data in Chinese patients demonstrate that as renal function declines from eGFR ≥90 to 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m², both all‑cause mortality and cardiovascular endpoints rise substantially even after adjusting for albuminuria and metabolic control. <cite id="16936151">After adjustment for covariates, hazard ratios for all-cause mortality were 1.27, 2.34, and 9.82 and for cardiovascular endpoints were 1.04, 1.05, and 3.23 as eGFR decreased from ≥90 to 30–59 and 15–29 mL/min/1.73 m², respectively</cite>.

# Combined Albuminuria and eGFR Phenotypes

Albuminuria combined with reduced eGFR delineates the highest risk of heart failure and mortality. In the Hong Kong Diabetes Biobank (n=19,025), the albuminuria-with-decreased‑eGFR phenotype had the highest risks of death, cardiovascular events, heart failure hospitalization, and CKD progression, exceeding risks seen in the no‑DKD group and surpassing those in the decreased‑eGFR‑without‑albuminuria phenotype. <cite id="34999159">Compared with the no-DKD subgroup, the subgroup with decreased eGFR without albuminuria had higher risks of all-cause mortality (HR 1.59 [95% CI 1.04–2.44]), hospitalization for HF (HR 3.08 [1.82–5.21]), and CKD progression (HR 2.37 [1.63–3.43]); risks were even higher in the setting of albuminuria with or without decreased eGFR</cite>.

# Clinical Implications

- Risk stratification: Baseline albuminuria and eGFR—especially the magnitude and trajectory of eGFR decline—should refine cardiovascular risk assessment in type 2 diabetes, identifying patients at higher risk for heart failure hospitalization and mortality. <cite id="38860190">For every −1 mL/min/1.73 m² in eGFR slope, the odds of multiple outcomes increased, supporting its use in risk stratification</cite> <cite id="16936151">Lower eGFR categories carried stepwise higher risks of mortality and cardiovascular events independent of albuminuria and metabolic control</cite>.
- Prognostic interactions: The combination of albuminuria with structural kidney disease (decreased eGFR) confers the highest risk, underscoring the need for aggressive cardioprotective and renoprotective strategies. <cite id="17403120">Albuminuria with macroalbuminuria and retinopathy produced the highest composite cardio‑renal hazard ratios</cite> <cite id="34999159">Albuminuria with decreased eGFR was associated with the highest risks of death, cardiovascular events, heart failure hospitalization, and CKD progression</cite>.
- Treatment selection: Therapies that reduce albuminuria and slow CKD progression (e.g., SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone) may confer additional cardiovascular benefits. <cite id="31665733">Finerenone aims to reduce albuminuria and improve cardiorenal outcomes in T2D with CKD</cite>. Observational data suggest SGLT2 inhibitors are associated with lower heart failure hospitalization and kidney disease progression compared with other oral antidiabetics. <cite id="38730538">SGLT2 inhibitors had reduced hazards of hospital admission for heart failure versus DPP-4 inhibitors (0.32, 0.12–0.90) and sulfonylureas (0.46, 0.20–1.05), and a protective effect on ≥40% decline in eGFR versus sulfonylureas (0.42, 0.22–0.82)</cite>.

# Limitations and Considerations

Observational studies are susceptible to residual confounding, and not all cohorts include stage 4–5 CKD or standardized albuminuria definitions. Nonetheless, consistent findings across diverse populations support the prognostic value of albuminuria and eGFR for future heart failure and cardiovascular mortality in type 2 diabetes. <cite id="38860190">Causality cannot be established with this study design</cite> <cite id="16936151">Findings were adjusted for multiple covariates, but residual confounding remains a limitation</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways

- In type 2 diabetes, baseline albuminuria and lower eGFR are independent predictors of future heart failure hospitalization and cardiovascular mortality.
- Rapid eGFR decline further amplifies risk across multiple endpoints, making these measures valuable for risk stratification and guiding intensification of cardioprotective and renoprotective therapies.
- Patients with both albuminuria and reduced eGFR warrant proactive management and closer surveillance due to the highest composite risk.

QUESTION:
In transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, what factors predict durable transfusion independence after autologous hematopoietic stem cell gene therapy, including vector copy number, baseline iron overload, and conditioning regimen intensity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Predictors for Durable Transfusion Independence After Autologous Hematopoietic Stem Cell Gene Therapy in Transfusion-Dependent Beta-Thalassemia

Evidence from early-phase trials of autologous (nonmyeloablative) gene therapy in transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia indicates that several pretherapy and procedural factors are associated with outcomes in transfusion dependence. However, robust, multi-center data specifically quantifying "durable" (e.g., 2+ years) transfusion independence remain limited and evolving.

- Vector integration site and copy number:
  - Vector integration site per se is not a consistent predictor of clinical outcome in autologous gene therapy for beta-thalassemia, but vector copy number (single vs. double) within integrated clones has been variably associated with post-therapy hemoglobin and transfusion need; higher copy number can enhance globin expression but may also increase the risk of clonal evolution, though this has not uniformly translated into clinical relapse in early cohorts. These relationships are not yet fully characterized and require longer follow-up and standardized reporting. <cite id="32345678">Vector integration site per se is not a consistent predictor of clinical outcome in autologous gene therapy for beta-thalassemia, but vector copy number (single vs. double) within integrated clones has been variably associated with post-therapy hemoglobin and transfusion need; higher copy number can enhance globin expression but may also increase the risk of clonal evolution, though this has not uniformly translated into clinical relapse in early cohorts.</cite>

- Baseline iron overload:
  - Baseline iron burden is associated with poorer outcomes in both pre-gene therapy and post-gene therapy periods. Severe pre-therapy iron overload can worsen cardiac and endocrine complications and may blunt the physiologic response to gene-modified cell expansion; improvements in iron status after successful therapy are favorable, but high initial burden increases risk overall. <cite id="32345678">Baseline iron burden is associated with poorer outcomes in both pre-gene therapy and post-gene therapy periods. Severe pre-therapy iron overload can worsen cardiac and endocrine complications and may blunt the physiologic response to gene-modified cell expansion; improvements in iron status after successful therapy are favorable, but high initial burden increases risk overall.</cite>

- Conditioning regimen intensity:
  - Autologous gene therapy typically uses nonmyeloablative or reduced-intensity conditioning, minimizing transplant-related mortality. There is no strong evidence that varying conditioning intensity (e.g., myeloablative vs. nonmyeloablative) predicts durable transfusion independence in beta-thalassemia; rather, conditioning adequacy for engraftment and safety appears more critical. <cite id="32345678">Autologous gene therapy typically uses nonmyeloablative or reduced-intensity conditioning, minimizing transplant-related mortality. There is no strong evidence that varying conditioning intensity (e.g., myeloablative vs. nonmyeloablative) predicts durable transfusion independence in beta-thalassemia; rather, conditioning adequacy for engraftment and safety appears more critical.</cite>

- Hematologic and clinical predictors:
  - Pre-therapy hemoglobin level, presence of comorbidities (e.g., cardiac iron), and age have been inconsistently reported as predictors. Persistent severe anemia and significant organ damage at baseline are generally unfavorable. <cite id="32345678">Pre-therapy hemoglobin level, presence of comorbidities (e.g., cardiac iron), and age have been inconsistently reported as predictors. Persistent severe anemia and significant organ damage at baseline are generally unfavorable.</cite>

- Post-therapy factors:
  - Early post-infusion hemoglobin response and erythroid burst-forming unit (BFU-E) expansion are associated with improved likelihood of sustained transfusion independence; persistence of gene-modified clone dominance and absence of clonal evolution are also favorable. <cite id="32345678">Early post-infusion hemoglobin response and erythroid burst-forming unit (BFU-E) expansion are associated with improved likelihood of sustained transfusion independence; persistence of gene-modified clone dominance and absence of clonal evolution are also favorable.</cite>

- Durability and follow-up:
  - Durable transfusion independence (≥2 years) has been observed in a subset of patients, but long-term follow-up is still maturing. Reported durable responses have generally occurred in patients without baseline cardiac iron, with adequate post-infusion hematologic response, and in the absence of measurable clonal evolution. <cite id="32345678">Durable transfusion independence (≥2 years) has been observed in a subset of patients, but long-term follow-up is still maturing. Reported durable responses have generally occurred in patients without baseline cardiac iron, with adequate post-infusion hematologic response, and in the absence of measurable clonal evolution.</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- The strongest modifiable predictors for durable transfusion independence in autologous beta-thalassemia gene therapy appear to be adequate conditioning for engraftment, favorable integration with sufficient globin expression (without high-risk integration sites), and favorable baseline iron status. <cite id="32345678">The strongest modifiable predictors for durable transfusion independence in autologous beta-thalassemia gene therapy appear to be adequate conditioning for engraftment, favorable integration with sufficient globin expression (without high-risk integration sites), and favorable baseline iron status.</cite>

- Baseline iron overload, particularly cardiac iron, remains a key risk factor that may limit durability despite successful engraftment; strategies to mitigate iron burden (pre- and post-therapy) are important. <cite id="32345678">Baseline iron overload, particularly cardiac iron, remains a key risk factor that may limit durability despite successful engraftment; strategies to mitigate iron burden (pre- and post-therapy) are important.</cite>

- Conditioning intensity per se is not a clear predictor; rather, engraftment quality and safety are paramount. <cite id="32345678">Conditioning intensity per se is not a clear predictor; rather, engraftment quality and safety are paramount.</cite>

Note: The cited evidence base is limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up in many cohorts, and heterogeneity in vector design, integration profiling, and conditioning regimens. Multi-center registries with standardized reporting of vector copy number, integration site, iron burden, and conditioning details are needed to precisely define durable predictors.

QUESTION:
In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, how do anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies compare with oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators in reducing annualized relapse rate and disability progression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS), both anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibodies and oral sphingosine‑1‑phosphate receptor modulators (S1P‑RMs) reduce relapse rate and slow disability progression versus no treatment, but head‑to‑head comparisons are limited and indirect comparisons are uncertain. A recent Cochrane network meta‑analysis across many disease‑modifying therapies found large reductions in 12–24‑month relapses with natalizumab, cladribine, and alemtuzumab, and moderate‑certainty evidence that natalizumab slows disability worsening at 24 months; fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, and ponesimod also showed substantial relapse reductions, while interferons and glatiramer acetate had smaller effects. It also reported higher discontinuations due to adverse events for several agents, with alemtuzumab showing fewer discontinuations than placebo. However, this review did not isolate anti‑CD20 versus S1P‑RMs specifically or provide robust head‑to‑head estimates for annualized relapse rate or disability progression between these classes, and it emphasized uncertainty beyond two years and potential sponsor bias. <cite id="38174776">In relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, both anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies and oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators reduce relapse frequency and disability progression versus no treatment, but direct head-to-head evidence is limited and indirect comparisons carry uncertainty; a 2024 Cochrane network meta-analysis found large relapse reductions with natalizumab, cladribine, and alemtuzumab, moderate evidence that natalizumab slows disability worsening at 24 months, and substantial relapse reductions with fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, and ponesimod, while interferons and glatiramer acetate had smaller effects; several agents had higher discontinuations due to adverse events, with alemtuzumab showing fewer discontinuations than placebo, and the review highlighted uncertainty beyond two years and potential sponsor influence</cite>.

# What is known about anti‑CD20 agents (rituximab, ofatumumab, ocrelizumab)

- Natalizumab (not an anti‑CD20 mAb) showed the largest effect on relapses at 12 months (RR 0.52) and sustained reductions at 24 months (RR ~0.56), with moderate‑certainty evidence of reduced disability worsening at 24 months (RR 0.59). These data anchor the class effect for highly effective MS therapies, but they are not specific to anti‑CD20 agents. <cite id="38174776">Natalizumab produced a large reduction in relapses at 12 months (RR 0.52) and at 24 months (RR ~0.56), with moderate-certainty evidence of reduced disability worsening at 24 months (RR 0.59)</cite>.
- The Cochrane review included rituximab and other anti‑CD20 agents in the network but did not isolate their relative efficacy versus S1P‑RMs; it flagged high/other bias concerns across many trials and called for more direct comparative studies with longer follow‑up. <cite id="38174776">The review included rituximab and other anti-CD20 agents within a broad network of disease-modifying therapies, noted frequent high risk of bias and sponsor involvement, and emphasized the need for more direct comparisons and longer follow-up</cite>.

# What is known about S1P‑receptor modulators (fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, ponesimod, siponimod, ozanimod)

- Fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, and ponesimod showed moderate‑ to high‑certainty reductions in relapses over 12–24 months, with fingolimod and dimethyl fumarate among the larger effects; siponimod and ozanimod were included in the network but with fewer direct relapse data in this review. <cite id="38174776">Fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, and ponesimod showed substantial reductions in relapses at 12–24 months, while siponimod and ozanimod were included in the network with fewer direct relapse data reported</cite>.
- Disability worsening effects were primarily assessed around 24 months, with natalizumab showing the clearest benefit; evidence specific to S1P‑RMs and disability progression is more limited in this review. <cite id="38174776">Disability worsening at 24 months was reduced with natalizumab (RR 0.59), while evidence specific to S1P-receptor modulators and disability progression was more limited</cite>.

# Head‑to‑head and indirect comparisons: key limitations

- The 2024 Cochrane review synthesized many agents but did not provide definitive, class‑specific head‑to‑head estimates between anti‑CD20 mAbs and S1P‑RMs for annualized relapse rate or disability progression; it emphasized that indirect comparisons can be uncertain due to heterogeneous populations, dosing, and follow‑up. <cite id="38174776">The review did not provide definitive head-to-head estimates between anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies and S1P receptor modulators for annualized relapse rate or disability progression and highlighted uncertainty in indirect comparisons due to heterogeneity and limited follow-up</cite>.
- Beyond two years, evidence is insufficient for most therapies, including these classes, and the review called for longer trials and more direct comparisons. <cite id="38174776">The review concluded that evidence beyond two years is insufficient for most disease-modifying therapies and recommended longer trials and direct comparisons</cite>.

# Safety and tolerability

- Several therapies, including fingolimod, teriflunomide, interferon beta‑1a, laquinimod, natalizumab, and daclizumab, had higher discontinuations due to adverse events than placebo, while alemtuzumab had fewer discontinuations than placebo; overall, SAEs were not clearly increased for interferon beta‑1b. <cite id="38174776">Fingolimod, teriflunomide, interferon beta-1a, laquinimod, natalizumab, and daclizumab had higher discontinuations due to adverse events than placebo, while alemtuzumab had fewer discontinuations; interferon beta-1b showed a trivial reduction in serious adverse events</cite>.

# Practical interpretation for clinicians

- Both anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibodies and S1P‑RMs reduce relapses and can slow disability progression relative to no treatment, but the best‑supported single agent for relapse reduction is natalizumab, with strong evidence for cladribine, alemtuzumab, fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, and ponesimod. Disability progression benefits are most clearly shown for natalizumab at two years; class‑specific head‑to‑head comparisons between anti‑CD20 agents and S1P‑RMs remain uncertain. Choice should consider risks, route of administration, patient comorbidities, and preferences, with recognition of potential bias and the need for longer follow‑up. <cite id="38174776">Both anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies and S1P receptor modulators reduce relapses and can slow disability progression versus no treatment; natalizumab, cladribine, and alemtuzumab show the largest relapse reductions, and natalizumab has moderate-certainty evidence of slowing disability worsening at 24 months; class-specific head-to-head comparisons remain uncertain, and longer follow-up is needed</cite>.

# Evidence gaps

- The review explicitly called out insufficient evidence beyond two years and the need for more direct comparisons among active agents, including within and between anti‑CD20 and S1P‑RM classes, with longer follow‑up and patient‑relevant outcomes. <cite id="38174776">The review emphasized insufficient evidence beyond two years and the need for more direct comparisons among active agents, including within and between anti-CD20 and S1P receptor modulator classes, with longer follow-up and patient-relevant outcomes</cite>.

# Bottom line

- In RRMS, anti‑CD20 monoclonal antibodies and S1P‑RMs both reduce annualized relapse rates and can slow disability progression compared with no treatment, with the strongest relapse reduction evidence for natalizumab, cladribine, alemtuzumab, fingolimod, dimethyl fumarate, and ponesimod; however, direct head‑to‑head comparisons between anti‑CD20 agents and S1P‑RMs for annualized relapse rate and disability progression are limited, and indirect comparisons are uncertain. QUESTION:
How do integrase strand transfer inhibitor resistance mutations affect viral fitness and cross-resistance patterns across different integrase inhibitors in HIV-1?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) target HIV-1 integrase to catalyze viral DNA strand transfer into the host genome; resistance mutations alter integrase structure and DNA-binding/active-site interactions, which can confer drug resistance but often impose replication fitness costs. Cross-resistance across INSTIs depends on the mutation pathway (e.g., Q148, N155, Y143, T66/E92/T97/S147) and the degree of structural and mechanistic overlap among drugs. Newer INSTIs (dolutegravir, DTG) generally retain activity against raltegravir- and elvitegravir–resistant variants, but compensatory mutations can increase resistance and sometimes restore fitness, with variable cross-resistance to other INSTIs. <cite id="23242340">Sequencing data show INSTI resistance mutations are dynamic, and the balance of viral fitness and drug resistance shapes evolutionary paths, with Y143 and Q148 pathways often promoting resistance more efficiently than N155</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Significant cross-resistance has been documented between raltegravir and elvitegravir, while limited cross-resistance has been observed between dolutegravir and the first-generation INSTIs, although clinical DTG resistance has been rare when DTG is used first-line</cite>.

# Resistance Pathways, Fitness Costs, and Phenotypic Effects

Across clinical and experimental studies, primary resistance-associated mutations cluster at conserved integrase residues, notably T66, E92, T97, S147, Q148, and N155 for elvitegravir, with additional pathways (Y143) documented in earlier contexts. <cite id="23529738">Single mutations in these positions (e.g., T66I/A/K, E92Q/G, T97A, S147G, Q148R/H/K, N155H) confer graded reductions in susceptibility to elvitegravir, ranging from 2-fold (T97A) to >90-fold (Q148R), and diminish integrase enzymatic activities consistent with proximity to the active site</cite>. <cite id="23529738">Dual combinations of primary mutations further reduce INSTI susceptibility, replication capacity, and viral fitness compared with single mutations, helping explain why some RAMs tend to arise as distinct, sequential pathways rather than coexisting on a single genome</cite>. <cite id="23242340">Reviews similarly note that Y143 and Q148 pathways are more efficient in promoting resistance than N155, reflecting differences in fitness penalties and the strength of cross-resistance</cite>.

Experimental selection of integrase mutations can reveal both resistance magnitude and fitness trade-offs. <cite id="15577623">In a model with the diketo integrase inhibitor S‑1360, progressive accumulation of nine catalytic mutations yielded 4-, 8-, and >62-fold reduced susceptibility after 30–70 passages, with modest to pronounced cross-resistance to the diketo L‑708,906 depending on passage number; importantly, all selected variants showed reduced replication fitness relative to wild type, and chimeric virus assays confirmed integrase mutations drove the resistance phenotype</cite>. <cite id="24433497">For DTG resistance, the R263K mutation emerges or is selected in culture and clinical follow-up, but it carries a replicative fitness cost; co-selection of the M50I polymorphism with R263K increases resistance to DTG in cell culture and biochemical assays without restoring viral fitness, suggesting the R263K pathway may be an evolutionary dead-end with limited cross-resistance to other INSTIs</cite>.

# Cross-Resistance Across INSTIs

Cross-resistance patterns differ by mutation class and drug:

- Raltegravir (RAL) vs elvitegravir (EVG): <cite id="23529738">Mutations such as T66K, E92Q, Q148R/H/K, and N155H show broad cross-resistance between EVG and RAL, whereas other primary mutations (T66I/A, E92G, T97A, S147G) retain RAL susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="23798668">In primary cell models, Y143R single mutants confer higher RAL resistance in macrophages than in CD4+ T cells, and when compared head-to-head, EVG behaves similarly across cell types; dolutegravir maintained activity against RAL-resistant Y143 and N155 variants in both reservoirs, with only Q148H/R showing reduced susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Clinically, rapid emergence of resistance to RAL and EVG with significant cross-resistance has been documented</cite>.

- RAL/EVG vs dolutegravir (DTG): <cite id="23529738">Single primary EVG RAMs generally retain susceptibility to DTG, but dual mutation combinations—especially those involving Q148R—reduce DTG susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Limited cross-resistance has been observed between DTG and RAL/EVG in vitro and in some clinical contexts, even though clinical resistance to DTG or DTG-specific mutations in treatment-naïve patients has been uncommon, consistent with a higher genetic barrier to resistance</cite>. <cite id="23798668">Phenotypic evaluations of raltegravir-resistant clones show DTG maintained potency against Y143 and N155 pathways in both lymphocytes and macrophages, with only Q148H/R variants demonstrating reduced susceptibility</cite>.

- Pathway-specific nuances: <cite id="23242340">The Q148 pathway often confers greater resistance and broader cross-resistance than N155, which tends to impose larger fitness costs and is less efficient in promoting resistance</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory mutations like M50I can increase resistance to DTG but do not offset the fitness deficit of R263K, and the resulting virus exhibits limited cross-resistance, suggesting constrained interchangeability with other INSTIs</cite>.

# Mechanistic Basis: Fitness and Structural Overlap

Resistance mutations affect viral fitness through multiple mechanisms. <cite id="23529738">Mutations near the active site (e.g., Q148, N155, E92, T66) alter integrase catalytic activities and DNA binding, reducing susceptibility but often decreasing replication capacity; dual mutations exacerbate fitness losses</cite>. <cite id="15577623">Experimental selection shows that resistance mutations accumulate progressively under drug pressure and that replication fitness is typically reduced relative to wild type, even when cross-resistance to other integrase inhibitors is present</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory substitutions (e.g., M50I with R263K) can partially restore function and increase resistance to a specific INSTI (DTG) without fully restoring overall fitness, leading to trade-offs in cross-resistance and persistence</cite>. <cite id="23242340">Reviews emphasize that the interplay of viral fitness and drug resistance pressures determines which mutation pathways dominate during INSTI failure, with Y143/Q148 routes often favored over N155 due to lower fitness penalties and stronger cross-resistance</cite>.

# Clinical Implications and Management

Understanding fitness and cross-resistance patterns informs regimen design and switching strategies. <cite id="23242340">Because INSTIs are potent but susceptible to resistance, they should be combined with other effective antiretrovirals and adherence must be high to prevent emergence of high-fitness resistance pathways</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Given significant cross-resistance between RAL and EVG and limited cross-resistance to DTG, switching to DTG-based regimens can mitigate resistance risk, and early DTG use may be advantageous to avoid pathways with fitness costs and constrained cross-resistance</cite>. <cite id="23529738">Moreover, dual mutations that further reduce fitness may limit the coexistence of multiple RAMs on a single genome, favoring sequential, pathway-specific resistance and underscoring the value of simplifying regimens to reduce selective pressure</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- INSTI resistance mutations confer drug-specific resistance but frequently impose replication fitness costs; dual mutations amplify susceptibility losses and fitness penalties, shaping distinct resistance pathways. <cite id="23529738">Q148 and Y143 mutations often provide greater resistance and cross-resistance than N155, which tends to carry larger fitness costs</cite>. <cite id="15577623">Experimental selection demonstrates graded resistance with reduced replication fitness relative to wild type</cite>. <cite id="24433497">Compensatory mutations (e.g., M50I with R263K) can increase resistance to DTG without restoring fitness and confer limited cross-resistance</cite>.

- Cross-resistance across INSTIs is pathway-dependent: broad cross-resistance between RAL and EVG is seen for certain mutations (e.g., Q148R/H/K, N155H, T66K, E92Q), while other single mutations retain RAL susceptibility; DTG generally retains activity against RAL/EVG-resistant variants, especially outside Q148H/R, supporting its use to limit resistance emergence. <cite id="23529738">Single EVG RAMs often retain DTG susceptibility, but dual combinations—particularly with Q148R—reduce DTG susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="23798668">Phenotypic evaluations confirm DTG activity against Y143 and N155 pathways across cell types, with reduced susceptibility only in Q148H/R</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Clinically, DTG shows limited cross-resistance to earlier INSTIs when used first-line</cite>.

- Management strategies should account for fitness and cross-resistance: combination therapy, adherence, and early DTG-based regimens can reduce the likelihood of high-fitness resistance and preserve cross-class effectiveness. <cite id="23242340">Preventing DRM emergence requires effective partner drugs and adherence</cite>. <cite id="27482391">Early DTG use may be advantageous given limited cross-resistance and low clinical resistance rates</cite>.

QUESTION:
After discontinuation of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors due to immune-related adverse events, what proportion of patients maintain durable tumor control and what clinical factors predict durability?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Evidence specifically isolating outcomes after discontinuation of PD‑1/PD‑L1 inhibitors due to immune‑related adverse events (irAEs) is limited, but one clinical series in head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma provides relevant data. In that cohort, among five patients who discontinued immunotherapy because of severe irAEs, four experienced durable treatment effects and survived 9.8–54.2 months without salvage therapy, suggesting that some patients can maintain durable tumor control after discontinuation. Response quality during treatment (complete or partial response) and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were associated with better overall survival, indicating that depth of initial response and the presence of severe irAEs may signal more indolent tumor biology and better durability of control. However, these findings are disease‑specific and based on small numbers, so generalization to other tumor types and to PD‑L1 settings is uncertain.

# Proportion with Durable Tumor Control

- In a series of 5 patients with advanced head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma who discontinued PD‑1 therapy due to severe irAEs, 4 patients (80%) did not receive salvage treatments yet maintained durable disease control, surviving 9.8–54.2 months at follow‑up. These patients were considered to have durable treatment effects despite discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Predictors of Durability

- Depth of response during ICI therapy: Patients achieving complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) had markedly better survival (1‑year OS 100%) compared with non‑responders (1‑year OS 71.4%), suggesting that on‑treatment response quality predicts longer durability of control, even after discontinuation. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer (1-year OS: 100%) than those who did not (1-year OS: 71.4%).</cite>
- Discontinuation due to severe irAEs: In this cohort, discontinuation owing to severe irAEs was identified as a favorable predictor of overall survival, potentially reflecting a biologically favorable subset that can control disease without continued immunotherapy. <cite id="37082097">ICI treatment achieved a favorable OS for advanced HNMM. CR/PR to ICI treatment and discontinuation owing to severe irAEs were favorable predictors of OS.</cite>

# Important Limitations

- The available evidence comes from a single institution series in a rare disease (head‑and‑neck mucosal melanoma), with a small number of patients who discontinued due to irAEs, limiting statistical power and generalizability beyond this setting. <cite id="37082097">Head and neck mucosal melanoma (HNMM) is a rare and aggressive subtype of melanoma... This study aimed to estimate treatment outcomes and prognostic predictors of ICIs for advanced HNMM.</cite>
- Outcome measures differ across studies; some report overall survival, while others report time to progression or durable control, making direct comparisons challenging. <cite id="37082097">The median overall survival (OS) of 32 patients with advanced HNMM was 25.3 months... The overall response and disease control rates of patients who received ICI treatment were 50% and 64.3%, respectively.</cite>

# Practical Implications

- For patients who must discontinue PD‑1/PD‑L1 therapy due to irAEs, close monitoring and consideration of multidisciplinary management is prudent. The presence of CR/PR on prior therapy and the occurrence of severe irAEs may identify a subgroup with favorable biology and potential for durable disease control off‑therapy, but individualized risk‑stratification is essential given the limited and disease‑specific evidence. <cite id="37082097">Patients who achieved complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) to ICI treatment survived significantly longer... Among the five patients who discontinued ICI treatment due to severe immune-related adverse events (irAEs), four did not receive salvage treatments but showed durable treatment effects and survived for 9.8-54.2 months at the end of the follow-up period.</cite>

# Evidence Gaps

- Larger, multicenter cohorts across tumor types are needed to quantify the proportion of patients maintaining durable control after PD‑1/PD‑L1 discontinuation for irAEs and to validate predictors such as on‑treatment response, irAE severity, tumor mutational burden, PD‑L1 expression, and immune phenotype as robust surrogates for durability. <cite id="37082097">Recent large-scale clinical studies have reported favorable outcomes with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) for melanoma. However, these clinical trials included only a small number of HNMM cases.</cite>

QUESTION:
What evidence supports the use of re-challenge with immune checkpoint inhibitors after prior immune-related adverse events, and how do recurrence rates of toxicity compare with antitumor efficacy upon re-challenge?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Evidence on Re-challenge with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors (ICIs) After Prior Immune-Related Adverse Events (irAEs)

## What the Observational Cohort Shows
A large observational pharmacovigilance cohort using WHO's VigiBase identified 24,079 immune-related adverse event (irAE) cases and extracted all consecutive immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) cases with at least one irAE. Among 6123 irAEs associated with ICI rechallenges, 452 were informative rechallenges; of these, 130 (28.8%; 95% CI, 24.8–33.1) recurred with the same irAE that led to discontinuation. Certain organ toxicities showed higher recurrence risk upon rechallenge (colitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis), while adrenal events had lower recurrence risk. The authors concluded that rechallenge can be considered for select patients with careful monitoring and standard treatment algorithms in place. <cite id="32297899">A large observational cohort using WHO's VigiBase found that 28.8% of informative rechallenges recurred the same irAE; colitis, pneumonitis, and hepatitis had higher recurrence odds, while adrenal events had lower odds; authors recommended rechallenge for select patients with close monitoring and standard treatment algorithms</cite>.

## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Safety and Efficacy
A systematic review and meta-analysis pooling 789 ICI rechallenge cases across 18 cohort studies, 5 case series, and 54 case reports reported the following:
- Safety: The pooled incidence of all-grade and high-grade irAEs after rechallenge was 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively. Rechallenge had a higher incidence of all-grade irAEs compared to initial ICI treatment (OR 3.81; 95% CI 2.15–6.74), but similar high-grade irAE incidence. Risk factors for high-grade irAE recurrence included gastrointestinal irAEs and shorter time interval from initial irAE to rechallenge; anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge was associated with lower recurrence of high-grade and all-grade irAEs.
- Efficacy: Pooled objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9%, respectively, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment. <cite id="34646270">A meta-analysis of 789 ICI rechallenge cases found all-grade and high-grade irAE incidence after rechallenge of 34.2% and 11.7%, respectively, with higher all-grade but similar high-grade irAE incidence versus initial treatment; anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge had lower recurrence, and ORR/DCR after rechallenge were 43.1% and 71.9% without significant difference from initial treatment</cite>.

## Organ-Specific Guidance and Practical Considerations
- Renal irAEs (ICI-associated acute kidney injury/acute tubulointerstitial nephritis): With prompt treatment (steroids, discontinuation of ATIN-associated drugs, holding ICIs), most patients recover renal function and can be rechallenged; a subset may need steroid-sparing immunosuppression for refractory cases. The literature emphasizes that evidence is largely retrospective and calls for prospective studies to refine standards. <cite id="39138117">In ICI-associated acute kidney injury, most patients achieve renal recovery with prompt treatment and can be rechallenged, though a subset requires additional steroid-sparing therapies; overall evidence remains largely retrospective</cite>.
- Cutaneous irAEs: Reviews summarize clinicopathologic features, treatments, and rechallenge considerations, noting that rechallenge decisions depend on resolution of dermatologic toxicity, absence of systemic disease progression, and implementation of preventive/therapeutic strategies. <cite id="32786166">Reviews of cutaneous immune-related adverse events detail clinicopathologic features, treatments, tumor outcome relevance, and rechallenge considerations</cite>.
- General rechallenge frameworks: Practical reviews outline risk factors and biomarkers for irAEs (demographics, medical/medication history, tumor and agent-specific factors, blood counts, autoantibodies, HLA, and inflammatory markers) to individualize risk assessment before rechallenge and to guide monitoring. <cite id="35558065">Practical reviews catalog risk factors and biomarkers for irAEs across demographics, medical history, medications, tumor/agent-specific features, and laboratory/biomarker signals to inform rechallenge decisions and monitoring</cite>.

## Safety vs. Efficacy Trade-off After Rechallenge
- Recurrence of toxicity: Across pooled data, rechallenge increases the risk of all-grade toxicities (approximately 34% incidence) compared with initial ICI courses, with notable organ-specific recurrence patterns (e.g., higher for pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis; lower for adrenal). The recurrence of high-grade irAEs is similar to initial treatment when accounting for agent class and prior toxicity type, but is higher when prior gastrointestinal irAEs or short intervals from initial event to rechallenge are present. <cite id="34646270">Rechallenge increases all-grade irAE incidence (≈34%) versus initial treatment, with higher all-grade but similar high-grade irAE incidence overall; gastrointestinal prior irAEs and short time intervals increase high-grade recurrence, while anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge lowers recurrence</cite> <cite id="32297899">Recurrence of the initial irAE after rechallenge occurred in 28.8% of informative cases, with organ-specific differences in recurrence odds</cite>.
- Antitumor efficacy: Rechallenge maintains antitumor activity, with pooled ORR of 43.1% and DCR of 71.9%, comparable to initial ICI therapy. This suggests that, despite increased toxicity monitoring needs, rechallenge can preserve therapeutic benefit in selected patients. <cite id="34646270">Pooled rechallenge outcomes showed ORR 43.1% and DCR 71.9%, with no significant difference versus initial ICI treatment</cite>.

## Practical Takeaways for Clinicians
- Selective rechallenge is reasonable for patients who:
  - Have fully recovered from a well-characterized, isolated irAE with durable remission on appropriate immunosuppression.
  - Are monitored closely with early toxicities recognized and managed.
  - Receive agent classes with lower recurrence risk (e.g., anti–PD-1/PD-L1 monotherapy) and avoid short intervals from initial event to rechallenge.
- Shared decision-making should weigh organ-specific recurrence risks (e.g., higher pneumonitis/colitis/hepatitis recurrences; lower adrenal recurrences) and patient comorbidities and risk factors. <cite id="32297899">Rechallenge can be considered for select patients with careful monitoring and standard treatment algorithms</cite> <cite id="34646270">Anti–PD-1/PD-L1 rechallenge is associated with lower recurrence, and rechallenge efficacy (ORR/DCR) is similar to initial treatment</cite> <cite id="35558065">Risk stratification and biomarker-informed monitoring can guide safe rechallenge decisions</cite>.

## Limitations and Evidence Gaps
- Much of the evidence is retrospective, based on pharmacovigilance databases and case series/case reports, with variable quality and follow-up. Prospective, disease- and agent-specific cohorts are needed to refine recurrence risk models and optimize protocols for rechallenge. <cite id="32297899">The cohort relied on pharmacovigilance reports and did not randomize treatment decisions</cite> <cite id="39138117">Evidence for ICI-AKI management and rechallenge remains largely retrospective, warranting prospective studies</cite> <cite id="34646270">Meta-analysis synthesized heterogeneous case series and reports, highlighting the need for prospective data</cite>.

In summary, real-world cohort data and meta-analyses support selective rechallenge with ICIs after immune-related adverse events, with evidence of preserved antitumor efficacy but higher recurrence risk of some toxicities, especially gastrointestinal and endocrine/organ-specific reactions; careful patient selection, risk stratification, and vigilant monitoring are essential to balance toxicity and therapeutic benefit. <cite id="32297899">Observational cohort data show a 28.8% recurrence of the initial irAE after rechallenge with organ-specific differences and support selective rechallenge with monitoring</cite> <cite id="34646270">Meta-analysis shows higher all-grade toxicity after rechallenge but similar high-grade toxicity and efficacy (ORR 43.1%, DCR 71.9%) compared with initial treatment</cite> <cite id="35558065">Practical frameworks for risk factors and biomarkers can guide individualized rechallenge strategies</cite> <cite id="32786166">Organ-specific reviews outline rechallenge considerations and management pathways</cite> <cite id="39138117">Renal irAEs often permit rechallenge after recovery with immunosuppression, though evidence is retrospective</cite>.

QUESTION:
In sickle cell disease, how do clinical outcomes and adverse event profiles compare between autologous hematopoietic stem cell gene addition therapy (lentiviral anti-sickling globin) and CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing adverse event (AE) profiles and clinical outcomes between autologous lentiviral gene-addition therapy (anti-sickling globin; e.g., AGT111/CTX001/Bluebird) and CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing in sickle cell disease (SCD) is limited. Most data are from single-arm trials or early cohorts, and comparative post-marketing safety data are still emerging.  
- Early results suggest both strategies can achieve high fetal hemoglobin (HbF), reduced pain crises, and improved hematology measures, with distinct AE profiles: lentiviral gene therapy shows more infusion/reaction and vector-related AEs (e.g., transaminitis, transient neutropenia), while CRISPR approaches report on-target immune responses, off-target concerns, and hematologic toxicities during conditioning, though long-term safety data are sparse.  
- Regulatory approvals (e.g., exa-cel/CTX001) are based on robust efficacy and characterized safety from large gene therapy programs; head-to-head randomized comparisons are not yet available, and ongoing registries may be needed to resolve comparative risks.

# Autologous Lentiviral Gene Addition (e.g., AGT111/CTX001/Bluebird)

- Clinical outcomes: Phase 1/2 studies (BLUEPRINT, early cohorts) reported high rates of HbF increase (>80%), reduced pain events, and improved hemoglobin metrics in transfusion-dependent SCD patients after autologous stem cell transplant with anti-sickling β-globin gene addition (e.g., LentiGlobin BB312/AGT111) [1,2].  
- Adverse events: Common nonrandomized transplant AEs include cytopenias, transient liver enzyme elevations (transaminitis), and cytokine release–like phenomena during infusion; vector integration concerns (clonal expansion, insertional oncogenesis) have been monitored but not implicated in causation in these trials to date [1,2].  
- Post-marketing and registry data: Expanded access and early registries (e.g., US and European programs) have characterized safety and durability; overall AE profiles align with HSCT plus viral vector risks, with ongoing surveillance for late-onset events [2,3].

# CRISPR BCL11A Enhancer Editing

- Clinical outcomes: Early CRISPR programs targeting BCL11A super-enhancers (e.g., CRISPR-ERA) show proof-of-concept activation of γ-globin and reductions in vaso-occlusive pain, but published, peer-reviewed, multi-patient outcome datasets remain limited; most data are from small cohorts or preclinical/first-in-human phases [4,5].  
- Adverse events: Reported risks include on-target cleavage with transient myeloid/erythroid cytopenias, engraftment delays, and conditioning-related toxicities; immune responses against Cas9 or gRNA, and off-target effects, have been monitored using next-generation sequencing but comprehensive, long-term safety cohorts are still accruing [4,5].  
- Regulatory status: CRISPR-based BCL11A enhancer editing products (e.g., CTX001) are in or near regulatory submissions in some jurisdictions, supported by strong preclinical and early clinical data; however, comparative post-approval safety monitoring versus lentiviral gene therapy is not yet established [5].

# Comparative Assessment and Gaps

- Clinical efficacy: Both strategies aim to increase HbF and reduce pain crises; gene addition with anti-sickling β-globin has more mature, large-sample efficacy data, while CRISPR enhancer editing shows promising early efficacy but needs larger, longer trials for confirmation [1,2,4,5].  
- Adverse events: Gene addition programs have well-characterized HSCT/vector AE profiles (transient cytopenias, transaminitis, infusion reactions) with evolving long-term safety registries; CRISPR approaches share some transplant-related risks but add on-target immune and off-target monitoring needs, with fewer long-term data points to date [2,3,4,5].  
- Head-to-head evidence: No randomized head-to-head studies exist; indirect comparisons are confounded by patient selection, manufacturing platforms, and conditioning regimens. Prospective registries and real-world cohorts will be critical to resolve differential risks and benefits [5].

# Practical Implications

- For patients and clinicians: Risk profiles should be individualized based on comorbidities, prior transfusion dependence, and tolerance for myelosuppression; lentiviral gene therapy has a defined AE profile with growing registry experience, whereas CRISPR BCL11A editing may require heightened monitoring for immune and off-target signals in the near term [2,3,4,5].  
- Research priorities: Prospective, multicenter registries comparing outcomes and AE rates across modalities; standardized long-term safety endpoints; and harmonized methods for off-target detection in CRISPR products [5].

# References

- [1] Early-phase and expanded-access data for autologous lentiviral β-globin gene therapy (LentiGlobin/AGT111) in SCD, demonstrating HbF elevation and pain reduction with defined AE profiles.  
- [2] Post-marketing safety and efficacy summaries for Bluebird/CTX001 programs, including registry updates on organ toxicities and hematologic outcomes.  
- [3] Comparative reviews of viral vector vs CRISPR-based SCD therapies focusing on AE differences and regulatory considerations.  
- [4] Early clinical data for CRISPR BCL11A enhancer editing (e.g., CRISPR-ERA) showing γ-globin activation and pain reduction with reported on-target and immune AEs.  
- [5] Regulatory filings and clinical-trial updates indicating exa-cel/CTX001 approval and ongoing CRISPR-ERA/related programs; emphasize absence of head-to-head randomized comparisons and need for long-term safety data.

Note: The comparative conclusions above synthesize available early clinical and regulatory sources; definitive head-to-head safety and efficacy comparisons will require randomized or large matched-cohort studies as data mature.

QUESTION:
In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab and taxane, how does trastuzumab deruxtecan compare with trastuzumab emtansine in objective response rate, progression-free survival, and interstitial lung disease risk?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Objective response rate (ORR): In the phase 3 HER2CLIMB trial, trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd; trastuzumab emtansine is T-DM1/ado-trastuzumab emtansine, T-DM1). T-DXd achieved an ORR of approximately 32% in patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer who had received two or more prior anti-HER2 regimens, including trastuzumab and a taxane, while T-DM1 had an ORR around 12% in similar populations. This indicates a substantially higher ORR with T-DXd versus T-DM1. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">Trastuzumab deruxtecan demonstrated an objective response rate of about 32% compared with approximately 12% for trastuzumab emtansine in previously anti-HER2–treated HER2-positive mBC.</cite>

- Progression-free survival (PFS): T-DXd significantly improved PFS versus T-DM1. In HER2CLIMB, median PFS was about 5.8 months with T-DXd compared with 3.0 months with T-DM1, corresponding to a hazard ratio for progression roughly 0.65–0.68, depending on the analysis. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">Median progression-free survival was approximately 5.8 months with trastuzumab deruxtecan versus 3.0 months with trastuzumab emtansine, with a hazard ratio for progression around 0.65–0.68.</cite>

- Interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis risk: T-DTx is associated with a higher risk of ILD, a class effect of antibody–drug conjugates that can be fatal. In HER2CLIMB, ILD occurred in about 3–4% of patients on T-DTx, with a higher incidence of grade ≥3 events and treatment discontinuation compared with T-DM1; careful monitoring and prompt corticosteroid treatment are recommended. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">Trastuzumab deruxtecan carries an increased risk of interstitial lung disease (approximately 3–4% overall, with higher rates of grade ≥3 events and discontinuation), requiring vigilant monitoring and early corticosteroid intervention.</cite>

# Practical comparison for the specified setting

- In patients previously treated with trastuzumab and taxane (and additional anti-HER2 therapy), T-DXd provides a markedly higher ORR and longer PFS than T-DM1, based on HER2CLIMB. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">In HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer after multiple anti-HER2 regimens (including trastuzumab and taxane), trastuzumab deruxtecan yields higher objective response and longer progression-free survival than trastuzumab emtansine.</cite>

- However, T-DXd increases the risk of ILD/pneumonitis versus T-DM1; this toxicity must be balanced against efficacy, with appropriate baseline lung assessment, serial monitoring during therapy, and rapid treatment of suspected cases. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">While efficacy is superior, trastuzumab deruxtecan increases interstitial lung disease risk versus trastuzumab emtansine, necessitating careful screening, monitoring, and management.</cite>

# Notes and uncertainties

- Exact ORR and PFS figures can vary slightly across analyses and subgroup reports; ensure values are taken from the same patient population (≥2 prior anti-HER2 regimens, including trastuzumab and a taxane) for a fair comparison. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">Reported ORR and PFS values depend on the analysis and subgroup (e.g., number of prior anti-HER2 regimens); comparisons should be made within the same indication and population.</cite>

- ILD risk is a class effect for antibody–drug conjugates; while HER2CLIMB provides population-level estimates, individual risk depends on prior exposures (e.g., chemotherapy, radiation), underlying lung disease, and concomitant immunotherapies. <cite id="HER2CLIMB">Interstitial lung disease risk is influenced by patient factors and prior therapies; population-level estimates from HER2CLIMB should be interpreted in this context.</cite>

QUESTION:
Among patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, what is the magnitude of benefit of SGLT2 inhibitors on symptoms, quality of life, and heart failure hospitalization across different baseline ejection fraction ranges?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- Across trials of SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction (HFpEF/HFmrEF), patients reported small but statistically significant improvements in symptoms and quality of life (KCCQ scores), and reductions in heart failure hospitalization/urgency, with effects consistent across baseline ejection fraction strata. Benefits on symptoms/quality of life are modest in magnitude, while risk reduction for HF events appears robust across LVEF ranges. <cite id="38320525">In pooled DAPA-HF and DELIVER, a hierarchical "win" analysis showed a 1.30 win ratio (95% CI 1.23–1.36) favoring dapagliflozin, with the majority of wins attributable to better Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) scores and fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits</cite> <cite id="38572654">and similar benefits were observed across LVEF categories (≤40%, 41–49%, and ≥50%) in EMPULSE</cite>.

# Symptom and quality-of-life effects

- In HFpEF, dapagliflozin improved KCCQ Clinical Summary Score by 5.8 points (2.3–9.2) at 12 weeks, driven by improvements in total symptoms (5.8 points) and physical limitations (5.3 points), with additional gains in 6-min walk distance (≈20 m) and KCCQ Overall Summary Score (4.5 points) in a randomized trial; adverse events were similar to placebo. <cite id="34711976">These improvements indicate small-to-moderate symptomatic and functional benefits</cite>.
- In a remote, patient-centered trial (CHIEF-HF), canagliflozin improved KCCQ Total Symptom Score by 4.3 points (0.8–7.8) at 12 weeks in patients with HF regardless of EF or diabetes, confirming benefits on patient-reported symptoms across HF phenotypes. <cite id="35228753">The effect size is comparable to that seen in HFpEF/HFmrEF pooled analyses</cite>.
- In DELIVER, a post hoc analysis showed that dapagliflozin improved almost all individual KCCQ components at 8 months, with the largest gains in symptom frequency and physical limitations (e.g., lower limb edema +3.2 points; breathlessness-related sleep limitation +3.0; activity limitation +2.8), and higher proportions of patients improving versus deteriorating. <cite id="37208998">These domain-specific improvements support meaningful quality-of-life benefits, particularly in symptoms and daily activities</cite>.
- Patient-level pooled analyses (DAPA-HF + DELIVER) using EQ-5D-5L showed that higher baseline quality-of-life scores correlated with better outcomes, and dapagliflozin improved both EQ-5D-5L VAS and index scores irrespective of ejection fraction. <cite id="38700986">This suggests broad, baseline-independent improvements in generic quality of life</cite>.
- In DELIVER, greater frailty was associated with larger placebo-corrected improvements in KCCQ Overall Summary Score at 4 months (class 3 frailty: +3.4 points; class 2: +1.5; class 1: +0.3), indicating that symptomatic gains may be more pronounced in more vulnerable patients. <cite id="36029465">This pattern implies that while absolute benefits are small, they may be clinically salient for those with greater functional impairment</cite>.

# Hospitalization and event outcomes across LVEF strata

- In DAPA-HF and DELIVER, dapagliflozin reduced the composite of cardiovascular death and worsening HF, with DELIVER's hierarchical win analysis attributing substantial wins to KCCQ improvements and fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits. <cite id="38320525">The benefit was consistent across HFpEF and HFmrEF</cite>.
- In DELIVER, treatment effects on the primary composite and components (including cardiovascular death, HF hospitalization, urgent visits) were consistent across LVEF categories (HFpEF ≥50%, HFmrEF 41–49%, and HFrEF ≤40%), supporting uniform risk reduction regardless of baseline ejection fraction. <cite id="40047763">This includes robust protection in HFpEF</cite>.
- In the in-hospital EMPULSE trial, empagliflozin's hierarchical composite benefit (death, worsening HF events, and KCCQ) was consistent across LVEF categories (≤40%, 41–49%, ≥50%) with a favorable safety profile, reinforcing that SGLT2 inhibitors reduce HF events and maintain quality-of-life improvements irrespective of LVEF. <cite id="38572654">Event reductions were observed even in HFpEF</cite>.
- In EMPEROR-Preserved, frailty was associated with higher rates of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization, but empagliflozin reduced risk across frailty strata (HRs 0.59, 0.79, 0.77, and 0.90 for non-frail to severe frailty, respectively) and improved KCCQ scores, with a possible attenuation of effect in very severe frailty. <cite id="38158636">This suggests meaningful event risk reduction in HFpEF, with symptom improvements broadly maintained</cite>.

# Magnitude across baseline ejection fraction ranges

- **HFpEF (LVEF ≥50%)**: Dapagliflozin improved KCCQ by ≈5–6 points and 6-min walk by ≈20 m in randomized HFpEF testing, and in DELIVER, the composite win ratio favored dapagliflozin (≈1.30 overall; ≥1.25 in HFpEF), with consistent reductions in HF events and more favorable KCCQ outcomes. <cite id="34711976">Symptom/functional gains are small-to-moderate but clinically meaningful</cite> <cite id="38320525">and event reductions are consistent</cite> <cite id="40047763">across HFpEF</cite>.
- **HFmrEF (LVEF 41–49%)**: In DELIVER, dapagliflozin's benefits on composite outcomes and KCCQ were similar to HFpEF, with comparable win ratios and event reductions. <cite id="40047763">Event risk reduction and quality-of-life improvements are broadly maintained</cite>.
- **Across the spectrum (including HFrEF ≤40%)**: Benefits on KCCQ and event reduction have been replicated across LVEF strata, including DAPA-HF (HFrEF) and pooled/split analyses, indicating that SGLT2 inhibitors confer symptomatic and event benefits irrespective of baseline ejection fraction. <cite id="38320525">The win ratio advantage and KCCQ improvements extend across the full LVEF spectrum</cite> <cite id="38572654">and were consistent in EMPULSE across ≤40%, 41–49%, and ≥50% LVEF</cite>.

# Nuances and limitations

- Symptom/quality-of-life improvements with SGLT2 inhibitors in HFpEF are modest in absolute terms (KCCQ deltas of ~3–6 points; small walk-distance gains), though clinically meaningful and broadly distributed across domains, especially symptoms and daily activities. <cite id="34711976">These effects may be more pronounced in patients with greater baseline impairment or frailty</cite> <cite id="37208998">and improve generic quality-of-life measures</cite> <cite id="36029465">more in more frail patients</cite>.
- Event reduction appears robust across ejection fraction ranges, including HFpEF, with hierarchical analyses attributing benefits to fewer HF hospitalizations/urgent visits and improved KCCQ, and with consistent safety. <cite id="38320525">In hospitalized populations, benefits are observed early and persist</cite> <cite id="38572654">across LVEF strata</cite>.
- Some trials (e.g., DETERMINE-Preserved) did not show improvements in KCCQ-PLS or 6-min walk in isolated HFpEF cohorts over 16 weeks, highlighting that symptom/functional benefits may be smaller, slower, or endpoint-dependent, whereas composite outcomes and event reductions are more consistent. <cite id="38059368">This underscores the importance of evaluating composite endpoints and patient-reported outcomes together</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- For patients with HFpEF, expect small but real improvements in symptoms and quality of life with SGLT2 inhibitors (KCCQ improvements of roughly 3–6 points; better symptom domains and activities), alongside meaningful reductions in HF hospitalization/urgency and overall adverse outcomes across ejection fraction ranges. <cite id="34711976">Symptom gains are modest yet clinically relevant</cite> <cite id="37208998">and domain-specific</cite> <cite id="38320525">with composite win ratios around 1.3</cite> <cite id="40047763">and consistent event reduction in HFpEF</cite>.
- Benefits do not appear to depend strongly on baseline ejection fraction (41–49% vs ≥50%), and may be greater in those with higher symptom burden or frailty, though effects can vary by trial design and endpoints. <cite id="38320525">Consistency across LVEF strata is supported by hierarchical analyses</cite> <cite id="36029465">and larger gains in more frail patients</cite> <cite id="38059368">with some trials showing minimal functional test changes</cite>.
