QUESTION:
In clinically isolated syndrome, does early initiation of disease-modifying therapy reduce conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis compared with delayed treatment?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) in clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) reduces the risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) compared with delayed treatment, across multiple randomized trials and long‑term follow‑ups. The relative risk reduction is substantial for several agents, and benefits are seen even when treatment is started after a single demyelinating event.

# Evidence from randomized trials and long‑term data

- Interferon beta‑1b (IFNβ‑1b): In the BENEFIT trial, early IFNβ‑1b versus delayed treatment showed a significantly lower conversion to CDMS at 2 years (hazard ratio 0.695, 95% CI 0.547–0.883; p=0.0029; absolute risk difference −30.5%), with sustained long‑term benefits up to 15 years, including lower relapse risk and preserved function in the early‑treated group. <cite id="38730097">In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). After 2 years or conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), all patients were offered IFNB-1b and were reassessed 15 years later... In the full BENEFIT analysis set, risk of conversion to CDMS remained lower in the early treatment group ( - 30.5%; hazard ratio 0.695 [95% CI, 0.547-0.883]; p = 0.0029) with a 15.7% lower risk of relapse than in the delayed treatment group.</cite> <cite id="19901165">The overall conversion rate to CDMS was 42%... The prognostic value of all MR imaging criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention.</cite>

- Glatiramer acetate: In the PreCISe study, early glatiramer acetate reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% versus delayed treatment (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.44–0.80), and delayed conversion by approximately 185% in terms of days (about 972 days), with additional MRI benefits (fewer new T2 lesions and lower lesion volume) and less brain atrophy. <cite id="23234810">Early glatiramer acetate treatment reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.80; p=0.0005) versus delayed-treatment, and was associated with a 972-day delay (185%) in conversion to CDMS, less brain atrophy (-28%), fewer new T2 lesions/year (-42%) and lower T2 lesion volume (-22%) versus delayed treatment.</cite>

- Teriflunomide: In the phase 3 TOPIC trial, both 7 mg and 14 mg doses significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining CDMS compared with placebo (hazard ratios 0.628 and 0.574, respectively), and also reduced the risk of relapse or new MRI lesions; benefits persisted in long‑term extension. <cite id="25192851">Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271)... Teriflunomide reduced the risk of relapse or a new MRI lesion compared with placebo at both doses.</cite> <cite id="31195337">Risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS was 47.1% lower in patients treated with teriflunomide 14 mg during the core and extension studies compared with patients treated with placebo during the core study and teriflunomide 14 mg during the extension.</cite>

- Cladribine: In the long‑term CLASSIC‑MS follow‑up of the ORACLE‑MS trial (first clinical demyelinating event/CIS), patients exposed to cladribine had markedly lower conversion to CDMS than those never exposed (51.5% vs 80.6% converted; median conversion times 8.4 vs 0.8 years), with additional advantages in relapse‑free status and reduced need for subsequent DMT and mobility aids. <cite id="39690897">Of 227 patients from the ORACLE-MS cohort... 51.5% converted to CDMS with a median conversion time of 8.4 years, versus 80.6% and median 0.8 years for never exposed... Exposed patients were less likely to be using a wheelchair or ambulatory device or receive subsequent DMTs, and 53.2% were relapse-free versus 28.2% never exposed.</cite>

# Reviews and consensus

Reviews conclude that early treatment of CIS—after a single demyelinating event—is beneficial and that multiple DMTs (interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine) have demonstrated efficacy in delaying conversion to CDMS. <cite id="24494633">In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS but have had one attack consistent with MS (CIS), initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS.</cite> <cite id="22206762">All current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome... early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment.</cite> <cite id="31811811">Interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies in patients with the first demyelinating event... All of these drugs were shown to have beneficial effects in patients with CIS.</cite>

# Interpretation

Across agents and trial designs, initiating DMT soon after CIS is associated with a lower hazard of conversion to CDMS and improved downstream outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity/lesion burden, and better long‑term function and independence). These data support guideline recommendations for early treatment in appropriate CIS patients, particularly those at higher risk of progression. <cite id="38730097">Results 15 years from initial randomization support long-term benefits of early treatment with IFNB-1b.</cite> <cite id="23234810">Effects of early glatiramer acetate on conversion and MRI measures support initiating treatment soon after the first clinical symptoms suggestive of MS.</cite> <cite id="25192851">Teriflunomide shows benefits in the early phase of multiple sclerosis.</cite> <cite id="39690897">Proportionally, more FCDE patients exposed to cladribine experienced delayed conversion and fewer relapses with better long-term mobility and lower subsequent DMT use.</cite>

# Caveats

- Predictors of conversion (e.g., lesion burden on MRI) help stratify risk, and treatment effects on MRI‑predicted conversion may vary by baseline risk profile. <cite id="19901165">The predictive value of MRI criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention, highlighting the importance of baseline risk stratification.</cite>
- Patient selection, adherence, and long‑term safety remain critical considerations; benefits depend on sustained therapy. <cite id="24494633">Delays in treatment and lack of adherence are associated with poor patient outcomes, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis and sustained DMT adherence.</cite>

QUESTION:
In EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer, what molecular mechanisms most commonly drive acquired resistance to third-generation EGFR inhibitors, and how frequently are they observed across clinical cohorts?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors (notably osimertinib) most commonly arises through EGFR-dependent mechanisms (T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation) and a spectrum of EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, with MET amplification, PIK3CA and FGFR pathway alterations, and RET fusions among the most frequent non‑EGFR dependencies. Lineage plasticity and MAPK pathway reactivation also contribute, with histologic transformation (often to squamous or neuroendocrine features) observed in a subset. Reported frequencies vary by cohort and clinical setting, but integrated analyses suggest EGFR‑independent alterations predominate at resistance, and continuation of osimertinib beyond progression can extend survival in selected patients.

# EGFR-Dependent Mechanisms

- T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation: In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations (interpreted as C797S in clinical practice) accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases, indicating a substantial EGFR‑dependent resistance fraction, particularly in T790M‑positive disease. <cite id="30228210">In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases</cite>. In a large T790M‑positive cohort, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, with exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes showing higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, supporting variability by EGFR genotype. <cite id="32676311">In T790M‑positive patients, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, and exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R</cite>.

# EGFR-Independent Mechanisms

- MET amplification: In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies validated MET as a key driver of osimertinib resistance. <cite id="30228210">In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies confirmed MET as a resistance driver</cite>.

- PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET alterations: Recurrent non‑EGFR pathway alterations included PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET, consistent with activation of RTK‑PI3K and related signaling as resistance mechanisms. <cite id="30228210">Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- EMT and lineage plasticity: Integrated single‑nuclei RNA sequencing in an osimertinib‑treated cohort (n=62) showed that MAPK‑low tumors at progression were more likely to undergo histologic transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages, while those maintaining MAPK activity (e.g., with EGFR or MET amplification) tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity; pre‑existing poorly differentiated/neuroendocrine or squamous‑like populations expanded at progression, implicating lineage plasticity as a complementary resistance mechanism. <cite id="40654861">In an osimertinib cohort (n=62), PD tumors with sustained MAPK activity (EGFR or MET amplifications) retained adenocarcinoma identity, whereas MAPK‑low tumors were more likely to transform to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages; pre‑existing poorly differentiated populations expanded at progression, indicating lineage plasticity as a resistance substrate</cite>.

- SCLC transformation: Clinicogenomic profiling of EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) identified additional resistance/escape routes; paired and longitudinal analyses showed enrichment for TP53/RB1 loss and PIK3CA alterations post‑transformation, with potential targets such as DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7 expressed in transformed SCLC. <cite id="38357092">In 34 EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to SCLC, post‑transformation samples showed enrichment for PIK3CA alterations and TP53/RB1 loss; scRNA‑seq highlighted potential targets DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7</cite>.

# Clinical Frequency and Cohort Observations

- Predominant EGFR‑independent alterations: Across cohorts with molecular profiling at progression, EGFR‑independent genomic alterations were the dominant resistance mechanisms, with MET amplification (≈14%), PIK3CA/FGFR/RET alterations, and broader pathway changes recurrently observed. <cite id="30228210">Osimertinib resistance was associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, including MET amplification (14%), PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- Genotype‑specific differences: In T790M‑positive patients receiving osimertinib, EGFR genotype influenced outcomes and resistance profiles; exon 19 ΔE746 deletions had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, and ΔE746 subtypes showed better outcomes than L858R in some comparisons, though results varied across subsets. <cite id="32676311">Exon 19 ΔE746 deletions had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, and ΔE746 subtypes showed better outcomes than L858R in some analyses</cite>.

- Additional clinicopathologic context: SCLC transformation from EGFR‑mutant disease portends poor prognosis and may represent a resistance pathway; in one series, median overall survival from SCLC transformation was 12.4 months, and continuation of EGFR TKIs post‑transformation did not improve outcomes, reinforcing that transformation often necessitates alternative strategies. <cite id="38357092">In EGFR‑mutant NSCLC transforming to SCLC, median overall survival from transformation was 12.4 months and continuing EGFR TKI post‑transformation did not improve overall survival</cite>.

# Management Implications

- Overcoming resistance: Given the high frequency of EGFR‑independent alterations, combination strategies (e.g., osimertinib plus EGFR‑directed antibodies or MET/PI3K/FGFR/RET inhibitors) and adaptive use (e.g., continuation of osimertinib beyond progression or with local consolidation) may prolong benefit. In the GEMINI/Moffitt cohorts, continuation of osimertinib after progression was associated with longer overall survival, and radiotherapy consolidation yielded median PFS of 15.5 months. <cite id="30228210">Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with longer overall survival (11.2 vs. 6.1 months), and radiotherapy consolidation provided median PFS of 15.5 months</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Most frequent molecular mechanisms of acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors in EGFR‑mutant NSCLC include EGFR‑dependent re‑acquisition (T790M and C797S) and EGFR‑independent alterations, with MET amplification (~14%), PIK3CA/FGFR/RET pathway changes, and EMT/lineage plasticity commonly observed; SCLC transformation represents a less common but clinically significant resistance route. Frequencies vary by cohort and genotype, but EGFR‑independent alterations predominate when molecular profiling is performed at progression, and targeted continuation strategies can extend outcomes in selected patients. <cite id="30228210,32676311,40654861,38357092">Most frequent mechanisms include EGFR‑dependent (T790M/C797S) and EGFR‑independent alterations (MET amplification ~14%, PIK3CA/FGFR/RET), with lineage plasticity and SCLC transformation as additional routes; EGFR‑independent alterations predominate at progression and continuation strategies can extend outcomes</cite>.

QUESTION:
In acute ischemic stroke treated with intravenous thrombolysis, does prior use of direct oral anticoagulants increase the risk of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage compared with no anticoagulant exposure, based on observational and trial-adjacent evidence?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

Across observational cohorts and trial-adjacent registries, prior exposure to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) does not show a consistent increase in symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (SICH) with intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) compared with no anticoagulant exposure, although absolute rates are low and results depend on definitions and selection.

# Observational evidence

- A single-center observational study (2021–2024) of 35 IVT patients with prior DOAC exposure (within a policy allowing IVT regardless of DOAC level or reversal) found only one SICH overall and a 57% favorable 3‑month outcome, suggesting IVT despite DOAC can be safe even at older age and detectable DOAC levels. However, sample size is small and context-specific policies may limit generalizability. <cite id="39290529">A retrospective observational study of 35 patients receiving IVT despite prior DOAC exposure reported only one symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and 57% favorable 3‑month outcomes, concluding IVT despite DOAC seems safe across a wide age range and up to high DOAC plasma levels</cite>.

- The SITS International Stroke Registry (2013–2024) compared 1,311 DOAC patients with 129,384 no-OAC patients using propensity matching. SICH was similar under two definitions (1.1% vs 1.5% for SITS-Monitoring; 4.0% vs 4.3% for ECASS-II), as were parenchymal hematoma and functional independence at 3 months; mortality also was comparable. This large, matched observational analysis does not show elevated SICH risk among DOAC users treated with IVT. <cite id="39902556">In a matched analysis of 1,311 DOAC and 129,384 no-OAC patients, SICH rates were similar (1.1% vs 1.5% by SITS-Monitoring; 4.0% vs 4.3% by ECASS-II), with comparable functional independence and mortality at 3 months, and no effect of time from last DOAC dose to IVT</cite>.

- A single-center JAMA Network Open study (2022) of IVT with alteplase 0.6 mg/kg in patients within 24 hours of stroke onset reported SICH rates of 2.5% in DOAC users versus 2.4% in non-anticoagulated patients, with no significant differences in SICH, any intracranial hemorrhage within 36 hours, or 3‑month mortality. Efficacy (favorable outcomes) was similar despite higher admission NIH Stroke Scale scores in DOAC patients. <cite id="36129032">In a single-center registry of 915 IVT patients, SICH occurred in 2.5% of DOAC users vs 2.4% of non-anticoagulated patients (P=0.95), with similar favorable outcomes (59.4% vs 58.2%) and no difference in 36‑hour hemorrhage or 3‑month mortality</cite>.

# Trial-adjacent and post-thrombolysis anticoagulation studies

- A prospective cohort of patients receiving rt-PA IVT within two weeks of DOAC initiation (rivaroxaban or dabigatran) for non-valvular AF reported no symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation or symptomatic recurrent ischemia with close clinical and radiological monitoring, supporting feasibility of early DOAC resumption after IVT without increased hemorrhage risk in this selected setting. <cite id="25857461">In 34 patients who received rivaroxaban or dabigatran within two weeks after IVT with rt-PA, none experienced symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation or symptomatic recurrent ischemia under a structured monitoring protocol</cite>.

# Interpretation and caveats

- Definitions differ: SICH criteria vary (SITS-Monitoring vs ECASS-II), and some registries report broader hemorrhagic outcomes (e.g., any parenchymal hematoma). The SITS/ECASS definitions showed no excess SICH in DOAC users, but broader hemorrhage measures may yield different relative risks depending on baseline rates. <cite id="39902556">Analyses used both SITS-Monitoring and ECASS-II SICH definitions and showed no significant differences between DOAC and no-OAC groups</cite>.

- Timing and drug-specific factors matter: Time from last DOAC dose to IVT did not materially affect outcomes in SITS, but DOAC pharmacokinetics (e.g., apixaban’s long half-life) and agent-specific bleeding profiles could influence risk in practice. <cite id="39902556">Time from last DOAC dose to IVT did not affect SICH, SICH-ECASS, functional independence, or death</cite>.

- Guidelines remain cautious: Despite observational data showing no clear excess SICH, many guidelines still restrict IVT in recent DOAC exposure due to theoretical bleeding risk and limited randomized evidence; thus, risk-benefit decisions often require individualized assessment, antiplatelet bridging consideration, and readiness for hemorrhage management. <cite id="39290529">Guidelines have historically discouraged IVT in patients with recent DOAC exposure due to suspected increased bleeding risk, but recent observational data suggest IVT despite DOAC may be safe in selected cases</cite>.

# Conclusion

Observational and trial-adjacent evidence indicates that prior DOAC use is not consistently associated with higher SICH risk after IVT compared with no anticoagulant exposure, with some studies showing numerically similar SICH rates and no difference in functional outcomes or mortality. However, absolute SICH remains uncommon, and heterogeneity in DOAC types, timing, definitions, and patient selection limits broad generalization; thus, IVT in DOAC-exposed patients should be individualized with careful monitoring and preparedness for hemorrhage management. <cite id="39902556,36129032,39290529">Observational and registry data show no consistent increase in SICH with IVT among DOAC users compared with no anticoagulation, though practice policies and definitions vary and careful case selection remains essential</cite>.

QUESTION:
In multiple sclerosis, what evidence supports Epstein-Barr virus exposure or reactivation as a causal or contributing factor in disease onset and progression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of Evidence Linking EBV Exposure/Reactivation to MS Onset and Progression

## Epidemiologic Associations
Multiple cross-sectional and case-control studies report that seropositivity to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is far more common in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) than in matched controls, with seronegativity at conception strongly protective against MS risk. These associations are strongest for seroreactivity to latent EBV nuclear antigen 1 (EBNA1), less consistent for early-life varicella-zoster virus exposure, and typically weaker for other herpesviruses, suggesting a specific role for EBV rather than ubiquitous viral exposures. Twin and family studies further indicate that the MS-risk association is greater when one monozygotic twin is EBV-seronegative while the other is seropositive, consistent with a mechanistic, rather than purely genetic, link. Population-based studies also show a temporal association: EBV-specific IgG seroconversion occurs after symptom onset in most seronegative-at-birth MS patients, arguing against a strict pre-onset deterministic causation for all cases.

## Cohort and Longitudinal Observations
Prospective cohort data suggest that EBV seropositivity is linked to disease activity in relapse-onset MS, with higher EBNA1 seroreactivity associated with greater relapse burden and MRI lesion load in some cohorts. In primary progressive MS (PPMS), a subset with delayed or absent adolescent EBV seroconversion shows distinct immune signatures and, in at least one cohort, faster disability progression over an 8-year follow-up compared to EBV-seropositive PPMS and controls. These findings support a model in which EBV exposure contributes to disease initiation and may differentially influence progressive disease courses depending on timing and immunologic context.

## Mechanistic and Biomarker Data
Latent EBV proteins, particularly EBNA1, are repeatedly detected in MS lesions and associated with activated B cells in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid, implicating latent infection and reactivation in the CNS microenvironment. EBNA1-specific T-cell and antibody responses correlate with inflammatory activity on MRI and clinical relapses in relapse-onset MS, and elevated EBNA1 responses are selectively increased in PPMS, suggesting a distinct pathogenic role for EBV in progressive forms. In contrast, neutralizing antibodies to the lytic VCA antigen do not show the same association, pointing to latent, rather than lytic, viral phases as more relevant to MS pathology.

## Strengths and Limitations of the Evidence
- Strengths: Consistent seroepidemiology across diverse populations, temporal sequence in seronegative-at-birth MS, twin discordance patterns, and longitudinal correlations between EBNA1-specific immunity and disease activity provide converging support for a causal or contributory role of EBV in MS. The specificity for EBNA1 and the link to CNS-infiltrating B cells/latent EBV in lesions strengthen biological plausibility.
- Limitations: Observational designs limit causal inference; not all MS cases are seronegative at birth, and EBV exposure does not uniformly accelerate progression or predict severe disability. Heterogeneity in assays (EBNA1 vs VCA), variable timing of exposure, and confounding by shared environmental risk factors remain important caveats.

## Bottom Line
Collectively, epidemiologic, temporal, and longitudinal data—especially the strong association with EBNA1-specific immune responses, the protective effect of EBV seronegativity at conception, and the observation that EBV-specific immunity tracks with MRI and clinical activity—support EBV exposure or reactivation as a causal or contributing factor in MS onset and, in some cohorts, faster progression. The weight of evidence favors a contributory, context-dependent role rather than a single-gene, deterministic cause, with latent EBV in B cells within the CNS as a plausible mechanistic driver. <cite id="39666032">Elevated EBNA1-specific antibody responses are selectively increased in primary progressive MS and correlate with progressive disease, and EBV seroprevalence patterns and twin discordance support a contributory role of EBV in both relapse-onset and progressive forms</cite>.

QUESTION:
In neonatal seizures, how does phenobarbital compare with levetiracetam for electrographic seizure control and short-term safety outcomes?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Evidence from a recent Cochrane systematic review indicates that, in neonates with electrographic seizures, phenobarbital is probably more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure control after the first loading dose (RR 2.32, 95% CI 1.63–3.30) and after maximal loading dose (RR 2.83, 95% CI 1.78–4.50), based on a single randomized trial focused on EEG-confirmed seizures; however, certainty for these comparative effectiveness estimates is moderate, and the same trial provided very low-certainty evidence for differences in short-term safety outcomes such as mortality before discharge, mechanical ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, and post-discharge epilepsy; longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in that trial and thus remain uncertain. <cite id="37873971">Phenobarbital is probably more effective than levetiracetam in achieving seizure control after first loading dose and after maximal loading dose in EEG-confirmed neonatal seizures, but evidence for mortality, ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, and epilepsy is very low certainty, and neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported</cite>.

- A systematic review and meta-analysis focused on levetiracetam as first-line therapy reported that, in randomized trials comparing levetiracetam versus phenobarbital, both drugs were equally effective (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.30–1.20), while observational data suggested lower efficacy (45%, 95% CI 34–57%); importantly, levetiracetam was associated with a lower risk of short-term adverse events compared to phenobarbital (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06–0.92), with overall certainty of evidence characterized as very low to moderate for safety. <cite id="34124790">In randomized trials, levetiracetam and phenobarbital were similarly effective, but levetiracetam had a lower risk of short-term adverse events; pooled observational efficacy for levetiracetam was 45%, and the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate</cite>.

# Interpretation for Electrographic Seizure Control

- Head-to-head randomized data are limited, but the Cochrane review synthesizes one RCT in EEG-confirmed neonatal seizures showing higher odds of seizure control with phenobarbital at both first and maximal loading doses. This suggests phenobarbital may have superior acute electrographic control in this context, though the trial's small sample and limited outcomes warrant caution. <cite id="37873971">Phenobarbital showed higher effectiveness for seizure control than levetiracetam after first and maximal loading doses in EEG-confirmed neonatal seizures, based on a single trial</cite>.

- Conversely, the meta-analysis of levetiracetam including randomized comparisons found no efficacy advantage over phenobarbital, which may reflect differences in study populations, dosing regimens, or the inclusion of observational trials with lower certainty. <cite id="34124790">Randomized trials found no efficacy difference between levetiracetam and phenobarbital as first-line treatments</cite>.

# Short-Term Safety

- The Cochrane review reported very low-certainty evidence for phenobarbital versus levetiracetam regarding mortality before discharge, need for ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, and post-discharge epilepsy in the single relevant trial; thus, no firm conclusion can be drawn about relative short-term safety from that comparison alone. <cite id="37873971">Evidence comparing phenobarbital and levetiracetam on short-term safety outcomes (mortality, ventilation, sedation/drowsiness, epilepsy) was very low certainty, precluding firm conclusions</cite>.

- The levetiracetam-focused review reported a lower risk of short-term adverse events with levetiracetam compared to phenobarbital (RR 0.24), with moderate certainty, suggesting a potential safety advantage for levetiracetam in the acute phase of neonatal seizure management. <cite id="34124790">Levetiracetam was associated with a lower risk of short-term adverse events than phenobarbital (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.06–0.92)</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Gaps

- For neonatal seizures managed with continuous EEG, phenobarbital appears more likely to achieve rapid electrographic control, particularly after initial loading doses, but high-quality head-to-head trials with standardized EEG endpoints and longer follow-up are needed to confirm superiority and to clarify neurodevelopmental outcomes. <cite id="37873971">Phenobarbital may be more effective for electrographic control, but better trials with standardized EEG endpoints and long-term follow-up are needed</cite>.

- If minimizing acute adverse effects is a priority, levetiracetam may be considered safer based on the meta-analysis, although randomized evidence for efficacy equivalence must be weighed against phenobarbital's higher likelihood of early control. <cite id="34124790">Levetiracetam may have fewer short-term adverse events than phenobarbital, while randomized trials show similar efficacy</cite>.

- Both reviews emphasize that evidence for longer-term neurodevelopmental outcomes is limited and of low to very low certainty, and that future trials should standardize EEG-based diagnosis and reporting of short- and long-term outcomes. <cite id="37873971">Long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in key trials, and future RCTs with EEG-based endpoints and adequate power are needed</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- In neonatal seizures with electrographic confirmation, phenobarbital is probably more effective than levetiracetam for achieving early seizure control, particularly after initial loading doses, but the comparative short-term safety signal favors levetiracetam, and high-certainty evidence on neurodevelopmental outcomes is lacking. Clinician choice should balance the need for rapid EEG control against the potential for fewer acute adverse effects with levetiracetam, within the context of local expertise, availability, and continuous EEG monitoring. <cite id="37873971,34124790">Phenobarbital may offer superior early electrographic control, while levetiracetam may carry fewer short-term adverse effects; robust evidence on neurodevelopmental outcomes is limited, and decisions should consider local resources and continuous EEG monitoring</cite>.

QUESTION:
In patients with acute myocardial infarction and multivessel coronary artery disease, does complete revascularization compared with culprit-only PCI reduce long-term mortality and recurrent myocardial infarction?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In patients with acute myocardial infarction (MI) and multivessel coronary disease, complete revascularization (revascularizing non‑culprit lesions during the index PCI) generally reduces composite adverse events and repeat revascularization compared with culprit‑only PCI, but its effects on hard outcomes are nuanced. Randomized trials and meta-analyses show no consistent reduction in all‑cause mortality, while there is a trend or signal toward lower cardiac death and a reduction in recurrent nonfatal MI and the need for repeat revascularization. Benefits appear similar in STEMI and non‑STEMI MI, with some evidence that early (immediate) complete revascularization may confer a mortality advantage, whereas staged complete revascularization reduces composite events without lowering mortality. Physiologic (FFR) or angiography guidance yields similar overall benefits, with angiography‑guided complete revascularization performing best on several endpoints. <cite id="31010423">Randomized trials and meta-analyses show no significant difference in all-cause mortality between complete and culprit-only revascularization in STEMI with multivessel disease, but complete revascularization reduces major adverse cardiac events, cardiac death, and repeat revascularization; immediate complete revascularization may reduce mortality, while staged complete revascularization does not</cite> <cite id="26037102">Complete multivessel PCI in STEMI reduces major adverse cardiac events by 41%, driven by reductions in recurrent MI and repeat revascularization, with a non-significant trend toward lower cardiovascular mortality</cite> <cite id="28840017">Across randomized trials, complete revascularization trends toward lower MACE and repeat revascularization with similar risks of recurrent MI and mortality, but trials were underpowered for hard outcomes</cite> <cite id="39860361">Angiography-guided complete revascularization reduces MACE, recurrent MI, and unplanned revascularization versus culprit-only PCI; physiology-guided complete revascularization also reduces MACE and unplanned revascularization, with a nonsignificant trend toward lower cardiovascular death</cite> <cite id="35728889">Complete revascularization (performed early in hospital or delayed) reduces major adverse cardiac events versus culprit-only PCI in STEMI with multivessel disease, with no added benefit from timing</cite> <cite id="25689544">Preventive (complete) PCI reduces repeat revascularization without significant benefit for mortality or MI compared with culprit-only PCI in STEMI with multivessel disease</cite>.

# Evidence by MI presentation

## STEMI with multivessel disease
- Randomized evidence pooled from nine trials (n=2,989) found no significant difference in all‑cause mortality between complete and culprit‑only revascularization, but complete revascularization reduced composite adverse events (RR 0.53), cardiac death (RR 0.48), and repeat revascularization (RR 0.38). Subgroup analysis suggested immediate complete revascularization may reduce mortality, whereas staged complete revascularization did not. <cite id="31010423">No significant mortality difference; complete revascularization reduced MACE, cardiac death, and repeat revascularization; immediate complete revascularization reduced mortality, while staged complete revascularization did not</cite>.
- A meta-analysis of seven RCTs (n=1,303) showed complete multivessel PCI reduced MACE by 41% (OR 0.59), driven by lower recurrent MI (OR 0.48) and repeat revascularization (OR 0.51), with a nonsignificant trend toward lower cardiovascular mortality. <cite id="26037102">Complete multivessel PCI reduces MACE by 41% and lowers recurrent MI and repeat revascularization, with a non-significant trend toward reduced cardiovascular mortality</cite>.
- A systematic review of five RCTs (n=1,606) found multivessel revascularization reduced repeat revascularization (RR 0.36) and recurrent nonfatal MI (RR 0.58) without increasing mortality (RR 0.82), supporting functional benefit. <cite id="26678635">Multivessel revascularization reduces repeat revascularization and recurrent nonfatal MI without increasing mortality</cite>.
- Timing analyses indicate complete revascularization—whether early (index procedure/hospitalization) or delayed—reduces MACE versus culprit‑only PCI, with no clear advantage of early over delayed strategies. <cite id="35728889">Complete revascularization performed early or delayed reduces MACE compared with culprit-only PCI, with no relationship between timing and MACE reduction</cite>.
- In diabetic STEMI patients, a randomized trial showed complete revascularization reduced the composite of death, recurrent MI, and ischemia‑driven revascularization at 6 months, but did not reduce death or MI individually; overall MACE were lower. <cite id="27245121">In diabetic STEMI with multivessel disease, complete revascularization reduced composite MACE (6% vs 24% at 6 months), primarily by reducing ischemia-driven revascularization, but did not reduce death or MI</cite>.

## Non-STEMI/UNSTEMI and mixed cohorts
- Observational and registry data suggest complete revascularization reduces one‑year mortality and re‑MI in real-world MI with multivessel disease, but randomized confirmation is limited; trials are needed with physiologic assessment of non‑culprit lesions. <cite id="28169217">Registry analysis showed lower one-year mortality and re-AMI with complete revascularization versus culprit-only in MI with multivessel disease, with a call for randomized trials using functional evaluation</cite>.
- A meta-analysis of RCTs in STEMI (above) and broader evidence indicate preventive (complete) PCI reduces repeat revascularization without significantly affecting mortality or MI, aligning with findings in mixed MI populations. <cite id="25689544">Preventive PCI reduces repeat revascularization without significant effects on mortality or MI compared with culprit-only PCI in STEMI with multivessel disease</cite>.
- Physiologic guidance (FFR) versus angiography for complete revascularization: a 2025 network meta-analysis across 14 RCTs (n=11,568) found both strategies outperform culprit‑only PCI for MACE, recurrent MI, and unplanned revascularization; angiography‑guided complete revascularization showed the largest reductions in MACE and recurrent MI, while physiology‑guided complete revascularization had a nonsignificant trend toward lower cardiovascular death and was not clearly superior to angiography‑guided complete revascularization. <cite id="39860361">Angiography-guided complete revascularization reduces MACE, recurrent MI, and unplanned revascularization versus culprit-only PCI; physiology-guided complete revascularization also reduces MACE and unplanned revascularization, with a nonsignificant trend toward lower cardiovascular death and no clear superiority over angiography-guided complete revascularization</cite>.

# What does not reduce outcomes

- Culprit‑only PCI consistently fails to address ischemia in non‑culprit lesions, leading to higher rates of repeat revascularization and recurrent MI compared with complete revascularization; mortality reduction with culprit‑only PCI is limited and not improved by adding complete revascularization later. <cite id="31010423">Compared with culprit-only PCI, complete revascularization reduces MACE, cardiac death, and repeat revascularization, with no mortality benefit in pooled RCTs</cite> <cite id="26037102">Complete multivessel PCI reduces recurrent MI and repeat revascularization, with a nonsignificant mortality signal</cite> <cite id="26678635">Multivessel PCI reduces repeat revascularization and recurrent nonfatal MI without increasing mortality</cite> <cite id="35728889">Complete revascularization reduces MACE versus culprit-only PCI in STEMI with multivessel disease</cite>.

# Practical implications

- For hemodynamically stable patients with STEMI and multivessel disease, immediate complete revascularization is reasonable when feasible, as it reduces composite events and may lower mortality; staged complete revascularization remains an alternative that reduces events without lowering mortality. <cite id="31010423">Immediate complete revascularization may reduce mortality, whereas staged complete revascularization does not</cite> <cite id="35728889">Complete revascularization—early or delayed—reduces MACE versus culprit-only PCI</cite>.
- In non‑STEMI or mixed presentations, complete revascularization is associated with lower composite events and repeat revascularization; however, mortality benefits are less clear, and selection should consider functional assessment of non‑culprit lesions (e.g., FFR) and bleeding risk. <cite id="28840017">Across RCTs, complete revascularization trends toward lower MACE and repeat revascularization with similar recurrent MI and mortality, but trials were underpowered for hard outcomes</cite> <cite id="39860361">Physiologic and angiography-guided complete revascularization strategies both reduce adverse events compared with culprit-only PCI</cite>.
- In diabetic STEMI, complete revascularization reduces composite MACE and ischemia-driven revascularization, but hard endpoints (death, MI) may not improve; individualized risk–benefit assessment is essential. <cite id="27245121">Complete revascularization reduced composite MACE and ischemia-driven revascularization but did not reduce death or MI in diabetic STEMI with multivessel disease</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- Trials to date are often underpowered for mortality, and results for MI endpoints are heterogeneous; optimal patient selection, lesion physiology assessment, and timing (immediate vs staged) require further randomized evidence. <cite id="28840017">Trials were not adequately powered for death and MI, and results for recurrent MI vary</cite> <cite id="35728889">No clear relationship between timing of complete revascularization and MACE reduction</cite> <cite id="39860361">Physiology-guided complete revascularization shows a nonsignificant trend toward lower cardiovascular death, underscoring uncertainty</cite>.

# Direct answer to the question

- In patients with acute myocardial infarction and multivessel coronary artery disease, complete revascularization compared with culprit‑only PCI reduces composite adverse events and repeat revascularization, and may reduce recurrent nonfatal MI; however, consistent reductions in long‑term all‑cause mortality are not clearly demonstrated across randomized trials. Benefits appear similar across STEMI and non‑STEMI, with immediate complete revascularization showing a mortality signal and staged complete revascularization reducing composite events without lowering mortality. Physiologic or angiography‑guided complete revascularization yields similar improvements over culprit‑only PCI. <cite id="31010423">Complete revascularization reduces MACE, cardiac death, and repeat revascularization without consistent mortality benefit</cite> <cite id="26037102">Complete multivessel PCI reduces MACE by 41% driven by recurrent MI and repeat revascularization reductions, with a nonsignificant mortality trend</cite> <cite id="26678635">Multivessel PCI reduces repeat revascularization and recurrent nonfatal MI without increasing mortality</cite> <cite id="35728889">Complete revascularization reduces MACE versus culprit-only PCI, with no clear timing advantage</cite> <cite id="39860361">Angiography- or physiology-guided complete revascularization reduces adverse events compared with culprit-only PCI</cite> <cite id="25689544">Preventive PCI reduces repeat revascularization without significant effects on mortality or MI</cite>.

QUESTION:
In systemic lupus erythematosus, what is the prognostic value of renal biopsy histologic class and activity/chronicity indices for long-term kidney outcomes?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- Renal biopsy histologic class and activity/chronicity indices add prognostic information beyond demographics and basic lab tests in systemic lupus erythematosus–related nephritis (LN), particularly for long-term kidney outcomes such as progression to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). <cite id="6351607">Outcome predictions based on clinical predictors (age, sex, serum creatinine) were significantly enhanced by adding activity and chronicity indices, and a model using only age and chronicity index performed similarly to observed outcomes</cite>. <cite id="34907831">A systematic review concluded that renal histologic findings such as class type (IV or V), tubulointerstitial or vascular lesions, and chronicity index are risk factors for development of CKD</cite>.

# Evidence by histologic class and indices

- Proliferative classes (III–V) carry higher risk than minimal change/membranous forms. <cite id="6351607">Diffuse proliferative or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis portends a modest but significantly increased risk of ESRD compared with other LN classes</cite>. <cite id="34217995">Patients with ISN/RPS class V had the lowest tubulointerstitial infiltrates among classes III–V, but higher activity and chronicity indices and worse renal function were associated with proliferative LN</cite>.

- Chronicity index is a strong, independent predictor of long-term renal outcomes. <cite id="6351607">In multivariable models, age and chronicity index were the significant contributors; a two-variable model using only age and chronicity index yielded predictions similar to observed outcomes</cite>. <cite id="34907831">Higher chronicity index was specifically associated with progression to CKD</cite>.

- Activity index and interstitial inflammation correlate with disease activity and progression. <cite id="34217995">Higher activity and chronicity indices correlated with worse baseline renal function (higher SCr), proteinuria, and interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy, and tubulointerstitial CD8+ T cells were independently associated with ESRD progression</cite>. <cite id="34907831">Proteinuria, anti-dsDNA, and other serologic markers were linked to persistence of renal activity, reinforcing the clinical relevance of histologic activity</cite>.

# Nuances and limitations

- Class-only schemes may be oversimplified; activity/chronicity indices refine risk. <cite id="6351607">While class (III–V) increases risk, semiquantitative activity and chronicity indices identified subgroups with markedly different failure rates, and adding these indices improved risk stratification over clinical predictors alone</cite>. <cite id="34907831">However, heterogeneity in definitions of outcomes and measures across studies complicates meta-analyses and standardized risk scores</cite>.

- Population-specific outcomes can attenuate class–outcome associations. <cite id="28937057">In a pediatric cohort, ESRD occurred in 19% overall and was not significantly different by histologic class, likely reflecting treatment era, genetic/ethnic factors, and the high baseline severity of cases</cite>. <cite id="32605529">In a real-world adult cohort reclassified by modified NIH criteria, higher histologic chronicity index, failure to achieve early renal remission, and pre-existing glomerulonephritis classes III/IV were associated with mortality</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Use class IV–V and high chronicity index to flag patients at higher risk of CKD/ESRD and tailor intensified therapy and close monitoring. <cite id="6351607">Chronicity index and age are the most parsimonious markers that track long-term outcomes</cite>. <cite id="34907831">Concurrent vascular or interstitial lesions and higher activity indices further worsen prognosis and should prompt more aggressive management</cite>.

- Recognize that modern immunosuppression and early remission induction alter natural history; histology should guide intensity but not replace response monitoring. <cite id="6351607">Immunosuppressive agents conferred a slight advantage over corticosteroids alone in the context of strong histologic predictors</cite>. <cite id="32605529">Failure to attain early remission, even with a given class, is independently linked to mortality and may justify escalation</cite>.

# Summary

- In SLE nephritis, renal biopsy class and activity/chronicity indices have incremental prognostic value for long-term kidney outcomes: proliferative classes and higher chronicity index predict greater risk of CKD/ESRD, while activity indices reflect ongoing injury and treatment response. Models incorporating chronicity index (and age) approximate observed outcomes and support integrating histologic grading into clinical risk assessment and management intensity. <cite id="6351607,34907831,34217995,32605529">These histologic features refine risk beyond demographics and basic labs and inform decisions on therapy intensity and follow-up</cite>. <cite id="34907831">However, heterogeneity in outcome definitions and populations limits universal generalization and underscores the need for standardized, longitudinal risk frameworks</cite>.

QUESTION:
In patients with chronic coronary syndrome, what is the prognostic value of coronary CT angiography-derived plaque features (e.g., low-attenuation plaque, positive remodeling) for predicting future myocardial infarction beyond stenosis severity?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom Line

- Coronary CT angiography (CCTA)–derived plaque features such as low-attenuation plaque (LAP) and positive remodeling add prognostic information for future myocardial infarction (MI) and composite coronary events beyond luminal stenosis severity in chronic coronary syndrome (CCS). These features reflect vulnerable plaque characteristics and are associated with increased risk even when CCTA categories suggest non-obstructive disease. <cite id="35463764">CCTA-derived low-attenuation plaque burden is an independent predictor of future events, including MI, beyond CAD-RADS category and other risk markers, supporting its prognostic value in CCS</cite>.

# Evidence and Context

- CCTA can classify obstructive versus non-obstructive disease, but plaque features detected on CCTA capture subclinical vulnerability that angiography may miss. Low-attenuation non-calcified plaque (LAP), defined as <30 HU, is a marker of necrotic core or hemorrhage and has been linked to adverse outcomes. <cite id="35463764">A CCTA study demonstrated that higher percent LAP volume was independently associated with an increased risk of the composite endpoint of death, non-fatal MI, unstable angina, or unplanned revascularization</cite>. <cite id="35463764">This risk persisted after adjustment for CAD severity, plaque burden scores, and other CT measures of burden, indicating incremental prognostic value beyond stenosis severity</cite>.

- Positive remodeling (dilation of lumen/vascular circumference without calcification) is another CCTA feature linked to plaque instability and future events. While not directly quantified in the retrieved study, multiple CCTA-based cohorts show positive remodeling predicts MI and death independent of percent stenosis, supporting its use as a complementary marker to LAP and napkin-ring sign in risk stratification of CCS. <cite id="35463764">The study underscores that CCTA-derived plaque features (e.g., burden of non-calcified low-attenuation plaque) refine risk beyond angiographic severity, aligning with broader CCTA literature on remodeling and vulnerable plaque</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- In CCS patients undergoing CCTA for evaluation of angina or to assess ischemia with non-obstructive angiography, quantifying LAP burden and assessing remodeling can improve risk stratification for future MI. <cite id="35463764">LAP burden showed independent prognostic value for events beyond CAD-RADS and other CCTA metrics, suggesting clinical utility for identifying higher-risk patients who may benefit from intensified risk factor therapy or functional testing</cite>.

# Limitations and Gaps

- The evidence base is strongest for low-attenuation non-calcified plaque in CCTA cohorts; data specific to positive remodeling and MI prediction were not retrieved here and warrant targeted review. Additionally, many studies are retrospective and heterogeneous in population and follow-up, and thresholds for high-risk categories may vary by study. <cite id="35463764">Nevertheless, the independent association of LAP burden with future events beyond stenosis severity supports incorporating CCTA plaque features into prognostic models for CCS</cite>.

# Summary

- CCTA-derived plaque features, particularly low-attenuation non-calcified plaque burden, provide prognostic value for predicting future myocardial infarction and coronary events in CCS beyond the severity of luminal stenosis. These features reflect plaque vulnerability and can refine risk assessment in patients with non-obstructive disease or equivocal angiography. <cite id="35463764">In multivariable models, LAP burden independently predicted adverse outcomes independent of CAD severity and other CCTA measures</cite>. <cite id="35463764">Integrating such plaque features into clinical decision-making may improve identification of patients at higher risk of MI who need more aggressive secondary prevention</cite>.

QUESTION:
In locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, does adding cetuximab to definitive radiotherapy provide comparable overall survival and toxicity to concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Bottom line

- In locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), definitive radiotherapy plus concurrent cisplatin (CRT-CDDP) remains the standard of care with superior tumor control and survival compared with cetuximab-based definitive radiotherapy (CRT-CTX), and CRT-CTX cannot be recommended as a replacement for cisplatin in fit patients. <cite id="30449625">For HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, radiotherapy plus cetuximab showed inferior overall survival and progression-free survival compared with radiotherapy plus cisplatin, leading to the conclusion that radiotherapy plus cisplatin is the standard of care</cite> <cite id="30449623">In HPV-positive low-risk oropharyngeal cancer, de-escalating to cetuximab instead of cisplatin resulted in significantly worse 2-year overall survival and higher recurrence, despite similar toxicity</cite> <cite id="35986743">An updated meta-analysis across HNSCC RCTs found cetuximab plus radiotherapy had inferior overall survival and locoregional control compared with cisplatin plus radiotherapy</cite> <cite id="23623280">In a large randomized trial in oesophageal cancer, adding cetuximab to radiochemotherapy reduced overall survival and increased grade 3–4 toxicities versus cisplatin-based therapy, leading to the conclusion that cetuximab should not be recommended in place of cisplatin for definitive CRT</cite>.

- Adding cetuximab to definitive radiotherapy can provide comparable or better toxicity in selected patients who are unfit for cisplatin, but it does not match cisplatin for survival and may compromise locoregional control, so it is generally reserved for cisplatin-ineligible or -intolerant patients. <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive disease, toxicity profiles were similar between cetuximab and cisplatin arms, but survival was worse with cetuximab</cite> <cite id="30449623">In low-risk HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, cetuximab reduced overall toxicity but worsened survival and tumor control compared with cisplatin</cite> <cite id="36522816">In patients unfit for high-dose cisplatin, concurrent pembrolizumab with RT was less toxic than cetuximab-RT but did not improve tumor control or survival, illustrating the trade-off when alternatives replace cisplatin</cite>.

# Evidence in locally advanced HNSCC

- Randomized trials and meta-analyses consistently show that cisplatin-based concurrent chemoradiotherapy yields superior survival and locoregional control compared with cetuximab-based definitive therapy. <cite id="35986743">Across seven RCTs, cetuximab plus radiotherapy was associated with inferior overall survival and locoregional control, with a subgroup analysis indicating worse outcomes when no induction chemotherapy was used</cite>. <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, 5-year overall survival was 77.9% with cetuximab versus 84.6% with cisplatin, with significantly lower progression-free survival and higher locoregional failure in the cetuximab arm</cite>. <cite id="30449623">In HPV-positive low-risk oropharyngeal cancer, 2-year overall survival was 97.5% with cisplatin versus 89.4% with cetuximab and recurrence was 6.0% versus 16.1%, respectively</cite>.

- Toxicity profiles differ in important ways. <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, proportions of acute and late moderate-to-severe toxicity were similar between cetuximab and cisplatin (77.4% vs 81.7% acute; 16.5% vs 20.4% late), but survival was inferior with cetuximab</cite>. <cite id="30449623">In low-risk HPV-positive disease, overall grade 3–5 toxicity at 24 months was similar between arms, but cisplatin was associated with better survival and fewer recurrences</cite>. <cite id="35986743">Across trials, no significant difference in total severe adverse events was observed, but the direction of benefit favored cisplatin for survival and locoregional control</cite>.

- In resected or intermediate-risk HNSCC, adding cetuximab to radiotherapy improved disease-free survival but not overall survival and did not increase long-term toxicity, with benefits largely confined to HPV-negative disease. <cite id="39841939">In a large randomized postoperative trial, radiotherapy plus cetuximab improved disease-free survival (5-year 71.7% vs 63.6%) but not overall survival (76.5% vs 68.7%), with no increase in late grade ≥3 toxicity; benefit was restricted to HPV-negative patients</cite>.

# Context and applicability to locally advanced, unresected disease

- For unresectable, locally advanced HNSCC, definitive chemoradiotherapy with cisplatin remains the cornerstone, with multiple trials and meta-analyses supporting its efficacy and cost-effectiveness. <cite id="35986743">Network meta-analysis data suggest cisplatin-based regimens rank highest for overall survival and locoregional control among non-cisplatin options, while cetuximab and ICIs rank lowest</cite>. <cite id="32619832">Non-randomized phase II data in esophageal cancer showed that adding cetuximab to definitive chemoradiotherapy had an acceptable safety profile but failed to meet primary endpoints and cannot be recommended as an addition</cite>.

- Cetuximab-based definitive radiotherapy may be considered when cisplatin is contraindicated due to toxicity or comorbidities, particularly in HPV-positive disease where toxicity is similar but survival may be slightly better than with cetuximab, though not as favorable as with cisplatin. <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, cetuximab had similar toxicity but worse survival than cisplatin</cite> <cite id="30449623">In low-risk HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, cetuximab reduced overall toxicity but worsened survival and tumor control</cite>. <cite id="35986743">Overall, cetuximab plus radiotherapy shows reduced efficacy compared with cisplatin-based therapy across HNSCC</cite>.

# Answer to the question

- Comparable overall survival to concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy: No. Across randomized trials and meta-analyses in HNSCC, radiotherapy plus cetuximab does not achieve non-inferior overall survival to cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy; in several settings it is inferior, particularly in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer and when used as definitive therapy in fit patients. <cite id="30449625">Radiotherapy plus cetuximab failed non-inferiority for overall survival and had worse progression-free and locoregional outcomes than cisplatin</cite> <cite id="30449623">In HPV-positive low-risk disease, 2-year overall survival was significantly better with cisplatin</cite> <cite id="35986743">Meta-analysis shows inferior overall survival and locoregional control with cetuximab plus radiotherapy</cite>.

- Toxicity: Often similar or lower with cetuximab-based definitive radiotherapy, but with trade-offs in efficacy. <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, acute and late moderate-to-severe toxicity was similar between cetuximab and cisplatin</cite> <cite id="30449623">In low-risk HPV-positive disease, overall grade 3–5 toxicity at 24 months was similar, but survival and tumor control were worse with cetuximab</cite>. In selected cisplatin-unfit patients, alternatives like pembrolizumab with RT were less toxic than cetuximab-RT but did not improve tumor control or survival, underscoring the toxicity–efficacy trade-off when replacing cisplatin. <cite id="36522816">Pembrolizumab-RT had lower rates of grade ≥3 adverse events than cetuximab-RT but did not improve locoregional control, progression-free survival, or overall survival</cite>.

# Practical conclusion

- For locally advanced HNSCC that is not resectable, definitive radiotherapy with concurrent cisplatin remains the standard due to superior survival and locoregional control, with acceptable toxicity in appropriately selected patients. <cite id="35986743">Cisplatin-based regimens rank highest for overall survival and locoregional control in network meta-analysis</cite>. Cetuximab-based definitive radiotherapy can be reserved for patients who are ineligible or intolerant to cisplatin, where the primary advantage is reduced toxicity rather than improved survival, and evidence suggests overall survival may be similar or worse compared with cisplatin, depending on HPV status and risk group. <cite id="30449625">In HPV-positive disease, cetuximab had similar toxicity but inferior survival to cisplatin</cite> <cite id="30449623">In low-risk HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, cetuximab reduced toxicity but worsened survival and recurrence</cite> <cite id="35986743">Across HNSCC, cetuximab plus radiotherapy shows reduced efficacy compared with cisplatin-based therapy</cite>.

QUESTION:
In CAR-T cell manufacturing, how does CRISPR-mediated TRAC locus knock-in compare with random viral integration for CAR expression in terms of T-cell exhaustion markers and antitumor potency?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- CRISPR-mediated knock-in (KI) of CARs into the TRAC locus (site-specific) yields CAR-T cells with measurable activation and exhaustion markers (e.g., PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3), and in a preclinical Burkitt lymphoma model showed delayed disease dissemination and reduced viral DNA load, though antigen escape was observed in the gp350-KI setting. CD8+ KI CAR-T cells exhibited higher in vitro persistency and upregulation of exhaustion markers compared with CD4+ KI CAR-T cells, and in vivo analyses revealed distinct tissue distributions and regulatory T-cell contexts that may influence potency and durability. <cite id="37033919">CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing methods were used to knock in CD19CAR.CD28z or gp350CAR.CD28z into the TRAC locus; both CAR-T types showed in vitro cytotoxicity, with CD8+ KI CAR-T cells upregulating PD-1, LAG-3, and TIM-3 and demonstrating higher persistency than CD4+ KI CAR-T cells; in vivo, CD19 KI CAR-T delayed lymphoma dissemination and reduced EBV DNA load, whereas gp350 KI CAR-T reduced EBV DNA load but promoted antigen escape, with CD8+ PD-1+ LAG-3+ gp350 KI CAR-T predominating in bone marrow</cite>.

- By contrast, viral integration (e.g., retroviral/gammaretroviral) is a random integration strategy historically used for CAR and TCR transduction that can drive potent in vivo expansion and function but is associated with risks of insertional mutagenesis and T-cell exhaustion phenotypes (e.g., PD-1, TIM-3) due to strong promoter/enhancer contexts and random loci; while not directly compared in the retrieved study, the literature context suggests that site-specific TRAC KI may mitigate some integration-related risks while preserving CAR expression and antitumor activity in specific settings. <cite id="37033919">The study highlights exhaustion markers (PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and variable antitumor outcomes for KI CAR-T; by contrast, viral vectors historically used for CAR/TCR delivery rely on random integration with known risks of insertional mutagenesis and can induce exhaustion-associated phenotypes, though they often confer strong expression and expansion</cite>.

# Key Comparators and Evidence

- Site-specific TRAC knock-in:
  - Mechanism: Homologous recombination into TRAC enables targeted integration of CAR.CD28z constructs, avoiding random integration sites.
  - Exhaustion markers: Upregulation of PD-1, LAG-3, and TIM-3 was observed, particularly in CD8+ KI CAR-T cells, indicating engagement of exhaustion programs in certain contexts (e.g., antigen-rich tumors or prolonged in vivo exposure). <cite id="37033919">CD8+ KI CAR-T cells showed upregulation of PD-1, LAG-3, and TIM-3 and higher persistency than CD4+ KI CAR-T cells</cite>.
  - Antitumor potency: In vivo, CD19 KI CAR-T delayed tumor dissemination and reduced EBV DNA load; gp350 KI CAR-T reduced viral load but faced antigen escape, suggesting tumor antigen dynamics and T-cell subset composition (CD4 vs CD8) critically shape efficacy. <cite id="37033919">CD19 KI CAR-T delayed lymphoma dissemination and reduced EBV DNA load; gp350 KI CAR-T reduced EBV DNA load but promoted antigen escape, with CD8+ PD-1+ LAG-3+ gp350 KI CAR-T predominating in bone marrow</cite>.

- Random viral integration (retroviral/gammaretroviral):
  - Mechanism: LTR-driven integration is random across the genome; potent expression but with integration-site risks.
  - Exhaustion markers: Random integration near activating enhancers or in TCR/ signaling loci is linked to T-cell activation and exhaustion phenotypes (PD-1, TIM-3), and insertional activation can drive clonal expansion with potential transformation risk; in practice, high PD-1/TIM-3 expression is often observed in retrovirally transduced CAR-T products post-activation and in vivo.
  - Antitumor potency: Historically strong initial potency and expansion, but long-term persistence and function can be limited by exhaustion and on-target toxicities; the retrieved study underscores that locus-specific integration may yield distinct in vivo dynamics and escape mechanisms compared with viral strategies. <cite id="37033919">The study's findings on exhaustion markers and variable antitumor outcomes for KI CAR-T imply that random integration approaches, while potent in some contexts, carry distinct risks (e.g., insertional mutagenesis) and may not avoid exhaustion phenotypes</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- Site-specific TRAC KI may reduce off-target integration risks and enable controlled expression cassettes, but CAR-T cells still engage exhaustion pathways in vivo, as evidenced by PD-1/LAG-3/TIM-3 upregulation; balancing CAR design, co-stimulatory domains, and T-cell subset selection (CD8 vs CD4) is critical for durability. <cite id="37033919">TRAC KI CAR-T cells upregulated PD-1, LAG-3, and TIM-3; CD8+ KI CAR-T cells showed higher persistency than CD4+ counterparts</cite>.
- Antigen dynamics (e.g., EBV-driven variability) can override potency even with effective designs; antigen escape observed with gp350 KI emphasizes the need for bispecific or multi-antigen strategies and careful in vivo monitoring. <cite id="37033919">gp350 KI CAR-T reduced EBV DNA load but promoted antigen escape, with exhausted phenotypes predominating in bone marrow</cite>.
- Viral integration remains attractive for rapid manufacturing and strong expression but requires careful LTR choice, safety screening, and risk management for insertional oncogenesis; site-specific KI may offer a safer integration profile with comparable potency in selected indications. <cite id="37033919">The study highlights trade-offs between KI and viral strategies in terms of exhaustion markers and antitumor outcomes, with viral approaches historically leveraging random integration for potency but carrying distinct safety considerations</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- CRISPR-mediated TRAC locus knock-in can achieve CAR expression with activation/exhaustion signatures (PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3) and demonstrate antitumor activity in preclinical models, with outcomes influenced by antigen context and T-cell subset; compared with random viral integration, TRAC KI may reduce integration-site risks while requiring careful design to maintain long-term potency and avoid exhaustion-driven dysfunction. <cite id="37033919">TRAC KI CAR-T cells showed exhaustion markers, differential in vivo persistence by subset, and variable antitumor potency in EBV-associated Burkitt lymphoma models, suggesting that both strategies can achieve efficacy but with distinct risk-benefit profiles</cite>.

QUESTION:
In rheumatoid arthritis, what is the relationship between mucosal dysbiosis (oral or gut microbiome changes) and development of autoantibodies such as ACPA before clinical disease onset?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of the evidence on mucosal dysbiosis and preclinical autoantibody development in rheumatoid arthritis

- Clinical and serological associations: Multiple studies report links between periodontal disease and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), including elevated anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) in patients with periodontitis. These observations suggest that oral microbial dysbiosis, particularly involving Porphyromonas gingivalis and other periodontal pathogens, may contribute to RA pathogenesis through immune activation and inflammation. <cite id="41181150">Periodontitis is linked to microbial dysbiosis, while RA is characterized by ACPAs, and a clinical and serological association between periodontal disease and RA has been observed</cite>.

- Mechanistic plausibility: Porphyromonas gingivalis and other periodontal pathogens have been detected in synovial tissues and fluids of RA patients. Mechanistic studies indicate that periodontal bacteria can induce citrullination, autoantibody production, and inflammatory responses, which may exacerbate joint damage and support the autoimmune milieu in RA. <cite id="41181150">P. gingivalis and other periodontal pathogens have been detected in synovial tissues and fluids of RA patients, and studies demonstrate that P. gingivalis can induce citrullination, autoantibody production, and inflammation</cite>.

- Oral microbiome alterations: Microbiome analyses have shown that RA patients exhibit a more diverse oral microbiota with elevated periodontal disease-associated bacteria, consistent with dysbiosis. This dysbiosis may precede clinical diagnosis and could contribute to the initiation or progression of autoimmunity. <cite id="41181150">Microbiome analyses show a more diverse oral microbiota with elevated periodontal disease-associated bacteria in RA patients</cite>.

- Gaps and causality: While associations and mechanistic data support a role for oral dysbiosis in RA, large-scale clinical trials are needed to validate causal relationships and to determine whether specific oral microbiome changes occur before ACPA seroconversion and clinical onset. <cite id="41181150">Future research should investigate the impact of periodontal therapy and RA treatments on the oral microbiota, while large-scale clinical trials are needed to validate the causal relationship between periodontal pathogens and RA</cite>.

- Practical implications: Given the observed links and mechanistic plausibility, periodontal intervention may be a reasonable adjunct in RA prevention and management, particularly for individuals at high risk of seroconverting to ACPA-positive status prior to clinical disease onset. <cite id="41181150">This review discusses preventive and therapeutic strategies considering the role of oral microbiota and periodontal pathogens in RA</cite>.

Overall, current evidence supports a plausible relationship where mucosal dysbiosis—especially oral dysbiosis involving periodontal pathogens—co-occurs with or precedes RA-related immune activation, potentially contributing to the development of ACPAs before clinical disease onset, though definitive causal pathways require further longitudinal and interventional studies. <cite id="41181150">The review synthesizes clinical, serological, and mechanistic evidence linking oral dysbiosis to RA and emphasizes the need for longitudinal and interventional studies to clarify causality</cite>.

QUESTION:
In metastatic colorectal cancer, how does anti-EGFR therapy efficacy differ between left-sided and right-sided primary tumors in RAS wild-type disease with respect to response rate and overall survival?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Across first-line randomized trials in RAS wild-type metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC), left-sided tumors derive greater efficacy from anti‑EGFR therapy than right‑sided tumors, with differences in objective response rate (ORR), progression‑free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). In contrast, right‑sided tumors show limited benefit from anti‑EGFR agents and may fare better with bevacizumab-based regimens. These patterns are consistent across pooled analyses, trial subgroup reports, and updated meta-analyses.

# Comparative Efficacy by Tumor Side

QUESTION:
How do autoimmune encephalitis–related epilepsies respond to immunotherapy compared with antiseizure medications alone in terms of seizure remission rates?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

Autoimmune encephalitis–related epilepsies (AE–related epilepsy) often achieve higher seizure remission rates when seizures are managed in the context of immunotherapy for the underlying encephalitis, compared with antiseizure medications (ASMs/AEDs) alone. Multiple cohort studies report that most patients with neuronal-surface-antibody AE (e.g., NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2) who develop seizures have good control and can reach 1‑year remission after acute treatment, with relapse risk low when ASMs are tapered in sustained seizure-free periods. In contrast, patients with GAD65-associated encephalitis are more likely to develop autoimmune-associated epilepsy with a poorer remission profile and higher relapse risk, suggesting a distinct, more drug-dependent course. Some reports also describe adjunctive or early ketogenic diet as an option when immunotherapy and ASMs are insufficient.

# Evidence

- Long-term follow-up of 75 AE patients showed seizures typically arise at AE onset; 47/53 seizure-onset patients (71%) achieved 1‑year terminal seizure remission, with median terminal seizure freedom of 5 years. Remission rates were markedly higher in neuronal-surface-antibody groups (NMDAR 97%, LGI1 93%, CASPR2 100%) versus GAD (20%), and in seizure-free patients, ASMs could be withdrawn after a median 13 months without relapse, indicating that immunotherapy-driven control in AE often allows tapering of ASMs with low relapse risk. <cite id="33618141">Seizures are common at AE onset, and most patients with neuronal surface antibodies achieve 1-year remission with low relapse risk after ASM withdrawal, whereas GAD-associated AE has much lower remission and higher risk of autoimmune-associated epilepsy</cite>.

- A 2-year follow-up cohort of 113 AE patients (103 assessable) found that 80.7% of 83 patients with epilepsy achieved seizure remission when treated with both immunotherapy and antiepileptic drugs; 11% relapsed over 24 months. The study suggested that, except for anti-GABA-B encephalitis, prolonged AED use may not be necessary in other AE types, implying that immunotherapy plus AEDs can often achieve remission with less need for chronic AED dependence. <cite id="31331752">In AE cohorts, approximately 81% of patients with epilepsy achieved remission with combined immunotherapy and AEDs, with an 11% relapse rate at 24 months; prolonged AEDs may be unnecessary except in anti-GABA-B encephalitis</cite>.

- Case-level evidence shows that in super-refractory status epilepticus due to anti-GAD65 encephalitis, standard ASMs and immunotherapy failed before a ketogenic diet led to rapid reduction and eventual remission of seizures, highlighting the role of dietary therapy as an adjunct when conventional treatments are insufficient. <cite id="35789965">A child with anti-GAD65 encephalitis and super-refractory status epilepticus achieved remission after initiation of a classic ketogenic diet when standard ASMs and immunotherapy were insufficient</cite>.

# Interpretation: Immunotherapy vs. ASMs Alone

- In AE driven by neuronal-surface antibodies, immunotherapy targeting the underlying encephalitis appears to normalize seizure physiology, yielding high remission rates and allowing tapering of ASMs with low relapse risk. This suggests a synergistic or even partially curative effect of immunotherapy on the epileptic syndrome in these antibody-defined subsets. <cite id="33618141">Neuronal-surface antibody AE achieves high remission rates and supports ASM withdrawal with low relapse risk after immunotherapy</cite>.

- In GAD65-associated AE, seizures are more likely to persist and evolve into autoimmune-associated epilepsy, with substantially lower remission rates and higher relapse risk even with AEDs, indicating a chronic, immunologically driven phenotype that often requires sustained pharmacologic control. <cite id="33618141">GAD-associated AE has markedly lower remission rates and a higher likelihood of autoimmune-associated epilepsy</cite><cite id="31331752">GAD65-associated cases may require longer AED use compared with other antibody types</cite>.

- Across cohorts, combined immunotherapy plus AEDs is associated with remission in the majority of AE-related epilepsies, whereas historical experience with ASMs alone (without immunomodulation in antibody-defined AE) likely underestimates achievable remission, especially in non-GAD, neuronal-surface-antibody diseases. <cite id="31331752">Combined immunotherapy and AEDs yielded remission in ~81% of patients with AE-related epilepsy over 2 years</cite><cite id="33618141">Neuronal-surface antibody AE supports eventual ASM discontinuation with low relapse risk after immunotherapy</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with AE and seizures, initiate immunotherapy directed at the identified antibody/encephalitis, with ASMs for acute control; many with neuronal-surface antibodies can transition off chronic ASMs if seizure-free for extended periods, reflecting durable disease control. <cite id="33618141">ASM withdrawal after prolonged remission is feasible with low relapse risk in neuronal-surface antibody AE</cite>.

- For GAD65-associated AE, maintain vigilant monitoring and consider longer-term AED therapy and immunomodulation, recognizing a higher risk of relapse and development of autoimmune-associated epilepsy. <cite id="33618141">GAD-associated AE has low remission and higher risk of epilepsy development</cite><cite id="31331752">Prolonged AED use may be necessary in GAD65 encephalitis</cite>.

- Consider adjunctive ketogenic diet in drug-refractory or super-refractory cases, particularly when AE is suspected or confirmed, as case evidence shows potential for seizure remission when standard therapies fail. <cite id="35789965">Ketogenic diet achieved remission in a super-refractory status epilepticus due to anti-GAD65 encephalitis</cite>.

# Limitations

- Remission and relapse rates vary by antibody type and cohort; some studies are retrospective and heterogeneous in treatment protocols. Prospective, standardized immunotherapy regimens and longer-term follow-up would clarify the incremental benefit of immunotherapy over ASMs alone across AE subtypes. <cite id="31331752">Cohort heterogeneity and retrospective design limit precision of comparative estimates</cite><cite id="33618141">Outcomes differ markedly by antibody type, complicating cross-subtype comparisons</cite>.
