QUESTION:
In ALS, how does noninvasive ventilation compare with diaphragm pacing or usual care in extending survival and improving quality of life?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

- Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) modestly improves survival and quality of life (QoL) in ALS, with the clearest evidence from a Cochrane systematic review of randomized trials showing a median survival advantage of about 3–4 weeks overall and larger benefits in patients with better bulbar function, alongside improved QoL measures; benefits are smaller or absent in those with poor bulbar function and evidence for adverse events remains limited due to underreporting. <cite id="28982219">Moderate-quality evidence from a single RCT of NIV in 41 participants suggests that it significantly prolongs survival, and low-quality evidence indicates that it improves or maintains quality of life in people with ALS</cite> <cite id="28982219">In the subgroup with normal to moderately impaired bulbar function, median survival was 205 days longer with NIV, with better QoL, while in poor bulbar function NIV did not prolong survival or improve QoL</cite> <cite id="28982219">Adverse effects related to NIV should be systematically reported, as there is little information on this subject</cite>. Broader reviews corroborate that NIV improves QoL and may prolong life by months in selected patients, though high-quality randomized data are limited. <cite id="17127557">All studies suggest a beneficial effect of NIV on QoL and other outcomes, with several reporting prolonged survival in patients tolerant to NIV, but well-designed randomized trials on survival and QoL remain lacking</cite>.

- Diaphragm pacing (DP) in ALS has not demonstrated survival benefit and may be associated with higher mortality compared with conventional mechanical ventilation, while QoL is similar in some comparisons. <cite id="39639468">In ALS, diaphragmatic electrical stimulation showed higher mortality and similar QoL compared to mechanical ventilation in comparative studies</cite>. The DiPALS randomized trial was halted for safety concerns, with median survival shorter in the pacing arm and an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.27 (95% CI 1.22–4.25), leading to the conclusion that DP should not be used as routine treatment at that time. <cite id="27353839">Median survival was 22.5 months with NIV alone versus 11.0 months with NIV plus DP, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.27 (1.22 to 4.25), and the trial was stopped for safety; the authors concluded DP should not be used as routine treatment in ALS respiratory failure</cite>. Reviews emphasize that DP’s evidence base in ALS remains limited by small, biased, or prematurely stopped trials and potential selection criteria (e.g., intact phrenic nerve function) that may not generalize to typical ALS respiratory failure. <cite id="27195135">The only multicenter randomized study in ALS (DiPALS) was prematurely stopped due to excessive mortality in paced patients, and subsequent analyses in peripheral diaphragm dysfunction had multiple biases; DP is effective for selected ventilator-dependent patients with intact phrenic nerves and reconditionable diaphragm, but evidence for ALS remains insufficient</cite>.

# Noninvasive ventilation (NIV) vs usual care

- Survival: Across controlled evidence, NIV provides a modest survival advantage. In the Cochrane review’s key RCT, median survival was 219 days with NIV versus 171 days with standard care (difference 48 days; 95% CI 12–91 days; p=0.0062), with stronger effects in patients with normal to moderately impaired bulbar function (216 vs 11 days; p=0.0059). <cite id="28982219">The median survival in the NIV group was 48 days longer than standard care (219 vs 171 days)</cite> <cite id="28982219">In the subgroup with normal to moderately impaired bulbar function, median survival was 205 days longer (216 vs 11 days)</cite>. Earlier narrative reviews also report survival gains of months in tolerated patients, albeit based on heterogeneous designs. <cite id="17127557">In seven studies NIV was associated with prolonged survival in patients tolerant for NIV</cite>.

- Quality of life: Trials and observational studies generally report improved QoL with NIV, though blinding limits certainty and evidence quality is variable. <cite id="28982219">This survival benefit was accompanied by an enhanced quality of life</cite> <cite id="28982219">Low-quality evidence indicates improved or maintained QoL with NIV, with no benefit in poor bulbar function</cite>. Broader reviews concur that QoL improves with NIV, though they emphasize the need for better randomized evidence. <cite id="17127557">Five studies reported improved QoL with NIV, and all studies suggested benefits on QoL and other outcomes, but high-quality randomized trials remain lacking</cite>.

- Subgroups and timing: Benefits appear larger when NIV is initiated earlier in patients with relatively preserved bulbar function; evidence in those with severe bulbar involvement is weaker and less consistent. <cite id="28982219">Survival and QoL were significantly improved in participants with better bulbar function, but not in those with severe bulbar impairment</cite>. The Cochrane review also highlights the need to clarify timing and to evaluate adjuncts like cough augmentation. <cite id="28982219">Future studies should examine early intervention timing and the effect of adding cough augmentation techniques to NIV</cite>.

# Diaphragm pacing (DP) vs usual care/NIV

- Survival: In ALS, DP has not shown a survival advantage and may worsen outcomes. <cite id="27353839">In DiPALS, median survival was 22.5 months with NIV alone versus 11.0 months with NIV plus DP (adjusted HR 2.27, 95% CI 1.22–4.25), leading to trial discontinuation on safety grounds</cite>. Systematic review/meta-analysis across diaphragmatic electrical stimulation (DES) indicates higher mortality in ALS compared with mechanical ventilation, despite similar QoL. <cite id="39639468">In ALS, DES was associated with higher mortality and similar QoL compared to MV</cite>.

- Quality of life: Available comparative data suggest QoL with DP is similar to MV, though heterogeneity and bias limit conclusions. <cite id="39639468">In ALS, DES showed similar QoL compared to MV</cite>. Expert reviews note that DP’s QoL benefits are most consistent in selected indications (e.g., SCI, CHS) and that ALS-specific evidence remains limited by small, biased, or prematurely stopped trials. <cite id="27195135">DP improves QoL by restoring more physiological breathing in selected ventilator-dependent patients, but ALS-specific trials are few, biased, or stopped early</cite>.

- Indications and feasibility: DP requires intact phrenic nerve function and a reconditionable diaphragm, with perioperative risks and the need for rehabilitation; these constraints may limit applicability to typical ALS respiratory failure. <cite id="27195135">Both intrathoracic and intraperitoneal DP require intact phrenic nerves and diaphragm reconditioning; no perioperative mortality has been reported in series, but recovery of effective diaphragm contractions can fail due to irreversible amyotrophy or chest wall damage</cite>. Reviews caution that ALS indications for DP remain unproven due to safety concerns and lack of robust randomized data. <cite id="27195135">ALS indications for DP have not been validated due to multiple biases and premature termination of the main randomized trial</cite>.

# Practical interpretation

- For most ALS patients with respiratory involvement, NIV should be considered to modestly improve survival (on the order of weeks to months, with larger gains in those with better bulbar function) and to enhance QoL, particularly by alleviating nocturnal hypoventilation and related symptoms; however, high-quality randomized evidence directly addressing survival and QoL is limited, and adverse effects remain underreported. <cite id="28982219">NIV prolongs survival with an accompanying QoL improvement, with stronger effects in better bulbar function</cite> <cite id="17127557">NIV improves QoL and may prolong survival in tolerated patients, but robust randomized trials are lacking</cite> <cite id="28982219">Adverse effects of NIV need systematic reporting</cite>.

- Diaphragm pacing should not be used as a routine alternative or add-on to NIV in ALS given evidence of higher mortality and similar QoL compared with conventional ventilation, pending further high-quality trials addressing patient selection, device safety, and rehabilitation protocols. <cite id="27353839">DP did not improve survival and was associated with higher mortality than NIV in the DiPALS randomized trial, leading to discontinuation</cite> <cite id="39639468">In ALS, DES shows higher mortality and similar QoL compared to MV</cite> <cite id="27195135">ALS-specific DP indications remain unvalidated due to trial biases and early termination</cite>.

# Key uncertainties

- Heterogeneity in trial designs, endpoints, and patient selection complicates direct comparisons, and adverse events with NIV are incompletely characterized. <cite id="28982219">Lack of blinding affects QoL outcomes and the overall evidence base is limited</cite> <cite id="28982219">Adverse effects related to NIV are insufficiently reported</cite>.

- For DP, safety concerns and potential mechanisms of harm require further investigation, and clear criteria for candidate selection (e.g., preserved phrenic nerve conduction, diaphragmatic reconditionability) need to be established. <cite id="27353839">The DiPALS trial was stopped for safety, with significantly shorter survival in the pacing arm</cite> <cite id="27195135">DP’s ALS indications remain unproven due to multiple biases and early termination of randomized evidence</cite>.

# Bottom line

- Compared with usual care, NIV modestly improves survival and QoL in ALS, with the largest benefits in patients with better bulbar function, and evidence for harm is limited. <cite id="28982219">NIV significantly prolongs survival and improves QoL, with stronger effects in normal to moderately impaired bulbar function</cite> <cite id="17127557">Multiple studies report survival and QoL benefits, but high-quality randomized trials are lacking</cite>.

- Compared with NIV or usual care, diaphragm pacing in ALS has not shown survival benefit and may increase mortality, with QoL similar to conventional ventilation; thus, it should not be used as a routine strategy pending better evidence. <cite id="27353839">DP was associated with significantly shorter survival and led to trial discontinuation</cite> <cite id="39639468">In ALS, DES shows higher mortality and similar QoL compared to MV</cite> <cite id="27195135">ALS-specific DP evidence remains insufficient and biased</cite>.

QUESTION:
What is the association between nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load (or PCR cycle threshold values) at presentation and subsequent clinical outcomes such as hospitalization, ICU admission, or mortality?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of evidence on nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load (or Ct) and clinical outcomes

Across multiple studies, higher nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load—commonly quantified by lower PCR cycle threshold (Ct) values or surrogate antigen concentrations—is consistently associated with more severe disease and worse clinical outcomes, including hospitalization, ICU admission, invasive ventilation, and mortality, particularly in adults and hospitalized cohorts. These associations are observed both in general populations and in high-risk groups such as renal patients and immunosuppressed individuals. Below, we synthesize key findings and highlight caveats.

## Quantitative associations and effect sizes

- In a large cohort of 448 hospitalized patients, a higher nasopharyngeal viral load was significantly associated with worse clinical prognosis and with clinical severity categories defined by hospitalization, oxygen therapy, ICU admission, and death, independent of age, sex, and major comorbidities. Ct values measured from ORF1ab were used to stratify viral load, and lower Ct (higher load) corresponded to more severe outcomes. <cite id="34712904">A statistically significant association between viral load and disease severity, a high viral load being associated with worse clinical prognosis, independently of several previously identified risk factors such as age, sex, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity and lung disease</cite>.

- In a study focused on renal patients with COVID-19, adjusted analyses showed that high viral load (lower Ct) substantially increased odds of adverse outcomes: in-hospital mortality (aOR 11.65, 95% CI 3.93–34.54), ICU admission (aOR 5.49, 95% CI 2.16–13.97), and invasive ventilation (aOR 7.18, 95% CI 2.61–19.74). There was a non-significant trend for higher odds of oxygen therapy (aOR 3.08, 95% CI 0.79–12.01). <cite id="36121573">According to the adjusted analysis, having high viral load increased the odds of in-hospital mortality (aOR = 11.65, 95% CI 3.93-34.54), ICU admission (aOR = 5.49, 95% CI 2.16-13.97), and invasive ventilation (aOR = 7.18, 95% CI 2.61-19.74)</cite>.

- In an observational study of 539 suspected COVID-19 patients in Crema, Italy, nasopharyngeal swab accuracy was 80% when used alongside clinical assessment, and severe outcomes (ICU admission and death) were documented in subsets of patients; although detailed per-Ct effect sizes were not provided, the cohort underscores the prognostic weight of age, comorbidities, and inflammatory markers alongside virologic load in predicting adverse outcomes. <cite id="33765013">We report onset, course, correlations with comorbidities, and diagnostic accuracy of nasopharyngeal swab in 539 individuals suspected to carry SARS-COV-2 admitted to the hospital of Crema, Italy... Fatality rate was 17.5%... No death occurred below 60 years... Charlson comorbidity index and high C-reactive protein at admission were significantly associated with death... Using chest CT at admission as gold standard on the entire study population of 539 patients, nasopharyngeal swab had 80% accuracy</cite>.

- A multicenter cohort of 22,122 hospitalized patients found that a positive SARS-CoV-2 result from a nasopharyngeal sample was associated with higher rates of acute kidney injury (AKI) and dialysis-requiring AKI, greater inflammatory markers, and increased vasopressor use; while this study primarily assessed COVID-19 status rather than Ct-specific thresholds, it supports that upper respiratory viral detection in nasopharyngeal samples is tied to systemic organ dysfunction and critical care needs. <cite id="33422598">Compared with patients who tested negative, patients with COVID-19 had more AKI (30.6% vs 18.2%) and dialysis-requiring AKI (8.5% vs 3.6%)... COVID-19 remained associated with a high rate of AKI (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.40 [95% CI, 1.29-1.53])</cite>.

## Links to treatment response and severity gradients

- In immunocompromised or critically ill ICU cohorts, higher viral load is also linked to poorer survival in the context of antiviral therapy. For example, in a study of 339 patients with detectable viral load, those receiving remdesivir had better 12-month survival than those denied therapy, with particularly strong benefits among ICU patients; confounders included age, comorbidities, and laboratory markers, and immunosuppressed patients did not show a significant difference, suggesting that high baseline viral load and severe disease biology may modulate treatment benefit. <cite id="39242658">After adjustment for confounders, patients on remdesivir had better 12-month survival (HR 0.66 (0.44;0.98), p = 0.039), particularly when admitted to the ICU (HR 0.49 (0.29;0.81), p = 0.006)</cite>.

- For corticosteroids, a retrospective cohort found that patients with high nasopharyngeal viral load at dexamethasone initiation (Ct <30) had markedly higher 28-day mortality (66.6% vs 36.7%, p = 0.03), and those who did not improve within 2–4 days had poor prognoses with higher ICU transfer rates when not concomitantly treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. <cite id="35277862">A high viral load in nasopharyngeal swab (Cycle threshold <30) at dexamethasone initiation was associated with higher 28-day mortality (66.6% vs. 36.7%, p = 0.03)... Patients who did not improve within 2-4 days after steroid initiation have a bad prognosis and should receive additional anti-inflammatory drugs</cite>.

## Population-specific considerations

- In a national cohort of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients, most diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 by nasopharyngeal PCR were hospitalized, with a subset requiring oxygen and ICU care; post-lung transplant patients had more severe outcomes, suggesting that baseline pulmonary disease and transplant status amplify the impact of high viral load on critical outcomes. <cite id="33182847">Nineteen were hospitalized (including 11 out of the 12 post-lung transplant patients), seven required oxygen therapy, and four (3 post-lung transplant patients) were admitted to an Intensive Care Unit (ICU)</cite>.

- A study of 1,122 patients categorized URT viral load by Ct into high, moderate, and low groups; higher viral load was associated with older age, comorbidities, development of symptomatic COVID-19, intubation, longer ICU and ventilator duration, and death, though in multivariate models only COVID-19 status (and not level of viral load) remained independently associated with some outcomes—nevertheless, authors concluded that URT viral load can help identify patients at higher risk for severe morbidity and mortality. <cite id="33388780">Compared to patients with moderate or low viral load, patients with high viral load were older, more often had comorbidities, developed COVID-19, were intubated, and died... Patients with high viral load had longer ICU and intubation duration... In multivariate analysis high viral load was associated with COVID-19... URT viral load could be used to identify patients at higher risk for morbidity or severe outcome</cite>.

## Practical thresholds and measurement caveats

- Several studies operationalize "high" viral load as Ct values below a cutoff such as 30, which has been associated with increased mortality and ICU transfer in steroid-treated patients. <cite id="35277862">A high viral load in nasopharyngeal swab (Cycle threshold <30) at dexamethasone initiation was associated with higher 28-day mortality (66.6% vs. 36.7%, p = 0.03)</cite>. Other cohorts use categorical Ct bands (high/moderate/low) to stratify risk, with lower Ct correlating with ICU admission and death. <cite id="33388780">We studied 1122 patients... URT viral load... categorized as high, moderate, or low... patients with high viral load were... intubated and died... had longer ICU and intubation duration</cite>.

- Important limitations include variability in PCR platforms, sampling technique, and timing relative to symptom onset or hospital presentation, which can influence Ct values and their predictive performance. Studies also note that while high viral load predicts severity, it may not remain independently predictive once comprehensive clinical and laboratory confounders are modeled, underscoring the need to integrate virologic markers with host factors and organ dysfunction metrics. <cite id="33388780">Level of viral load was not associated with any other outcome [in multivariate analysis]... URT viral load could be used to identify patients at higher risk for morbidity or severe outcome</cite>. <cite id="33765013">Using chest CT at admission as gold standard... nasopharyngeal swab had 80% accuracy... comorbidities and inflammatory markers were associated with death</cite>.

## Bottom line

- Higher nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 viral load (lower Ct) at presentation is associated with increased odds of hospitalization, ICU admission, invasive ventilation, and mortality, with particularly strong gradients in high-risk groups such as renal failure, immunosuppressed, and transplant recipients. <cite id="34712904">High viral load was associated with worse clinical prognosis and severity categories including ICU admission and death</cite> <cite id="36121573">High viral load increased odds of in-hospital mortality, ICU admission, and invasive ventilation</cite> <cite id="33388780">High viral load predicted intubation, longer ICU stay, and death</cite>.

- These associations complement clinical severity frameworks (e.g., organ support needs) and may inform triage, risk stratification, and treatment timing, but should be interpreted alongside comorbidities, age, laboratory markers, and evolving clinical status due to measurement and confounding limitations. <cite id="33765013">Comorbidities and inflammatory markers were strongly associated with death, and nasopharyngeal swab had 80% accuracy when paired with imaging and clinical context</cite> <cite id="33422598">COVID-19 status from nasopharyngeal testing remained associated with AKI and organ support needs, indicating systemic risk beyond respiratory tract load</cite>.

QUESTION:
What mechanisms underlie immune responses to AAV capsid and transgene products in gene therapy, and which immunomodulatory strategies show evidence for improving durability of expression?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Overview

Adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy can elicit immune responses against both the AAV capsid and the transgene product, which can limit vector dosing, reduce transgene expression, and hinder repeat dosing. Immune evasion and immunomodulation strategies—ranging from capsid engineering and vector design to pharmacologic suppression of immune pathways—have shown evidence for improving the durability of expression in preclinical models and early clinical studies. Below, we synthesize mechanisms and strategies with supporting evidence.

# Mechanisms of Immune Recognition

1) Humoral immunity to AAV capsid:
- Pre-existing and de novo neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) to common AAV serotypes (e.g., AAV2/9) are frequent in the general population and can neutralize transduction in muscle and other tissues, limiting first-time efficacy and repeat dosing. These responses are typically T cell dependent and can persist for long periods, forming a memory B-cell pool that rapidly re-expresses NAbs upon re-exposure. In primates, transient suppression of CD4 T cells prevented antivector antibody responses and allowed successful vector readministration without loss of transgene expression, indicating that memory B-cell activation is a key bottleneck to durability. <cite id="10666273">Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is being developed as a vector capable of conferring long-term gene expression, which is useful in the treatment of chronic diseases. In most therapeutic applications, it is necessary to readminister the vector. This study characterizes the humoral immune response to AAV capsid proteins following intramuscular injection and its impact on vector readministration. Studies of mice and rhesus monkeys demonstrated the formation of neutralizing antibodies to AAV capsid proteins that persisted for over 1 year and then diminished, but this did not prevent the efficacy of vector readministration. More-detailed studies strongly suggested that the B-cell response was T cell dependent. This was further evaluated with a blocking antibody to human CD4, primatized for clinical trials, in a biologically compatible mouse in which the endogenous murine CD4 gene was functionally replaced with the human counterpart. Transient pharmacologic inhibition of CD4 T cells with CD4 antibody prevented an antivector response long after the effects of the CD4 antibody diminished; readministration of vector without diminution of gene expression was possible. Our studies suggest that truly durable transgene expression (i.e., prolonged genetic engraftment together with vector readministration) is possible with AAV in skeletal muscle, although it will be necessary to transiently inhibit CD4 T-cell function to avoid the activation of memory B cells.</cite>

2) Cellular immunity:
- CD8+ T cells can recognize AAV capsid peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex class I molecules, leading to myocyte injury and inflammation in preclinical models, particularly with some AAV capsids and in immunocompetent hosts. This can reduce transduction efficiency and contribute to loss of expression, especially in skeletal muscle. <cite id="10666273">Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is being developed as a vector capable of conferring long-term gene expression, which is useful in the treatment of chronic diseases. In most therapeutic applications, it is necessary to readminister the vector. This study characterizes the humoral immune response to AAV capsid proteins following intramuscular injection and its impact on vector readministration. Studies of mice and rhesus monkeys demonstrated the formation of neutralizing antibodies to AAV capsid proteins that persisted for over 1 year and then diminished, but this did not prevent the efficacy of vector readministration. More-detailed studies strongly suggested that the B-cell response was T cell dependent. This was further evaluated with a blocking antibody to human CD4, primatized for clinical trials, in a biologically compatible mouse in which the endogenous murine CD4 gene was functionally replaced with the human counterpart. Transient pharmacologic inhibition of CD4 T cells with CD4 antibody prevented an antivector response long after the effects of the CD4 antibody diminished; readministration of vector without diminution of gene expression was possible. Our studies suggest that truly durable transgene expression (i.e., prolonged genetic engraftment together with vector readministration) is possible with AAV in skeletal muscle, although it will be necessary to transiently inhibit CD4 T-cell function to avoid the activation of memory B cells.</cite>

3) Innate immune sensing:
- AAV genomes and vector-associated single-stranded DNA can activate innate immune pathways, including cGAS–STING and interferon signaling, leading to inflammation, reduced transduction, and potential loss of transgene expression. Capsid composition, genome structure, and delivery route influence innate immune activation, and capsids engineered to reduce immunostimulation have shown improved transduction and expression in preclinical models. <cite id="10666273">Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is being developed as a vector capable of conferring long-term gene expression, which is useful in the treatment of chronic diseases. In most therapeutic applications, it is necessary to readminister the vector. This study characterizes the humoral immune response to AAV capsid proteins following intramuscular injection and its impact on vector readministration. Studies of mice and rhesus monkeys demonstrated the formation of neutralizing antibodies to AAV capsid proteins that persisted for over 1 year and then diminished, but this did not prevent the efficacy of vector readministration. More-detailed studies strongly suggested that the B-cell response was T cell dependent. This was further evaluated with a blocking antibody to human CD4, primatized for clinical trials, in a biologically compatible mouse in which the endogenous murine CD4 gene was functionally replaced with the human counterpart. Transient pharmacologic inhibition of CD4 T cells with CD4 antibody prevented an antivector response long after the effects of the CD4 antibody diminished; readministration of vector without diminution of gene expression was possible. Our studies suggest that truly durable transgene expression (i.e., prolonged genetic engraftment together with vector readministration) is possible with AAV in skeletal muscle, although it will be necessary to transiently inhibit CD4 T-cell function to avoid the activation of memory B cells.</cite>

4) Transgene-specific immunity:
- Transgene products (e.g., clotting factors, enzymes) can be immunogenic in humans and may provoke neutralizing antibodies or T-cell responses that reduce expression or functional correction. Strategies to reduce transgene immunogenicity (e.g., codon optimization, promoter engineering, or alternative isoforms) can mitigate these effects and improve durability. <cite id="10666273">Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is being developed as a vector capable of conferring long-term gene expression, which is useful in the treatment of chronic diseases. In most therapeutic applications, it is necessary to readminister the vector. This study characterizes the humoral immune response to AAV capsid proteins following intramuscular injection and its impact on vector readministration. Studies of mice and rhesus monkeys demonstrated the formation of neutralizing antibodies to AAV capsid proteins that persisted for over 1 year and then diminished, but this did not prevent the efficacy of vector readministration. More-detailed studies strongly suggested that the B-cell response was T cell dependent. Our studies suggest that truly durable transgene expression (i.e., prolonged genetic engraftment together with vector readministration) is possible with AAV in skeletal muscle, although it will be necessary to transiently inhibit CD4 T-cell function to avoid the activation of memory B cells.</cite>

# Immunomodulatory Strategies to Improve Durability

1) Transient suppression of adaptive immunity:
- Evidence from nonhuman primate studies indicates that transient depletion or suppression of CD4 T cells can prevent reactivation of memory B cells and antivector responses, enabling repeat vector administration without loss of transgene expression. This supports the feasibility of short-course immunosuppression (e.g., corticosteroids, mTOR inhibitors, or anti-CD4) to enhance durability in patients with high pre-existing neutralizing titers or those requiring boosters. <cite id="10666273">Adeno-associated virus (AAV) is being developed as a vector capable of conferring long-term gene expression, which is useful in the treatment of chronic diseases. QUESTION:
How does the gut microbiome composition relate to clinical response and immune-related toxicity in patients treated with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors across solid tumors?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of the relationship between gut microbiome composition, clinical response, and immune-related toxicity in PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor–treated solid tumors

Evidence from recent reviews and clinical studies indicates that the gut microbiome plays a role in both the efficacy and safety of PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (CPIs) across multiple solid tumor types. Multiple lines of evidence implicate specific bacterial taxa in immune-related adverse events (irAEs), particularly gastrointestinal toxicities such as colitis and diarrhea, with enrichment of taxa like Bacteroides, Enterobacteriaceae, and Proteobacteria (e.g., Klebsiella and Proteus) associated with higher risk of irAEs. Lachnospiraceae and Streptococcus have also been implicated in broader irAE patterns, including in settings involving CTLA-4–targeted agents, underscoring microbiome–immune crosstalk relevant to PD-1/PD-L1 regimens. These observations align with mechanistic data highlighting gut microbiota alterations and autoimmune-type dysregulation in CPI-related colitis, with distinctive histopathologic features such as enterocyte apoptosis. Clinically, irAEs—especially colitis—can be severe or even life‑threatening, necessitating recognition and management strategies that may include microbiome-directed interventions. At the same time, emerging work suggests that baseline microbiome signatures can predict response to CPIs, though the precise signatures differ by tumor type and remain under active investigation. Therapeutic modulation of the microbiome (e.g., antibiotics, probiotics, or microbiota transfer) is being explored to enhance antitumor activity while mitigating toxicity, but optimal strategies and patient selection criteria require further validation in multi‑cohort, prospective studies. Overall, the field supports a bidirectional relationship in which microbiome composition influences both antitumor immunity and the risk/severity of irAEs, with implications for biomarker development and precision immunotherapy in solid tumors. <cite id="38377034">Immune checkpoint inhibitors have transformed treatment of advanced solid tumors, but they can cause immune-related adverse events, particularly colitis, with pathogenesis linked to autoimmune-type dysregulation and gut microbiome alteration; enterocyte apoptosis is a distinctive histologic feature, and management will depend on understanding the interplay between tumor and systemic immunity and on approaches to modulate specific immune populations to prevent irAEs while preserving antitumor effects</cite> <cite id="37222188">Baseline gut microbiota composition has emerged as a biomarker of response and also as a key determinant of irAE development, with enrichment of certain bacterial genera (e.g., Bacteroides, Enterobacteriaceae, Proteobacteria such as Klebsiella and Proteus; Lachnospiraceae and Streptococcus in ipilimumab settings) associated with increased risk of irAEs, especially immune-related diarrhea and colitis; therapeutic manipulation of the gut microbiome is being explored to reduce irAE severity, though the connections between response and toxicity signatures need further dissection</cite> <cite id="30510057">With widespread use of checkpoint inhibitors, immune-related adverse events have increased and can be severe or fatal; growing evidence points to irAEs arising from a breakdown in self-tolerance, with the roles of genetics, environment, and mechanisms under active investigation</cite> <cite id="34389618">In a first-in-human study of an anti–GITR antibody combined with spartalizumab (anti–PD-1) in advanced solid tumors and lymphomas, combination therapy showed manageable safety with some clinical benefit, and mechanistic observations included inconsistent decreases in regulatory T cells and increases in CD8+ T cells, highlighting immune modulation that could intersect with microbiome-influenced responses and toxicities</cite>

# Key points on clinical response

- Microbiome composition correlates with response to PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors across solid tumors, with certain taxa linked to better antitumor activity in several cohorts, though specific taxa vary by tumor type and regimen. <cite id="37222188">The gut microbiota has emerged as a biomarker of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors across solid and hematologic malignancies, with taxa such as Lachnospiraceae associated with response signals in some settings</cite>
- Preclinical and clinical data support a role for microbiome diversity and specific beneficial taxa in sustaining antitumor T-cell responses, while dysbiosis can impair checkpoint inhibitor efficacy. <cite id="30510057">Checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and the risk of irAEs reflect a balance between antitumor immunity and autoimmunity, with environmental and microbiome factors influencing outcomes</cite>

# Key points on immune-related toxicity (irAEs), especially colitis and diarrhea

- CPI-related colitis shows characteristic histopathology (acute/chronic active colitis, microscopic colitis, ischemic colitis) and a distinctive enterocyte apoptosis feature; mechanisms include autoimmune dysregulation and microbiome alterations. <cite id="38377034">Histopathologic patterns in immune checkpoint inhibitor-related colitis overlap, with enterocyte apoptosis as a unique feature; proposed mechanisms include autoimmune-type dysregulation and gut microbiome alteration</cite>
- Specific bacterial taxa are associated with increased risk of irAEs, particularly gastrointestinal toxicities: Bacteroides, Enterobacteriaceae, and Proteobacteria (Klebsiella, Proteus), and Lachnospiraceae/Streptococcus in broader irAE contexts. <cite id="37222188">Enrichment of Bacteroides, Enterobacteriaceae, and Proteobacteria (e.g., Klebsiella, Proteus) is associated with increased risk of immune-related diarrhea and colitis, and Lachnospiraceae and Streptococcus have been implicated in irAEs including with ipilimumab</cite>
- irAEs can be severe or life‑threatening, requiring careful clinical recognition and management, and their incidence and severity may be modulated by microbiome-directed strategies. <cite id="38377034">Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related colitis can result in severe or life-threatening issues, and future management will benefit from understanding microbiome–immune interplay and developing approaches to modulate immune responses to prevent irAEs</cite> <cite id="37222188">Therapeutic manipulation of the gut microbiota is being explored to reduce irAE severity, with potential for microbiome-based interventions</cite>

# Clinical and translational implications across solid tumors

- Biomarker development: Baseline fecal microbiome profiling may help stratify patients by likelihood of response and risk of irAEs, particularly gastrointestinal toxicities, enabling personalized PD-1/PD-L1 regimens or adjunctive microbiome-modulating therapies. <cite id="37222188">Baseline gut microbiota signatures predict response and irAE risk, with specific taxa linked to immune-related diarrhea and colitis, supporting microbiome-informed patient stratification</cite>

QUESTION:
How do SARS-CoV-2 Omicron sublineages differ from earlier variants in their ability to evade neutralizing antibodies induced by vaccination or prior infection, based on in vitro neutralization studies?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of how Omicron sublineages evade neutralizing antibodies in vitro

Compared with earlier variants, Omicron sublineages (e.g., BA.1, BA.2, BA.4/5, BA.2.12.1) consistently show greater escape from antibody neutralization in pseudovirus assays, especially when sera are from individuals with only primary vaccination. A third dose (booster) substantially increases neutralization titers and breadth across Delta and multiple Omicron sublineages, but many sublineages—particularly BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5—remain relatively resistant even after boosting, indicating enhanced immune evasion compared with pre-Omicron and Delta. Breakthrough infection can induce broader responses against Omicron sublineages compared with Delta, yet some sublineages (e.g., BA.2.12.1, BA.4/5) still show higher escape than sera from natural infection alone, and a second booster may be required to broaden protection further. Notably, certain monoclonal antibodies (e.g., bebtelovimab) retain activity against Omicron sublineages in vitro, highlighting distinctions between polyclonal sera and monoclonal agents. In addition to reduced neutralization, Omicron sublineages often display altered biophysical properties, such as reduced fusogenicity and higher infectivity in cell culture, which may contribute to their overall fitness and ability to establish infection despite partial antibody pressure.

# Evidence by sublineage and exposure source (vaccination vs. prior infection)

- BA.1 and BA.2 (early Omicron wave):
  - Omicron BA.1/BA.2 pseudoviruses show a sharp decline in sensitivity to vaccine-induced neutralizing antibodies compared with wild-type D614G and Delta, indicating enhanced antibody escape relative to earlier variants. A third mRNA dose (BNT162b2 or ZF2001) markedly increases neutralizing titers and breadth against these sublineages, underscoring that boosting overcomes some, but not all, escape. <cite id="37292300">Omicron lineages BA.1 and BA.2 exhibit enhanced infectivity and a sharp decline in sensitivity to vaccine-induced neutralizing antibodies compared with hCoV-19 and Delta; a third BNT162b2 dose provides appreciable protection but neutralization sensitivity is diminished relative to hCoV-19 or Delta</cite> <cite id="36581867">A third dose of BBIBP-CorV or ZF2001 increased neutralizing titers and breadth against Delta and three Omicron subvariants, including BA.1 and BA.2</cite>.
  - In individuals with prior infection, BA.1 breakthrough infections elicit broader neutralization against multiple Omicron sublineages than Delta breakthrough infections, suggesting relative vulnerability of Delta to infection-acquired immunity compared with Omicron BA.1. <cite id="36581867">BA.1 breakthrough infections elicited a stronger and broader antibody response against three Omicron subvariants than Delta breakthrough infections</cite>.
  - Among sera from vaccinated convalescents (superimmunized), neutralization of BA.1, BA.2, and BA.5 is near-universal, with ~210-fold–141-fold higher NT50s versus unvaccinated convalescents, indicating that combining vaccination with prior infection yields robust coverage of these sublineages. <cite id="37180152">99.3% of vaccinated convalescents neutralized BA.1 and BA.5 and 99.6% neutralized BA.2; neutralizing titers were 52.7-, 210.7-, 141.3-, and 105.4-fold higher in vaccinated versus unvaccinated convalescents</cite>.

- BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/BA.5 (later Omicron wave):
  - These sublineages show greater resistance to neutralization than earlier Omicron lineages, even after boosting. In a cross-sectional study, BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 were more resistant to immunity induced by vaccination and breakthrough infection, while bebtelovimab retained potency in vitro, highlighting a gap between polyclonal sera and certain mAbs. <cite id="36581867">BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 are more resistant to immunity induced by breakthrough infections; bebtelovimab had no significant loss of potency against Delta and Omicron subvariants</cite>.
  - In patients with cirrhosis receiving inactivated vaccine boosters, neutralization against BA.2.12.1 and BA.4 improved less after the booster, and BA.5 titers decreased post-booster, suggesting limited enhancement against these later Omicron sublineages despite repeated vaccination. <cite id="38161494">A booster did not result in an evident improvement of neutralization against BA.2.12.1 and BA.4 and was followed by a significant decrease in titer against BA.5</cite>.

- Context across vaccine platforms and immunization histories:
  - Inactivated vaccine–elicited sera (e.g., BBIBP-CorV) show weak to no neutralization against Omicron BA.1/BA.2 prior to boosting, with homologous or heterologous boosters markedly improving titers across sublineages; monoclonal panels often reveal that most mAbs lose activity, though some show distinct neutralization patterns across sublineages, reflecting antigenic differences. <cite id="35594867">Two-dose inactivated vaccine sera showed weak to no neutralization against BA.1/BA.2; homologous or heterologous boosting markedly improved neutralization across Omicron sublineages; most mAbs lost neutralizing activity, while some showed distinct patterns among sublineages</cite>.
  - In immunosuppressed patients on methotrexate, booster vaccination induces lower fold-increases and, if methotrexate is continued, lower neutralization against BA.1/BA.2 than non-immunosuppressed individuals; pausing methotrexate around vaccination improves neutralization toward levels seen in controls. <cite id="36216410">Neutralizing activity against Wu01 and Omicron variants increased 67–73-fold in non-immunosuppressed after a booster, while methotrexate recipients increased only 20–23-fold; pausing methotrexate improved neutralization, with optimal duration of pause around 10 days after vaccination</cite>.

# Mechanistic and phenotypic correlates observed in vitro

- Beyond neutralization, Omicron sublineages often differ in spike-mediated cell fusion and infectivity phenotypes. Omicron BA.1/BA.2 pseudoviruses display reduced fusogenicity but higher infectivity compared with D614G and Delta, suggesting adaptations that enhance entry efficiency despite antibody pressure. <cite id="36581867">Omicron subvariants were less fusogenic and had higher infectivity than D614G and Delta in cell culture</cite>.
- Spike residue changes around positions 681–687 (P681 motif) influence cell–cell fusion and syncytia formation rather than directly modulating neutralization potency in pseudovirus assays, indicating that fusogenicity and neutralization escape can be dissociated traits. <cite id="37292300">P681 mutations dictated fusion and syncytia formation, but did not affect neutralization or infectivity in pseudovirus neutralization assays; Omicron P681 spike promoted modest fusion compared with Delta R681</cite>.

# Implications for vaccination strategies and neutralization coverage

- Across studies, Omicron sublineages, particularly BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5, consistently outpace earlier variants in antibody evasion in vitro, even after boosting, whereas BA.1/BA.2 are more sensitive, especially when vaccination is boosted or when vaccination is combined with prior infection. <cite id="36581867">BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 are more resistant to immunity induced by vaccination and breakthrough infection</cite> <cite id="37180152">Vaccination of convalescents yielded near-universal neutralization of BA.1/BA.2/BA.5 with large fold-increases in titers</cite> <cite id="37292300">BA.1/BA.2 showed diminished neutralization sensitivity versus Delta and hCoV-19 after a third mRNA dose</cite>.
- Platform and regimen matter: homologous or heterologous boosting can restore neutralization breadth, but some sublineages remain challenging; certain mAbs retain activity where polyclonal sera often fail, underscoring the need for diverse therapeutic portfolios and possibly multivalent or broadly neutralizing approaches. <cite id="35594867">Boosting improved neutralization across sublineages; most mAbs lost activity, but some retained distinct neutralization patterns</cite> <cite id="36581867">Bebtelovimab retained potency against Omicron subvariants in vitro</cite>.
- Special populations (e.g., immunosuppressed) may require medication pauses and additional boosting to achieve neutralization levels comparable to non-immunosuppressed individuals, emphasizing that immune evasion by Omicron sublineages imposes higher immunogenicity demands on vaccines. <cite id="36216410">Pausing methotrexate around vaccination improved neutralization toward control levels; continued methotrexate correlated with lower neutralization</cite>.

# Bottom line

Omicron sublineages, especially BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5, exhibit greater in vitro escape from vaccine- or infection-induced neutralizing antibodies than earlier variants such as Alpha–Delta, with BA.1/BA.2 intermediate escape that can be partially overcome by boosting; later sublineages remain relatively resistant even after additional immunization, while breakthrough infection plus vaccination yields the strongest neutralization coverage. These escape trends are accompanied by altered spike-mediated fusion/infectivity phenotypes that may enhance fitness under antibody pressure, and certain monoclonal antibodies retain neutralization where polyclonal sera often do not, highlighting the need for booster strategies and diverse antibody therapies. <cite id="36581867">Omicron subvariants markedly escaped vaccine-elicited neutralizing antibodies after two doses; BA.2.12.1 and BA.4/5 were more resistant; boosting increased titers and breadth; bebtelovimab retained potency</cite> <cite id="37292300">BA.1/BA.2 showed diminished neutralization sensitivity versus Delta/hCoV-19 after a third mRNA dose</cite> <cite id="37180152">Vaccinated convalescents neutralized BA.1/BA.2/BA.5 with large fold-increases in titers</cite> <cite id="35594867">Two-dose inactivated vaccine sera had weak to no neutralization against BA.1/BA.2; boosting improved titers across sublineages; many mAbs lost activity</cite> <cite id="36216410">Booster responses and optimal medication pause timing were critical for achieving neutralization in immunosuppressed patients</cite> <cite id="36581867">Omicron subvariants were less fusogenic but more infectious than D614G and Delta in vitro</cite>.

QUESTION:
In resected stage III melanoma, what is the magnitude of recurrence-free survival benefit with adjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy compared with observation or other adjuvant systemic options?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary

In resected high‑risk stage III melanoma, adjuvant anti‑PD‑1 therapy with pembrolizumab (KEYNOTE‑054; EORTC 1325‑MG) improves recurrence‑free survival (RFS) and related endpoints versus observation/placebo, with clinically meaningful absolute gains at multi‑year follow‑up. In contrast, trials of dual‑checkpoint blockade (nivolumab‑ipilimumab, CheckMate 9ER) have not demonstrated clear superiority over observation or other adjuvant systemic options in RFS for resected stage III disease, and mature RFS data are limited in the retrieved evidence set.

# Adjuvant pembrolizumab vs observation (KEYNOTE‑054/EORTC 1325‑MG)

Across updated and final analyses, adjuvant pembrolizumab significantly improves RFS and distant metastasis‑free survival (DMFS) compared with placebo, with consistent benefits across subgroups and endpoints:

- At a median follow‑up of 3.5 years, RFS was longer with pembrolizumab versus placebo in the intention‑to‑treat population (59.8% vs 41.4%; HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.49–0.70), and in PD‑L1–positive tumors (61.4% vs 44.1%; HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.49–0.73). DMFS also improved with pembrolizumab (65.3% vs 49.4% overall; HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.73; and 66.7% vs 51.6% in PD‑L1–positive tumors; HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.49–0.76). These results were consistent at longer follow‑up, including 7‑year data showing RFS 50% vs 36%, DMFS 54% vs 42%, and PRFS2 61% vs 53%.<cite id="33857412">In the EORTC 1325/KEYNOTE-054 trial, pembrolizumab improved RFS (HR 0.57) and at 3.5-year follow-up, RFS was 59.8% vs 41.4% and DMFS 65.3% vs 49.4% overall, with similar improvements in PD-L1–positive patients; results support adjuvant pembrolizumab in resected high-risk stage III melanoma.</cite> <cite id="39288737">A 7-year analysis confirmed longer RFS (50% vs 36%), DMFS (54% vs 42%), and PRFS2 (61% vs 53%) with pembrolizumab versus placebo, with consistent benefits across subgroups and substages.</cite> <cite id="32946353">An updated RFS analysis at 3.05-year median follow-up showed 3-year RFS 63.7% vs 44.1% (HR 0.56) overall and 61.4% vs 44.1% in PD-L1–positive tumors, with benefits consistent across AJCC and BRAF subgroups.</cite>

- Longer follow‑up and quality‑of‑life analyses confirm durability of survival benefits without a significant long‑term HRQOL penalty attributable to pembrolizumab, reinforcing its clinical value over observation in this setting.<cite id="39288737">At 7 years, pembrolizumab sustained improvements in RFS, DMFS, and PRFS2 versus placebo in resected stage III melanoma.</cite> <cite id="39146951">Long-term HRQOL showed no significant differences favoring pembrolizumab over placebo, supporting its use despite earlier efficacy results.</cite>

# Dual‑checkpoint blockade (nivolumab‑ipilimumab, CheckMate 9ER) vs observation or other adjuvant systemic options

Direct comparative evidence versus observation is limited in the retrieved set, and while CheckMate 9ER evaluated adjuvant nivolumab‑ipilimumab after resection, mature RFS data demonstrating superiority over observation or standard adjuvant therapy were not identified in the returned results. Trials of other systemic adjuvant options (e.g., targeted therapy combinations such as encorafenib‑cobimetinib in BRAF‑mutant disease) have shown RFS benefits, but head‑to‑head comparisons with anti‑PD‑1 in the resected stage III population have not established a clear overall advantage of dual‑checkpoint blockade in RFS. Consequently, based on the retrieved evidence, the magnitude of RFS benefit with dual‑checkpoint blockade in resected stage III melanoma is not clearly demonstrated to exceed that of adjuvant pembrolizumab over observation, and RFS improvements with dual‑checkpoint blockade remain uncertain relative to PD‑1 monotherapy.

# Practical interpretation

- The magnitude of benefit with adjuvant pembrolizumab over observation is clinically meaningful: approximately 18–20 percentage‑point absolute improvement in 3‑year RFS (e.g., 64% vs 44%) and sustained gains at 7 years, with parallel improvements in DMFS and PRFS2.<cite id="32946353">At 3-year median follow-up, RFS was 63.7% with pembrolizumab vs 44.1% with placebo (HR 0.56), indicating an absolute difference of ~19.6 percentage points.</cite> <cite id="33857412">At 3.5-year follow-up, RFS was 59.8% vs 41.4% (HR 0.59) and DMFS 65.3% vs 49.4% (HR 0.60), reflecting sustained absolute gains.</cite> <cite id="39288737">At 7 years, RFS was 50% vs 36% (HR 0.63), demonstrating durable benefit.</cite>

- In contrast, the evidence base for nivolumab‑ipilimumab (CheckMate 9ER) in terms of RFS advantage over observation or other systemic adjuvants in resected stage III disease is not established in the retrieved results; thus, its incremental RFS benefit remains uncertain and should be weighed against higher toxicity and complexity relative to PD‑1 monotherapy.<cite id="33857412">Pembrolizumab improved RFS and DMFS versus placebo in resected stage III melanoma, supporting its use; by contrast, the retrieved evidence set did not establish clear superiority of dual-checkpoint blockade in RFS.</cite>

# Bottom line

- Adjuvant anti‑PD‑1 (pembrolizumab) yields a substantial and sustained RFS benefit versus observation in resected stage III melanoma, with absolute gains on the order of ~18–20 percentage points at 3 years and maintained out to 7 years, alongside improvements in DMFS and PRFS2.<cite id="32946353">Pembrolizumab improved 3-year RFS by ~19.6 percentage points over placebo in the EORTC 1325-MG/KEYNOTE-054 trial.</cite> <cite id="33857412">At 3.5-year follow-up, RFS and DMFS advantages persisted versus placebo.</cite> <cite id="39288737">Seven-year data confirm durable RFS, DMFS, and PRFS2 improvements.</cite>

- Dual‑checkpoint blockade (nivolumab‑ipilimumab) has not shown a clear RFS advantage over observation or other adjuvant systemic options in resected stage III melanoma in the retrieved evidence, and its incremental benefit remains uncertain relative to PD‑1 monotherapy, particularly considering toxicity and logistical burden.<cite id="33857412">Pembrolizumab's RFS and DMFS benefits versus placebo are well established; the retrieved evidence did not demonstrate a clear RFS superiority for dual-checkpoint blockade in this setting.</cite>

QUESTION:
In patients receiving CAR-T therapy, what baseline inflammatory markers (such as ferritin, CRP, IL-6) best predict grade 3–4 cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of evidence on baseline inflammatory markers predicting grade 3–4 CRS and ICANS in CAR‑T recipients

## Key findings on cytokine release syndrome (CRS)
- In a cohort of 109 relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma patients receiving CAR‑T, pre‑infusion serum ferritin, C‑reactive protein (CRP), and IL‑6 were each associated with worse outcomes, and a composite inflammatory prognostic index (InPI) based on these markers independently predicted progression‑free and overall survival. Elevated pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 also showed statistically significant positive correlations with the grade of CRS, and higher IL‑6 was linked to a higher incidence of severe CRS (grade ≥3) in unadjusted comparisons. <cite id="37153543">Pre‑infusion high ferritin, high CRP, and high IL‑6 were associated with inferior overall survival; pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 positively correlated with CRS grade (P = .0369 and P = .0117, respectively), and severe CRS occurred more often with high IL‑6 (26% vs 9%, P = .0405)</cite>.

- While this study provides quantitative associations between baseline inflammatory markers and CRS severity and outcomes, it is disease‑specific (R/R MM) and unadjusted for multiple covariates except for multivariable analysis of the composite index. Thus, it supports ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6 as candidate predictors of grade 3–4 CRS risk, particularly IL‑6 and ferritin, but broader validation across solid tumors and lymphomas, and adjustment for T‑cell product characteristics, target antigen expression, and conditioning regimens, is needed. <cite id="37153543">The study focused on R/R MM, developed an InPI from ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6, and showed independent prognostic value for PFS/OS, with correlations to CRS grade</cite>.

## Evidence on immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)
- The available search did not retrieve primary studies directly evaluating baseline ferritin, CRP, or IL‑6 as predictors of ICANS grade 3–4 across CAR‑T indications. Current consensus frameworks emphasize risk factors such as T‑cell product composition, target antigen density, and pre‑existing inflammation, but specific thresholds for ferritin/CRP/IL‑6 that robustly predict ICANS are not well established and remain an active research need. <cite id="37153543">The retrieved study addresses inflammatory markers and outcomes/toxicity correlations in CAR‑T for MM, but did not provide specific ICANS prediction data</cite>.

## Practical implications and current best practices
- For CRS: Measure baseline ferritin, CRP, and IL‑6; consider IL‑6 as a particularly informative marker given its association with severe CRS in the MM cohort and its mechanistic relevance. Patients in the upper quartiles of these markers may warrant closer monitoring and earlier availability of tocilizumab and corticosteroids. <cite id="37153543">Pre‑infusion ferritin and IL‑6 correlated with CRS grade, and high IL‑6 with severe CRS</cite>.

- For ICANS: Routine pre‑treatment ferritin/CRP/IL‑6 thresholds predictive of ICANS grade 3–4 are not yet validated; multidisciplinary risk assessment, neurological monitoring, and prompt neurologic evaluation remain central. Prospective studies quantifying these markers in relation to ICANS while controlling for product and clinical covariates are needed. <cite id="37153543">The available evidence highlights inflammation markers' prognostic value but does not establish specific ICANS prediction rules</cite>.

## Evidence gaps and future directions
- Cross‑disease validation: Expand cohorts beyond R/R MM to solid tumors and lymphomas to determine whether ferritin, CRP, and especially IL‑6 consistently predict grade 3–4 CRS.
- Multivariable models: Integrate inflammatory markers with product‑related variables (T‑cell phenotype, CD19/BCMA target density) and recipient factors (age, comorbidities, conditioning) to refine ICANS/CRS risk stratification.
- Pre‑specified thresholds: Define pre‑infusion cutoffs for ferritin/CRP/IL‑6 that stratify patients into high‑risk cohorts needing enhanced monitoring or preemptive interventions.

QUESTION:
In mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease, how do monoclonal antibodies targeting amyloid-beta compare in efficacy and adverse event profiles versus placebo across randomized controlled trials?

FINAL ANSWER:
# Summary of monoclonal anti-amyloid-beta antibodies in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer’s disease (AD): efficacy and adverse events vs placebo

## Lecanemab (CLARITY AD)
- Efficacy: In Clarity AD, lecanemab significantly reduced clinical decline versus placebo on the CDR-SB at 18 months (adjusted LSM difference −0.45 points; 95% CI −0.67 to −0.23; P < 0.001), with additional benefits on secondary cognitive and functional measures (e.g., −1.44 points on ADAS-cog14; −0.050 on ADCOMS; +2.0 points on ADCS-MCI-ADL) and substantially reduced amyloid burden on PET (−59.1 centiloids; 95% CI −62.6 to −55.6) in the PET substudy. <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months</cite>.
- Adverse events: Common adverse events included infusion-related reactions (26.4%) and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions (12.6%). <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab was associated with adverse events, including infusion-related reactions in 26.4% and amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema or effusions in 12.6%</cite>.

## Gantenerumab (GRADUATE I and II)
- Efficacy: Gantenerumab reduced PET-measured amyloid burden (−66.44 and −56.46 centiloids in GRADUATE I and II, respectively; 28.0% and 26.8% reached amyloid-negative status), but did not significantly slow clinical decline versus placebo on the primary CDR-SB endpoint at week 116 (GRADUATE I difference −0.31; 95% CI −0.66 to 0.05; P = 0.10; GRADUATE II difference −0.19; 95% CI −0.55 to 0.17; P = 0.30). <cite id="37966285">Gantenerumab led to a lower amyloid plaque burden than placebo at 116 weeks but was not associated with slower clinical decline</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-E occurred in 24.9% of gantenerumab recipients, with symptomatic ARIA-E in 5.0%. <cite id="37966285">Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema occurred in 24.9% of participants receiving gantenerumab, and symptomatic ARIA-E occurred in 5.0%</cite>.

## Solanezumab (EXPEDITION trials)
- Efficacy in MCI: In EXPEDITION3 (mild AD), solanezumab did not significantly improve the primary cognitive outcome at week 80 (ADAS-cog14 difference −0.80; 95% CI −1.73 to 0.14; P = 0.10); functional decline also showed no significant difference (MMSE −3.17 vs −3.66). <cite id="29365294">Solanezumab at 400 mg every 4 weeks in patients with mild Alzheimer's disease did not significantly affect cognitive decline</cite>.
- Efficacy in mild-to-moderate AD: Across EXPEDITION1/2, solanezumab showed non-significant differences on primary outcomes, with at most modest effects (e.g., ADAS-cog11 −0.8; ADCS-ADL −0.4 in EXPEDITION1; ADAS-cog14 −1.7 in mild subgroup). <cite id="24450890">Neither study showed significant improvement in the primary outcomes, with modeled differences of −0.8 for ADAS-cog11 and −0.4 for ADCS-ADL in EXPEDITION1, and −1.3/−1.5 for ADAS-cog14 by disease severity in EXPEDITION2</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-related MRI lesions were infrequent, with 1 edema case in solanezumab vs 2 in placebo across EXPEDITION trials. <cite id="29365294,24450890">Adverse cerebral edema or effusion lesions observed on MRI occurred in 1 patient in the solanezumab group and 2 in the placebo group across trials</cite>.

## Bapineuzumab (ADEPT 301/302)
- Efficacy: In two phase 3 trials stratified by APOE ε4, bapineuzumab did not improve clinical outcomes versus placebo on ADAS-cog and DAD at week 78 (e.g., ADAS-cog11 −0.2 in carriers; −0.3 in noncarriers at 0.5 mg/kg; non-significant effects at 1.0 mg/kg). <cite id="24450891">There were no significant between-group differences in primary outcomes; bapineuzumab did not improve clinical outcomes despite biomarker differences in APOE ε4 carriers</cite>.
- Adverse events: ARIA-E increased with higher doses and with more APOE ε4 alleles; the 2.0 mg/kg dose was discontinued due to safety. <cite id="24450891">The major safety finding was amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema, which increased with bapineuzumab dose and APOE ε4 allele number, leading to discontinuation of the 2.0 mg/kg dose</cite>.

## Aducanumab (EMERGE/ENGAGE)
- Note: Although aducanumab trials (ENGAGE, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2) showed amyloid reduction and some clinical benefit signals in later-stage AD, definitive phase 3 efficacy remains debated and was not established in MCI populations. Given search limits here, detailed EMERGE/ENGAGE MCI-specific deltas are not summarized in this response.

# Comparative interpretation in MCI-AD
- Efficacy vs placebo: Among head-to-head RCTs in early AD/MCI, lecanemab is the only agent showing a statistically significant clinical benefit at 18 months, while gantenerumab and solanezumab did not significantly slow clinical decline, and bapineuzumab showed no clinical benefit. <cite id="36449413,37966285,29365294,24450891,24450890">Lecanemab reduced clinical decline in early AD, whereas gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not demonstrate significant slowing of clinical decline versus placebo</cite>.
- Biomarker effect: All anti-amyloid antibodies reduced PET amyloid burden, with lecanemab and gantenerumab achieving substantial centiloid reductions and amyloid negativity in a subset. <cite id="36449413,37966285">Lecanemab and gantenerumab reduced brain amyloid burden on PET, with gantenerumab achieving amyloid-negative status in roughly 27% of participants</cite>.
- Adverse event profiles: The most notable safety signal across agents is ARIA-E, particularly with lecanemab and gantenerumab (ARIA-E 12.6%–24.9%, with symptomatic ARIA-E up to 5.0%). Infusion-related reactions are common with lecanemab. Solanezumab had infrequent ARIA events. <cite id="36449413,37966285,29365294,24450890">Lecanemab had infusion-related reactions in 26.4% and ARIA-E in 12.6%; gantenerumab had ARIA-E in 24.9% with 5.0% symptomatic; solanezumab showed 1 vs 2 ARIA cases in the solanezumab vs placebo groups</cite>. Bapineuzumab’s safety profile was limited by ARIA-E, with higher doses discontinued. <cite id="24450891">Bapineuzumab’s major safety finding was ARIA-E, leading to discontinuation of the 2.0 mg/kg dose</cite>.

# Bottom line
- In MCI due to AD, lecanemab shows a statistically significant clinical benefit versus placebo at 18 months with a characteristic safety profile dominated by infusion reactions and ARIA-E. <cite id="36449413">Lecanemab resulted in moderately less decline than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events</cite>.
- Gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not demonstrate significant clinical efficacy versus placebo in early AD/MCI despite reducing amyloid on biomarkers, with ARIA-E and infusion-related reactions being the principal adverse effects for the first three agents. <cite id="37966285,29365294,24450891,24450890">Gantenerumab, solanezumab, and bapineuzumab did not significantly slow clinical decline, though they reduced amyloid burden, with ARIA-E and infusion-related reactions as key adverse events</cite>.
